- A rival agent tips its hat, 'Thanks!'.
- The Sleeping Dragon snores on a Zzz cushion, but only after it is revealed. No card ever animates or hovers differently before its flip, so nothing leaks.

PRINTABLE SPY KIT (PDF): spy-chief badges; paper spy glasses for kids; phrase cards per level; laminated key cards; cell whiteboard templates with 1-16 and A1-E5 grids; a 'Poker face!' rule card.

RITUALS
- Gogo demos the game in 25 s.
- A 'Spy walk... freeze!' stirrer between boards.

ACCESSIBILITY
- Colour-blind safe: team cards carry stripes vs dots plus the emblem, and the trap has its own shape.
- Reduced motion swaps every effect for a static stamp.

ENDING
- 'Reveal all' sweeps the key across the board at the end.
- Then a 'TOP SECRET' manila Dossier: what each spymaster meant vs what the team picked, and the Best link of the game ('heavy · 3 → rain, traffic, bag'). Misread words appear with picture, definition and TR gloss and export as flashcards.
- The kids' class album collects a spy badge per mission. Arena emblems and mottos return at the next Match.
catalog.risks:
KEY LEAKAGE on a mirrored projector or smartboard
- The key is never rendered on the projector and is held only in memory.
- The key code is entered masked.
- No per-card DOM attributes, animations or hover states before a flip.

ONE-WORD ASSOCIATION IS TOO HARD BELOW B1
- The clue ladder (describe, then category, then one word), HQ/Gogo mode and the Clue helper.

SLOW SPYMASTERS
- The clue timer, one +10 s, then an automatic HQ clue.

LARGE CLASSES AND DOMINANT STUDENTS
- Cells with mini-whiteboards and rotating Captain, Scribe and Checker roles.
- 3-team and co-op modes; the seat spinner, never names.

TURKISH DISCUSSION
- The phrase strip, the Checker role and a teacher-tapped English bonus.
- Some L1 talk is accepted at A1.

UNKNOWN BOARD WORDS OR AMBIGUOUS PICTURES
- The words.js band check, Swap card before the first clue, labels on flip and the card-help ladder.

ILLEGAL CLUES (Turkish, gestures, spelling or position clues)
- The validator plus a teacher ruling, with a gentle redo in Nazik.

UNFAIR KEYS
- The balancer and alternating starters.

PHONES BANNED FOR STUDENTS in many schools
- The spy-desk teacher phone, printed key cards, or HQ mode.

NO REALTIME INFRA in C:/lg today
- The MVP uses a deterministic seed plus a masked key code.
- Later: Supabase Realtime broadcast for live flips on the spy phone, clue entry from the phone, and intended-target marking.

PACING
- A 5x5 board can take 15 min, so the Arena and A-level defaults use 5x4 or 4x4.

TRADEMARK
- Never show the 'Codenames' name, logo or card art to students. Use 'Gizli Ajan Kelimeler / Spy Words'.

issues: The pacing numbers don't hold up. In Oyun Parkı every clue has number 1, so the board needs about 11 turns to finish (6+5 agents, plus second tries). Each turn is Gogo's clue (~10 s), the 3 s lock, a stand-up vote that spotlights several cards (30-45 s), the call, the flip and the sticker, so about 60-75 s. That makes a 4x4 board 10-14 min, not 5-7, and 3 boards is 35+ min. Arena 5x4 has 13 agents, a 45 s clue, a 45 s first pick and 15 s later picks, so a board takes 12-18 min and best-of-3 does not fit in a 40-min Turkish lesson.

Dead time while the spymaster thinks. For 45-60 s one child thinks and 26 wait, and nobody waiting has a task because the Shadow read only starts after the clue. With 28 kids this is where the noise starts, and it happens every turn.

The kids' stand-up vote leaks and invites sabotage. Both teams stand for their pick in front of each other, so the active team can copy the crowd, and the waiting team can stand for wrong cards on purpose. Spotlighting candidates one at a time also means the teacher decides which cards count as candidates, which gives the answer away.

In Oyun Parkı A1 the Codenames mechanic is mostly gone. Gogo describes exactly one card with number 1, so the team key, the rival agents and the dragon only matter when someone misunderstands. It is really a listen-and-point riddle game with a spy skin. That is fine pedagogically, but it overlaps the riddle and 'Bil bakalım' games in the suite, and the long key and balancer machinery does nothing here.

The second miss auto-flips the card, and it is unclear whose agent it becomes. If it counts for the active team, there is no cost to guessing and the key barely matters. If it doesn't, the team was punished and the 'effort star' is the only consolation.

Setup is well over 2-3 min in real conditions. The steps: open languago.site/ajan on the phone, type the table code, then type a 5-character key code into a masked field. On a smart board that means the on-screen keyboard, where the pressed keys highlight in full view of the class, so the masked field still leaks. Then spin the seat numbers, hand out badges, whiteboards and markers, and move desks. The first session takes 8-12 min.

Seating and supplies. Turkish public classrooms have fixed rows of paired desks, so making 'cells of 4-5 around a mini-whiteboard' means moving furniture (noise, 3-5 min). Many schools also don't have 6-7 whiteboards with working markers.

Front-row children sit about 1 m from the teacher's desk, where the spy-desk phone stands. Two spymasters leaning over one phone draws a crowd, and a front-row child can glimpse the key. A printed key card held by a child leaks the same way.

The teacher has too much to do at the board. They type every clue on the smart board (slow, and the on-screen keyboard covers the grid), rule on the validator, tap Kabul or Kural dışı, do the two-step flips, check 6-7 Shadow-read whiteboards and tap Intel matches, tap the English bonus, and run +10 s and the timers. In a class of 28 they cannot do all of this and manage behaviour too.

The seat spinner can put a weak or anxious 12-year-old alone at the spy desk for a whole B1 board, where a single-word clue is required. The stall happens publicly, the whole team loses that board, and the automatic HQ clue after 10 s marks the child as having failed. Only Oyun Parkı pairs the spymasters.

Dominance inside the cells. The Captain 'goes with the majority', but in practice the 2 strongest students in each cell of 5 decide, and the Checker role doesn't police English in a 14-child team. Actual speaking per student is low. In the 3-team mode each team waits through two other turns, which is even more idle time.

Stopping at any moment is not defined. When the bell rings mid-board, the race has no winner. Kids' boards end 'Mission complete' for both teams, but Arena best-of-3 and the Stüdyo campaign have no rule for scoring an unfinished board.

The build is too big for the value. There are 5 key-delivery routes, 3 skins, gadgets at 3 harshness levels, bid rounds, constraint cards, idiom boards, intercepts, a campaign, a 3-team key and a co-op mode. That is L+ scope, and teachers will not find or remember most of the dials.

The adult evening class (10 people) is the strong case. Codenames is proven with adults, own phones are fine, 5x5 in 12-15 min is realistic, and the reason rule and debrief give real speaking. The main risk there is A1-A2 adults, where HQ 'describe one' turns it back into a listening quiz.
fixes: Re-derive the board sizes from turn counts and set session defaults to fit. Oyun Parkı: a 3x3 or 4x3 board with 3 agents each and first team to 3 wins, or a whole-class co-op board of 5 agents. Arena: 4x4 with 5/4 agents, one board of ~10 min, and best-of-3 only when the lesson-fit dial gives 40+ min. The lesson-fit dial should always show a realistic minutes estimate.

Kill the idle time. Both spymasters think at the same time: the next team's clue is prepared during the current team's guessing (the real Codenames etiquette). While a clue is being prepared, the waiting class does a 20 s micro-task on screen, such as 'Pick any 2 cards that go together, write why'. The Shadow read is locked before the clue appears.

Make the kids' vote secret and simultaneous. Use a heads-down, eyes-closed hand vote, or a number-card flash on '3-2-1 show!'. Spotlight the cards in fixed order 1-16 (or show all numbers at once) so the teacher's choice of candidates cannot hint. The active team votes first; the other team's vote is shown only after the flip, as a prediction.

Be honest about kids A1 and simplify. Either reuse the shared riddle/listen-and-point engine behind a spy skin (no balancer, no key routes), or give children one real Codenames decision: Gogo gives a category + 2 ('Animals, 2') over a picture board. Count a second miss as the rival's point, not a free flip, so the key still matters.

Cut key delivery to 3 routes for the MVP: (1) the teacher's phone with a QR code on the projector that encodes only the table seed, with the key derived on the phone and a 1-digit 'key variant' tapped on the board (no 5-character typing); (2) printed key cards; (3) HQ with no key. Add 'hold-to-peek' on the phone so the key is dark unless a thumb is on the screen, and a privacy-dim reminder.

No furniture moves. Default cells = 'desk pair + the pair behind turns around' (4 students). Default response = an A4 sheet folded with the codes written large, or a printable 1-16 / A-E + 1-5 answer fan. Whiteboards stay optional.

One-tap teacher flow as the default. Clue typing is OFF; the teacher taps the number pips only (validator off in speech mode, with a single 'Kural dışı' button). Shadow reads are self-checked (the teams tick themselves on the reveal) rather than teacher-scored. Also give the teacher a phone remote once Realtime exists (flip, undo, timer), so they can stand among the students.

Pair the spymasters in every mode (a 'spy desk duo'), and add a no-stigma 'Ask HQ' button that the duo can press at any time with no point cost in Nazik mode. Let the teacher veto the spinner result silently with 'Tekrar çevir' (spin again).

Fairness in the cells. Rotate the Captain by seat number on screen each clue, give the Captain a 'the quietest member picks first' rule, and in Arena let each cell's board count as one vote on screen (the teacher taps cell picks), so the majority is visible and no single loud student decides.

Define 'Bitir şimdi' (end now) for every mode. Score = agents found, with the team that has fewer remaining agents winning (the tie goes to both). The Dossier debrief still runs in a 2-min short form.
For the 3-team mode, cap it at B1+ with a turn timer, and suggest co-op for large classes instead, because 2 turns of waiting is too long for teens.

Trim the MVP to the classic rules, 2 teams, co-op, Nazik/Standard traps, the debrief and flashcard export. Ship gadgets, bid rounds, constraint cards, idiom boards, intercept and the campaign as a later 'Stüdyo extras' pack, since these mostly serve B2 adults.

Adults A1-A2: have HQ give category + number clues from the cluster labels (not 'describe one') so there is still a linking decision, and let a student act as spymaster with the on-phone Clue helper from A2.

issues: What makes Codenames work is lateral association with one-word clues, and that only happens at B1+. Below B1 the clue ladder turns the game into something else. 'Describe one, number always 1' plus Gogo reading a riddle is a listen-and-pick-the-picture quiz, and the secret key, the phones, the key code and the balancer add setup cost with no learning gain. For A1 kids and A1 adults, the Codenames label oversells what is really a picture riddle game.

The Oyun Parkı 'THREE RULES' card is honest for students but hides about 8 teacher-side branches: clue 2 after a townsperson, the second-miss name-and-repeat, rival agent, dragon snore removing a rival agent, stand-up vote, effort stars, mission stars, co-op torches. For 9-11 year olds the 20 s explanation holds, but the teacher has to run a large state machine live. The mini-game risks feeling fiddly next to Baamboozle.

The kids' Stand-up vote undermines the team race and cues the answer. Both teams stand for the active team's clue, so the active team can just follow the whole-class majority. The teacher spotlights 'candidate cards' one by one, and that choice itself is a hint. With 16 cards the spotlight walk is slow, about 30-60 s per turn.

The kids' default key delivery is over-engineered. With Gogo or the teacher as spymaster (A1 Genç), the app already knows the key, so no phone, table code or masked key code is needed. At A2 Genç, standing a spy-chief pair of 10-year-olds behind the teacher's phone on a stand is practical only in small classes, and every other child sees the phone screen's glow and angle (leak and crowding).

Language production is thin for most students. Cells write a CARD CODE (A3, 7) on whiteboards, not language. The Shadow read is also a code. Per turn, only 1-2 students (spymaster and captain) produce English, and the captain's line is a fixed formula at A1-A2. For a 30-student class this is mostly receptive vocabulary recognition.

The A2 kids' frame cards ('It's ___. It lives in ___. You can ___ it.') only fit animals and objects. For free-prompt topics like jobs, feelings, daily routines or places, the frames produce nonsense, and 10-year-olds will fall back to Turkish or gestures.

The 'unpicturable items are dropped' rule for A1/A2 Genç collides with free-text LLM prompts. A teacher prompt like 'daily routines' or 'feelings, adjectives' leaves too few emoji-safe, non-ambiguous items to fill 3-5 clusters × 4-6 members plus a 1.4x swap pool (23 for 4x4). The spec gives no fallback, and emoji ambiguity (🏠 house/home, 🍳 cook/egg/pan) creates arguments about 'wrong' picks at A1.

Bridge words (bank, spring, match, light) are the B1+ selling point, but neither source is reliable. words.js stores essentially one sense per headword, so code cannot verify that the second sense exists at the group's level. DeepSeek will invent weak bridges ('tree' in nature/family). Arena teens at B1 (12-14) often do not know the second sense (spring = water source, match = football game in TR-English usage), which turns 'aha' into confusion.

The clue validator is mostly theatre in spoken play. The teacher has to type every spoken clue into the teacher bar in real time to get stem, family and Turkish checks. In practice they will tap only the number pips, so illegal-clue rulings fall back to teacher judgment. B2 constraint rounds (collocations only, no nouns) are also unenforceable without typed clues.

Arena has two competing win conditions: the race (first to find all agents) and points (10 per agent, x1.5 or x2 combo, Intel, backup-hint costs). A team can win the board but lose the points, which confuses 12-14 year olds and weakens the tension of a best-of-3.

The adult A1 board (words with emoji, HQ describing one card) risks feeling like a children's quiz. The index-card styling helps, but emoji on adult cards plus 'The banana, please!' framing reads babyish to Turkish adult A1 learners, who are often professionals.

B2 Genç is described as 'richer but concrete, no abstract debate'. That is sensible for teenSafe, but it caps the game exactly where polysemy and collocation would teach the most. B2 Genç risks playing like B1 Genç with harder nouns.

Setup time is optimistic: 5 key routes, swaps, emblem and motto choices, seat spinner and role badges. '2-3 min' is realistic only after the class profile exists. The first run in a 40-min lesson will eat 8-10 min.

Multi-number clues at A2 adults ('Animals, 2') mostly reduce to category membership, and the Clue helper on the spy phone hands spymasters the category label directly. The spymaster's productive task shrinks to reading a label aloud.
fixes: Split the design honestly by level. For A1 Genç, A2 Genç and A1 adults, ship 'Spy Words: Listening Mission': the app is HQ, it holds the key internally, there is no phone, key code or balancer, and it runs co-op by default ('Whole class mission'). Real key and spymaster play unlock at A2 adults (describe or category clues) and B1+ (one word + number). Hide the key-delivery chooser entirely when the clue source is HQ.

Replace the kids' Stand-up vote. The ACTIVE team's cells hold up picture numbers (1-16) on whiteboards, the Captain calls the majority, and the WAITING team simultaneously holds up its own guess as a Shadow read that can earn a star. No teacher spotlighting. Gogo then says the picked word and the whole class echoes it: that is the whole-class moment, with no cueing.

Collapse the kids' teacher-side branches to three outcomes on screen: Agent (stamp), Not an agent (Gogo gives clue 2 once, then names the card, class repeats, turn passes), Dragon (turn passes, no bonus to the rival). Drop the snore-removes-rival-agent rule and effort stars from the default, and keep them as options.

Make the whiteboards produce language: from A2 upward, cells write the WORD, not the code. That gives spelling practice, and the teacher can say 'show me' and read the spelling. At B1+ they write word + 3-word reason ('money → bank'). The Shadow read becomes 'write the word you think + one link word'.

Give frame cards per cluster TYPE (animal/object: It's / It lives / You can; person/job: He/She works in / He/She uses; place: You go there to / It has; food: It tastes / You eat it for). The LLM schema returns a 'frameType' per cluster, and HQ uses the same frames so kids hear a model before producing.

Add a picturability fallback. If fewer than 23 pictured items survive for a Genç board, auto-drop to a 3x4 or 3x3 board, or switch the face to 'word + small emoji' at A2 Genç with a teacher warning. Add an emoji-ambiguity blacklist and dedupe by emoji, and always show the label on flip. Suggest topics that are picture-rich when the prompt looks abstract ('feelings' becomes face emojis only).

Build bridges only from a curated built-in list (about 150 hand-checked polysemes tagged with the CEFR level of EACH sense). Accept LLM bridges only if both members appear in the curated list or the teacher confirms them. At B1 Genç, turn bridges off by default and use only same-cluster cards.

Make the validator practical. Offer a spymaster clue-entry keypad on the spy phone for student spymasters at B1+, so the clue is typed once there and appears on the projector teleprinter. Otherwise label the validator 'teacher judgment' in spoken mode, and hide B2 constraint rounds unless typed clues are on.
In Arena, use one scoring system: the race decides the board, and points only feed series tiebreaks and stat awards. Or drop the race and play fixed turns for points. Show one bar, not both.

For adult A1/A2, default the card face to word-only with an optional thumbnail icon, and use call frames that sound adult ('Card C3: umbrella.' / 'We're going with umbrella.'). Keep emoji-heavy faces off in Stüdyo unless the teacher turns them on.
For B2 Genç, allow curated concrete polysemes (bat, bark, ring, trunk, match) and collocation clues with a picture-free board, so B2 teens get the 'aha' layer without abstract adult content.
Add a 'Hızlı başlat' preset per profile. The first launch skips emblems, mottos, roles and badges, then offers them after board 1. Show realistic lesson-fit numbers (first run +5 min).

Guarantee meaningful production for the spymaster at A2 adults: the Clue helper shows the category label only after a 20 s attempt, or shows two cards to be linked instead of the label. Add a 'Say it in a sentence' bonus ('They're all animals that live in the sea').

issues: The scope is XL, not L. Five key routes, three skins, co-op, 3-team boards, gadgets across three harshness levels, bid rounds, B2 constraint cards, idiom boards, campaign scoring, the validator, the balancer, the dossier export and a printable PDF kit add up to 3-4x the build of /sinif-oyunu. The polish will be spread thin, and Codenames only feels right if the core loop (key sync, flip, clue rail, reveal) is flawless.

The key-sync handshake is the biggest risk to launch and to feel. The phone and the projector must run the same seeded generator plus the 50-try balancer and get the same result. A cached older JS bundle on the phone, a change to the float or RNG code, or a board swap after the key is generated all silently desync the key, and a wrong flip ruins a round in front of 30 students. Also, typing 5 characters on a smartboard's on-screen keyboard is slow, and on some Pardus smartboards the OS keyboard is unreliable.
Swap card (before the first clue) changes the board. If the key code has already been exchanged, the phone never learns about the swap, and its key covers a card that no longer exists.

The printed key cards (24 patterns x 4 rotations) are specified only as generic patterns. There are different grid sizes (4x4, 5x4, 5x5) and team counts (2 or 3), and a fixed pattern ignores the cluster balancer entirely, so printed keys are unbalanced unless the code does something about it.

The Oyun Parkı A1 version is not really Codenames. Every clue describes one card with number 1, Gogo gives the clue, and there is no association across cards. That makes it a listen-and-find picture quiz with team colours, which overlaps with any 'Listen and find', Bingo or picture-MCQ candidate. It is also slow: the Stand-up vote needs the teacher to spotlight candidate cards one by one, and a second try follows every townsperson hit.

The TTS dependency breaks on real school hardware. The Gogo 0.8x voice needs an English speechSynthesis voice, but MEB smartboards (Pardus) and many school Windows installs have no English voice, or only a robotic one. The A1 kids' listening game then has no audio at all.

The picture requirement is a large, hidden asset cost. A1/A2 Genç needs a consistent self-hosted SVG icon set, realistically 400-800 icons to cover the built-in topics, and it drops every unpicturable item. With a free prompt, the LLM will produce words that no icon exists for, so boards come out short. Emoji fallback looks different across Windows, Android and Pardus, some glyphs are ambiguous (the classic ambiguous-picture problem) or missing (tofu boxes), and the look is not 'polished'.

The LLM is not reliable at bridge words (polysemy across two clusters). DeepSeek will produce false bridges, overlapping clusters where one member fits three clusters, and near-synonyms that make the key unfair ('cup' and 'mug' in different clusters). Dedupe plus the words.js band check will throw out 30-50% of the output, so hitting a 1.4x pool is not guaranteed on the first call.

The validator's rule 'shared stems of 4 letters or more' gives false positives if it is implemented as a substring or prefix test: rain/train, card/cardigan, 'plan' vs 'planet'. words.js likely has no morphological family field, so family[] has to come from the LLM or a heuristic stemmer. Also, requiring the teacher to TYPE every clue during live play is heavy friction, and many teachers will skip it, which makes the validator dead code.

Leaks and interaction risks on a smartboard. Long-press to Swap conflicts with the two-step lock and flip on touchscreens, because a slow press becomes a swap. Hover states are already banned, which is good. But a focus ring left by keyboard or touch, the DOM order, or a devtools or screen-reader aria-label containing the card's role would also leak, and so would CSS classes applied at render time.

The Shadow read, the card-help ladder, Intel points, combos, gadgets and commentator strips all fight for one projected screen. Too many overlays will make a 5x5 board of 12-character words illegible at the back of a classroom (only about 110 px per card at 1080p, with a rail on the side).
Adults at A1/A2 fit weakly. 'Describe one' with number 1, given by the teacher or HQ, removes the core tension, so at those levels this is a slower Taboo, Hot Seat or riddle game.
fixes: Cut the MVP down hard. v1 = 2 teams; 4x4, 5x4 and 5x5; clue ladder steps 1-3; HQ auto-clue mode; the two-step flip, undo and clue-history rail; 'Reveal all'; the dossier (no export yet). Key routes in v1: the teacher phone (a) and printed cards (d) only. Only the Nazik and Standard trap rules. Push the rest to v2: 3 teams, co-op, gadgets, bid rounds, B2 constraint cards, idiom boards, campaign, Intel/Shadow scoring, the PDF spy kit, and Supabase Realtime.

Make the key sync tamper-proof. Encode an algorithm version byte plus the seed in the key code, and have the projector show a 2-character checksum of the resulting key colouring pattern, which the phone also shows ('Kontrol: K7'). The teacher confirms the two match before play. The checksum is a hash, so it leaks nothing. Take the key code on the projector with a big custom numeric or base-20 on-screen pad (not the OS keyboard). Store the board and key in the class profile so a reload never loses them.

Lock the board before the key exists. Swap cards is only allowed in a 'Tahtayı hazırla' step, and 'Tahtayı kilitle' then shows the table code. If the teacher needs a swap afterwards, they go through 'Yeni anahtar', which issues a new key code.

For printed keys, let the words fit the key. Keep a fixed set of printed patterns per grid size (for example 16 each for 4x4, 5x4 and 5x5, used in 4 rotations). Once the teacher enters the card number and rotation, the code assigns words to cells so the balancer constraints hold (clusters split fairly, trap placement by mode). This is easy because the key is fixed and the word placement is free.

Present the Oyun Parkı A1 version honestly as 'Gizli Ajan: Dinle ve Bul', a listening variant, and give it a little Codenames spirit at A2. Once the class has played twice, Gogo gives category clues with 2 ('Animals, 2'). Replace the one-by-one spotlight vote with a quicker move: children hold up fingers showing the card NUMBER (1-16) all at once, and then the captain calls. That keeps a whole-class response every turn at a fraction of the time.

Pre-render the audio instead of relying on runtime TTS. Build-time generated MP3/Opus clips for every built-in word and riddle clue (a few MB, lazy-loaded per topic). Runtime speechSynthesis only as a fallback for LLM content, and a clear 'Öğretmen okur' mode with the clue shown in large type on the teacher bar when no English voice is detected.

Limit picture boards to a curated icon catalog. Ship roughly 400 consistent SVG icons first, tagged with lemma and topic. For kids' free prompts, pass the LLM the list of available icon keys, so it may only pick from those plus clusters, and reject anything else. Allow emoji only in Stüdyo and Arena, and there only as decoration next to the word, never as the only carrier of meaning.

Harden LLM generation. Use JSON-schema output, then run code checks: every member must be in words.js at level+1 or below; each member belongs to exactly one cluster unless it is marked as a bridge; bridges must have two distinct words.js senses, or appear in a curated polysemy list of about 150 items (bank, match, spring, light, fair, ring, bat...). If the pool is short, make one repair call ('need 6 more for cluster X'), then top up from built-in banks for the same topic. Cache good generated packs per prompt so the class can replay them.

Validator: use a real lightweight stemmer (Porter or Snowball-lite) plus the plural and -er/-ing rules, not substring checks. Make clue entry optional, as a quick pip tap for the number with the text optional. Run the validator only when text is entered, and show its verdict as advice ('Uyarı: "rainy" ~ RAIN') that the teacher overrides with 'Kabul'.

Smartboard input: replace long-press with an explicit 'Kart değiştir' mode toggle in the setup step. Render cards with role-free markup; keep roles only in a closure Map, and never in classes or aria. Use the same focus style for every card. Add a hidden 'leak test' in QA that dumps the DOM before any flip and checks that nothing differs between cards.

Projector legibility: at the 5x5 size, words are 12 characters or fewer and at least 48 px. Keep the clue rail on the side and collapsible. Show at most one transient overlay at a time. Test from the back of a 10 m classroom photo before shipping.
Scope the adult A1/A2 version as 'HQ listening round plus Describe one', and label the classic Codenames as B1+ in the picker, so A1 adults are not promised the association game.

Fix the build-size label to XL, or split it: v1 at M-L with the core loop plus the kids' listening variant, v2 adding the Arena and Stüdyo extras. There is no merge. The association and polysemy mechanic is distinct from the Taboo, Hot Seat and MCQ candidates, and it is the only candidate that directly trains semantic networks.

catalog.rankReason: Codenames (adult 8): rich clue-giving and negotiation at B1+. Split it honestly by level: A1-A2 and kids play 'Listening Mission' (the app is HQ, no phone key), and real spymaster play starts at B1. Both spymasters think at the same time to remove idle time. The key sync uses the seed plus an algorithm byte, with an on-screen checksum. It waits for the key-delivery decision.

catalog.name: Gizli Görev (Secret Mission Info-Gap Pairs)
catalog.familiarAs: Info-gap role-play cards / secret-mission speaking game (A/B role cards with a surprise twist)
catalog.oneLiner: The whole class plays in pairs at once. Each partner holds a secret role card with hidden facts and up to three goals, and neither can finish without asking the other. Midway a twist card changes the plan. At the end, partners check each other's missions with a quick report and earn a MISSION ACCOMPLISHED stamp for their squad.
catalog.howItPlays:
ROUND STRUCTURE (the projector runs it and the teacher presses one big button per phase: 'Sonraki adım').
0) Setup, about 1 min, once per lesson. The teacher picks a scenario: a built-in category, or a free-text prompt such as '8-B, hastanede randevu alma, telefon' that the LLM turns into a roleplay item, which the validator then checks. Pairs are seat neighbours. The window-side student is BLUE (role A) and the door-side student is ORANGE (role B). Colour labels are used instead of 'A/B' so a harder role never looks like a rank. Pairs are grouped into 3-5 SQUADS, usually by rows, and each squad gets the skin's mascot, emblem or name. Odd student out: they join a neighbouring pair as the OBSERVER (a trio).
1) BRIEF, 30-60 s. The projector shows the scenario title, a scene picture, the two role badges (e.g. 'Customer' / 'Waiter') and the Useful Language box of 5-8 phrases, which the class says together twice. At Oyun Parkı, Gogo and the teacher first act a 20-30 s demo mission that does not score, with the teacher as Blue and Gogo as Orange through TTS.
2) ENVELOPES. Print mode is the default for Genç groups: each pair gets a folded A4 strip with Blue on one side and Orange on the other, and a sealed twist flap marked 'Öğretmen söyleyince aç!'. Phone mode is the default for adults: the projector shows only two QR codes, a Blue one and an Orange one, and each student scans their colour. The card arrives LOCKED as a wax-sealed envelope. When everyone is ready, the projector shows an open code (3 digits, or 3 animal pictures for kids), students type or tap it, and the seal cracks open for everyone at the same moment. No login, and no server state: the card content travels inside the QR.
3) PREP, 45 s-2 min by level. Students read their card silently. It holds: MY FACTS (info lines such as prices, times or problems; some slots are empty and must be learned from the partner), MY MISSION (1-3 goals, each with an icon), and a HELP button (the hint ladder: sentence frames, then a model question, then the TR gloss where allowed). Rule shown on every card: 'Don't show. Tell!' Phone-call scenarios are played BACK TO BACK (sırt sırta), which forces real listening.
4) MISSION, 2-4 min. Pairs talk. The projector shows a calm progress visual in place of a harsh countdown, plus the Useful Language box and an optional 'English only' banner. Each pair has 2 Türkçe jetonu: holding one up allows ONE Turkish word or question, with no penalty. At kids level this is Gogo's 'help feather', a card they raise to call the teacher. The teacher walks around with the Walkabout view on their phone: a grid of seat numbers where they tap a pair number and pick a quick note ('good repair', 'past tense', 'too much Turkish'). Notes are anonymous and feed the end-of-lesson review.
5) TWIST, near the halfway point. A siren or sparkle sound plays and the twist card arrives. PUBLIC twists appear on the projector for everyone ('The restaurant is closing at 9!'). PRIVATE twists, used from B1 up, reach only one colour: the projector says 'Orange cards: open flap 2' or shows an unlock code, so the partner has to be told, which creates a new information gap. A 'Freeze and think' pause follows at the huddle length (kids 10 s, Arena 15 s, adults 20 s), then the mission continues. Each twist changes one fact or adds one goal, and the validator records which goal it affects.
6) REPORT, 60-90 s. Each student answers 1-3 report questions about what they learned from their partner: 'What time is your table?' with options 7:30 / 8:00 / 9:00, or a tap on a picture at kids level. Following the options delay, the question appears first and the options follow. A correct report auto-verifies a 'find' goal. 'Agree' or negotiation goals ('Get a discount') are ticked by the PARTNER ('Did Blue get a discount? yes / partly / no'), and the observer ticks the phrases they heard on a 3x3 PHRASE BINGO board. On paper, the report questions sit at the bottom of the card; pairs hold up 0-3 fingers per partner and the teacher taps the squad totals into the projector, which takes about 20 s per squad. Missed goals are never hidden: a SHOW AND CHECK moment follows in which partners show each other their cards and fix the report together. The learning happens here.
7) STAMPS, then an optional SHOWTIME, about 2 min. Squad totals roll up on the projector, and every pair that completed its missions gets the MISSION ACCOMPLISHED stamp animation on its seat number. Showtime: the seat-number spinner picks 2 pairs from those who raised a 'we'll perform' card (volunteers only for kids; the whole class for adults). They perform for 60 s, and the class votes by hands on 'Best twist handling'. Nobody is picked by name.
8) ROUND 2 = SWAP ROLES on the same scenario with a NEW twist, so the same language is repeated with more fluency. Round 3 = a new scenario, chosen by the trailing squad from 3 options (Comeback: Light).
SCORING, never shown as an individual ranking. Pair points: 1 per goal completed (max 3 each, so 6 per pair), +1 for twist handled (both partners report the new fact correctly), +1 per bingo line of target phrases (observer), +1 if no Türkçe jetonu was used (Arena and adults only). SQUAD score = the average of its pairs x 10, so squad size never matters. The finale uses the mode-specific ending (see the adult and teen versions).
catalog.playerSetup: The whole class in simultaneous pairs, Blue (role A) and Orange (role B), with a trio of Blue, Orange and Observer for odd numbers or to rotate a strong student into observing. Pairs are grouped into 3-5 squads (usually rows) for the score and the finale, and a squad's score is the average of its pairs, so squads of 3 pairs and 5 pairs compete fairly. 'Karışık görev' option: each squad gets a different scenario (one pair of QR codes per squad colour), and they swap scenarios in round 3. Absent partner: the teacher's phone plays that role with TTS lines and tap replies ('Öğretmen/Gogo ortak'). Devices: one projector plus either printed card strips (the default for Genç groups and phone-free schools) or student phones via QR (the default for adults). The teacher's phone is optional and runs the Walkabout view and the remote 'Sonraki adım'.
catalog.contentShape:
CORE = roleplay items, extended in a backward-compatible way so the information gap can be checked by code:
{ scenario, setting, scene (sticker/background key), secs, checklist[] (teacher success criteria),
  facts[{id, value, slot?:'time'|'price'|'day'|'number'|'place'|'item'|'name'}] (ONE shared fact table; code fills the numbers, times and prices, never the LLM, so both cards always agree and the confusable pairs are deliberate: 13/30, 15/50, 7:15/7:50),
  roleA/roleB { title, badge (sticker key or emblem), persona? (character item: fictional name from the name pool plus avatar), info[{id, text with {factId} placeholders, known:bool}] (known=false renders as an empty slot to find out), goals[1-3]{id, text, kind:'find'|'get'|'agree', needs[factId] (facts that live ONLY on the partner's card), blocked?:bool (cannot be met as asked, so the partner must negotiate an alternative)}, useful[] (phrases, linked to vocab ids), secret? (B2 bottom line, e.g. 'You can go down to £850, not lower') },
  twist { at (fraction of mission, default 0.5), to:'both'|'A'|'B', text, textTr?, emoji?, changes{factId:newValue} | addGoal{...}, kind:'fact'|'register'|'mishear'|'fun' },
  report[{goalId, owner:'A'|'B', q, options[3] (answer at any index; shuffled at presentation), answer, why (1 line, e.g. 'You agreed on 9:00, not 7:30')}],
  strip? (A1/A1 Genç only: a 4-6 turn dialogue whose 3 gaps are gap items with a tap bank of pictures or words that live on the partner's card) }.
SUPPORTING ITEMS: vocab (the Useful Language box, TTS, picture keys for kids, phrase-bingo cells); order items of kind 'dialogue' (optional 60 s warm-up: unjumble the model dialogue before the mission); chance-card items of kind 'task' (a generic twist deck for the 'fun' twists, e.g. 'Whisper for 30 seconds!', 'Speak like a robot!', 'Use the word ‘actually’ twice!'); character items (role personas and badges).
VALIDATOR (runs on built-in and LLM content alike): (1) every goal's needs[] points to a fact that is known ONLY on the partner's card, so neither student can finish alone; (2) each role has at least as many things to ASK as the other, within ±1, and card word counts are within 20% of each other, so talk time is balanced; (3) from A2 up, at least one blocked goal forces negotiation, and every blocked goal has a reachable compromise inside the fact table; (4) the twist changes a fact or adds a goal that a report question actually checks; (5) text caps per line follow the group's text-load cap (A1 Genç 0-4 words plus a picture, A2 Genç 8, B1 Genç 14, B2 Genç 20; A1 10, A2 15, B1 25, B2 40), and a card holds at most 3 info lines at A1, 4 at A2, 5 at B1 and 6 at B2; (6) no personal-data prompts (never the student's real address, phone, family, weight or money; all 'my' info is the card's); (7) Genç groups pass the teenSafe filter (no romance, brands, horror, alcohol or adult money domains; prices are in 'coins' or small pocket-money sums); (8) the words in the Useful box stay within the group's CEFR band from words.js, plus at most 2 'level+1' words with a TR gloss. A failure makes the generator regenerate only the failing role or twist, up to 2 times, before it asks the teacher.
catalog.adultVersion:
STÜDYO rule variant: 'Mission Brief'. Editorial quiz-night look: cream, or the dark 'Karartılmış sınıf' theme, with system sans and no mascot or voice lines. Cards look like realistic documents (a booking slip, an email printout, a ticket), and role badges are name tags with a fictional name and job ('Ms Demir · Front desk'). Squad names come from cities or grammar puns ('The Irregular Verbs'). The twist arrives as a soft phone-notification ping with a caption strip ('Round 2 · Twist'). Pairs or trios, with the OBSERVER holding a rubric: goals met, phrases heard (bingo), English kept, twist handled, register (B2).
Scenario categories, all life and work tasks: restaurant booking or complaint; hotel check-in problem (room not ready, wrong dates); doctor's appointment; job interview (the interviewer holds the job facts, the candidate holds a CV card); flat viewing and rent negotiation; returning a faulty product; scheduling a meeting across time zones; lost luggage at the airport; car rental add-ons; the neighbour's noise; a customer-support call played back to back; planning a team event on a budget; salary or freelance-rate negotiation (B2).
Example (A2, restaurant, from the raw idea): Blue wants a table for 4 at 8 pm, asks about vegetarian food and pays by card. Orange has only 7:30 or 9:00 free (blocked goal: agree an alternative), has 2 vegetarian dishes, and the card machine is broken today, so cash only (blocked; a compromise exists: the bank machine next door). Public twist: 'The kitchen closes at 9:30!', which makes 9:00 risky and forces renegotiation.
B2 example: a flat viewing. Blue needs to move in on the 1st, has a cat and a secret ceiling of £900. Orange's secret bottom line is £850 with no pets, but the flat is only free from the 15th and a bigger deposit is acceptable. Private twist to Blue: 'Your flatmate just texted: you need a 6-month contract, not 12.' A register twist is also possible: 'The agency manager joins the call. Switch to formal.'
Adult extras: an optional WAGER before the mission, where each pair secretly predicts how many of its 6 goals it will complete (+2 if exact, 0 otherwise, never negative); optional minus points (default OFF); the Showtime vote. The finale shows full squad scores plus a 'Kaçırılanlar' review: the teacher's anonymous Walkabout notes grouped into 3-5 lines ('We said: “I want pay card.” Better: “Can I pay by card?”') and the useful language actually heard, printable as a one-page handout. Hint ladder: phrase list, then a model sentence, then the TR gloss, each optionally costing 1 point with a floor of 0; the TR gloss can be switched off for immersion classes. Pacing: rounds of 8-12 min, 2-3 rounds, 20-40 min in total.
catalog.teenVersion:
Two stripped rule variants for 9-13, with the same engine and different rules. The group label never appears on screen.
OYUN PARKI (9-11), 'Gogo's Secret Errand'. Kids checklist: THREE rules, shown as pictograms and read by the teacher from a Turkish rule card in under 20 s: (1) 'Don't show. Tell!' (a card with an eye crossed out), (2) 'Ask in English' (an EN speech bubble), (3) 'Check and stamp!' (a stamp). Cards are PICTURE cards. Blue sees a pet-shop shelf whose price tags are blank; Orange has the prices (rabbit 8 coins, fish 5, hamster 12) and a 'sold out' sticker on one pet. Blue has a purse with 10 coins; the mission is 'Buy a pet!'. Frames are printed on the card ('How much is the ___?' / 'It's ___ coins.'). At A1 Genç the card is a DIALOGUE STRIP with 3 picture gaps. There are no goal lists to read, just 1 mission icon.
Every round has whole-class response moments. A choral rehearsal: Gogo says each phrase and the class repeats it twice. A funny PUBLIC twist that the whole class performs: 'The puppy is sleeping! Whisper!', 'A monkey is in the shop! Speak like a monkey for 5 seconds!', 'Everyone stand up and count to 10!'. And a SHOW ME report: the projector asks 'Which pet?' and the whole class holds up picture cards or fingers.
There is no elimination and no timer pressure: the mission 'timer' is a sun moving slowly across the sky, and the teacher ends it. Nothing can go below zero. A missed goal shows 'Nearly! Let's check!' with Gogo holding a magnifying glass. The partners show their cards, fix the answer and the class repeats the correct line twice, and the pair still earns an EFFORT STAR for the class album. Every pair's stamps fill ONE shared CLASS MISSION METER: at 20 stamps Gogo does a 2 s dance, and the class album gets the scenario sticker. Squads are animal mascots (panda, fox, lion, frog...). The ending gives titles, not ranks: Best Helpers, Super Listeners, Bravest Askers, Twist Masters. Sound is a marimba pack: a sparkle glissando for the twist and no buzzers. Hints are all free: picture, then the frame, then Gogo reads the question aloud. Showtime is volunteers only. Pacing: 3 rounds of about 5-6 min with a 45 s 'Gogo says' TPR stirrer between rounds, 18-22 min in total. Print mode is the default. Categories (YLE and MEB-aligned, all pictured): pet shop, fruit market, toy shop, lost at the zoo, class picnic, birthday present with pocket money, school club sign-up, library, canteen lunch, an alien visitor asking about Earth, a theme-park ticket booth, summer camp packing.
ARENA (12-14), 'Undercover Challenge'. The same mission, reframed as a spy MATCH: a dark navy dossier UI with neon in the squad colours, a condensed display font, squad emblems (bolt, flame, wave, comet, crown, diamond), and codenames built from the emblem plus a seat number ('Comet-7'). Squads spend 10 s choosing an emblem, a colour and a 3-word motto. Cards are stamped CLASSIFIED and flip to MISSION CLEAR. The twist is an 'INTEL UPDATE' with a radio-static blip. From B1 Genç it is PRIVATE to one colour, so one agent has to brief the other. There is no talking mascot, only a commentator strip at most once per turn ('CLEAN RUN', 'ADAPTED!'). Scoring is points: goals, adapt bonus, phrase bingo and a clean-English bonus. The streak counts consecutive rounds in which ALL of the squad's pairs clear at least 2 goals (x1.5 at 3 in a row), and scores never go below 0. Hints: the frame is free, and the model question costs 1 point, floored at 0. The finale is a podium plus stat awards (Smooth Operators, Best Adapters, Clean English, Phrase Hunters), never a last place. Nazik stays underneath: no individual naming, volunteer or spinner Showtime, no public last place. Mild steals do not apply to this game.
Genç content is always teenSafe: fictional names only, no romance, no adult money (only coins or pocket money), no brands. B2 Genç means rich language on concrete topics: planning a charity bake sale on a budget, choosing a school-trip destination, organising a sports day, a school radio interview. It does not mean abstract debate. Arena examples: a 'Class Picnic Planner' (Blue has the weather for Saturday and Sunday and the bus times; Orange has the park's opening days and who can't come on Saturday; goals: choose the day, the meeting time and 3 foods within a 20-point budget; private intel to Orange: 'The park café is closed on Sunday. Bring water!'); an 8th-grade 'On the Phone' unit call played back to back; a 'Tourism' unit hotel desk for a school trip. Arena is auto-suggested for grades 6-8 or when the teacher ticks 'Bu sınıf çocuksu görsellerden hoşlanmıyor', including for an A1 Genç class (Arena visuals with full picture and TTS support).
catalog.levelTuning:
A1 / A1 Genç. One goal each, 'find' only. At most 3 info lines; for kids the card is a picture card or a dialogue strip with 3 gaps and a picture bank. Functions: asking for and giving prices, numbers, colours and places ('How much is...?', 'Where is...?', 'Have you got...?'). An optional 60 s unjumble of the model dialogue comes first. Prep: 2 min for adults, 45 s for kids (pictures carry the meaning). The report is a tap on a picture or number. The twist is either none or public and 'fun' (whisper, robot voice) or a single visible fact change ('No fish today!'). Automatic TTS at 0.8x for kids, and TR glosses are on for adults. Mishear traps are OFF.
A2 / A2 Genç. Two goals each: one 'find' and one 'get' that is BLOCKED, so the student must accept an alternative ('Is 9:00 OK?' / 'Sorry, we only have...'). Up to 4 info lines. Functions: times, prices and days, polite requests ('Can I...?', 'I'd like...', 'Could you...?'), accepting and refusing. Deliberate number pairs (13/30, 15/50) train checking ('Sorry, fifteen or fifty?'). Public fact twist. Prep 90 s. The report has 3 options.
B1 / B1 Genç. Three goals each, one of them an 'agree' goal (a joint decision). Up to 5 info lines. Functions: suggesting ('How about...?', 'Why don't we...?'), problem-solving, complaints that contain a short past narrative ('I bought it last week and it stopped working'), and giving reasons. The PRIVATE twist goes to one colour, creating a new gap. Prep 60 s. The report has 3 options plus a partner tick for the 'agree' goal, and whyEn lines appear in the review. Adults also get a job-interview and a complaint pack; teens get planning and club tasks.
B2 / B2 Genç. Three goals that CONFLICT between the roles, plus a secret bottom line (adults: a price or date floor; teens: a budget or rule limit). Up to 6 info lines. Functions: negotiating, hedging ('I'm not sure that would work for us'), conceding and conditional offers ('If you..., we could...'), and clarification strategies (checking, paraphrasing, summarising: 'So what you're saying is...'). The twist is private and is either a REGISTER switch ('The manager joins the call', or for teens 'You're live on the school radio now') or a MISHEAR twist: an ambiguous new fact that must be clarified. Prep 45-60 s. The report is a partner rubric plus a typed one-line 'We agreed that...' summary that the teacher can show anonymously. Across all levels, 'Kolay / Orta / Zor' shifts the word band and card length, and the teacher can give the lighter card (Orange at A levels, which is mostly answering) to a weaker student without any visible label; 'Bir seviye kolaylaştır' drops the whole mission one level.
catalog.sessionMinutes: 15-40 (one mission round is about 5-6 min at Oyun Parkı, 6-7 min at Arena and 8-12 min at Stüdyo; 2-3 rounds with a role swap)
catalog.teacherControls: Setup: the scenario picker (built-in categories filtered by audience, MEB unit tags for grades 5-8, or an LLM prompt in Turkish or English), 'Karışık görev' (a different scenario per squad), a preview of both cards side by side with inline editing of any line or fact, 'Bu senaryoyu yenile' (regenerate one scenario) or regenerate only the twist, and the profile summary line ('A2 Genç · Oyun Parkı · Nazik · Süresiz · 20 dk · Değiştir'). Pairing: seat-number pairing, trio/observer toggle, number of squads, and a 'Gogo/Öğretmen ortak' stand-in for an absent partner. Delivery: print (A4 with 4 pairs per sheet, cut and fold lines, a sealed twist flap, a report strip at the bottom; with or without colour) or QR (one Blue and one Orange code; the open code shown on demand). Timing: the prep and mission lengths, 'Süresiz' (teacher-ended), +30 s, T to pause, and one 'Sonraki adım' button that also works from the teacher's phone. Twist: on or off, timing (auto at half, or a manual 'Twist!' button), public or private, twist type (fact / fun / register / mishear), and 'Gizle' to skip it for a struggling class mid-round. Language support: show or hide the Useful box, the TR gloss for A levels, the phrase-bingo board for observers, an 'English only' banner, the 2 Türkçe jetonu per pair (0-3), and a silence signal (a chime plus a full-screen 'Freeze!' with a hand icon; kids get a marimba 'Gogo is sleeping, shhh'). Monitoring: the Walkabout view (tap a seat number, add a quick note), and an optional noise meter that reads mic amplitude only and never records (off by default). Wrap-up: the Showtime spinner (volunteers only or everyone), 'Rolleri değiştir' for round 2, manual squad score entry for print mode, reduced motion, and a printable 'Kaçırılanlar' or 'Class fix-it' sheet.
catalog.delightDetails: Wax-sealed envelopes that crack open on every phone at the same moment once the class types the projector's open code (3 animal pictures for kids). Paper cards have a real sealed flap marked 'Öğretmen söyleyince aç!'. Role badges: kids get a picture badge ('Shopkeeper' with an apron sticker); Arena gets codenames such as 'Comet-7' on a CLASSIFIED dossier; adults get a realistic name tag and a document-style card (booking slip, boarding pass, email). A MISSION ACCOMPLISHED rubber-stamp animation lands on each pair's seat number: the kids' stamp is Gogo's paw print, Arena flips CLASSIFIED to MISSION CLEAR in neon, and adults get a quiet ink stamp. Twist arrival sounds: a marimba sparkle for kids, radio static plus 'INTEL UPDATE' for Arena, a soft phone ping for adults. The twist also shakes the envelope icon on the card. A 3x3 PHRASE BINGO for observers, where a completed line makes a little 'ding'. Back-to-back seating for phone scenarios, prompted by an icon of two chairs. The Türkçe jetonu is a coin-shaped token printed on the card that students physically fold over when used. For kids it is a 'help feather' card that calls the teacher. SHOW AND CHECK turns a mistake into a reveal moment: partners compare cards and laugh at the mix-up, with no loss. The class MISSION METER is a rocket (Arena) or a hot-air balloon (kids) that rises as stamps arrive. The mishear twist uses deliberately confusable numbers so 'Sorry, did you say fifteen or fifty?' becomes a real, rewarded move. The final 'Mission Log' shows kids a class-album page with the scenario sticker and team titles, Arena a dossier with squad stats and the podium, and adults the Kaçırılanlar sheet plus the 'Language we actually used' list. Gogo sleeps on the pause screen holding a tiny envelope.
catalog.risks: Noise and management: 15 pairs talking at once. Mitigations are the silence signal, the visible phase screen, back-to-back seating and the optional amplitude-only noise meter. Slipping into Turkish: the Useful box on screen and on the card, choral rehearsal, the Türkçe jetonu (rationed, never punished) and the observer tick. Students simply showing each other their cards: 'Don't show. Tell!' on every card, back-to-back seating and the fold-over paper design. Report questions reward real listening, but the game assumes some peeking and SHOW AND CHECK makes it harmless. A strong partner dominating: balanced cards (±1 question each, validated), the observer role rotating per round, role swap in round 2, and the lighter Orange card for weaker students without labels. Phones banned or under-13s without phones: print mode is the default for Genç groups and play works fully offline from paper plus the projector. An inconsistent or solvable-alone gap from the LLM: a code-filled shared fact table, the needs[] and blocked-goal validator, partial regeneration and the teacher preview. Self-reported goals being inflated: 'find' goals are auto-checked by report questions, and scoring is by squad average, so the payoff for one pair lying is small. Performance anxiety: Showtime is optional, volunteers only for kids, spinner by seat number, never by name. Kids overwhelmed by reading: picture cards, 0-4 words, TTS, a single mission icon. Teachers unable to monitor everyone: the Walkabout view plus the observer rubric. Privacy: no personal-data prompts, no recording, no student names stored; the QR carries only the card content. Round length over-running: 'Süresiz' is teacher-ended, and a 'Gizle twist' allows a fast finish.

reviewVerdicts: feasibility: keep-with-changes -> Merge in any separate 'role-play card' or 'speaking card' candidate that uses the roleplay type. This should be the only info-gap pair engine. Keep it separate from Alibi / Kim Yaptı (case frames). They can reuse its shared-fact-table validator.

issues: ROUND 2 BREAKS. SHOW AND CHECK has both partners compare cards, so when they swap roles on the same scenario each already knows the other card's facts. Round 2 has no information gap left, only the new twist. In a real class, round 2 turns into reading the answers aloud.

TECHNICAL CONTRADICTION. The design says 'no login, no server state, the card content travels inside the QR', yet it also says report answers auto-verify goals, stamps land on each pair's seat number, squad totals roll up and a class meter rises. Nothing links phones to the projector, so in phone mode either the aggregation does not exist or the teacher has to type it in by hand. That hidden manual step is exactly where the flow stalls.

PRINT MODE IS HEAVY. For 28 kids that means 14 folded strips, a colour print, cut lines and sealed twist flaps, every lesson and for every scenario. Many Turkish public schools have one shared black-and-white printer and a copy quota. The first run costs 15-20 minutes of teacher prep outside class, and 'Karışık görev' multiplies it.

ONE DOUBLE-SIDED STRIP PER PAIR IS PHYSICALLY AWKWARD. Blue is on one side and Orange on the other, so either one child holds it and reads the other's side by flipping it, or it has to stand up as a tent between them, which rules out back-to-back seating. Kids will read both sides within 10 seconds. The report questions at the bottom of the strip also sit next to the partner's facts.
SEALED FLAPS WILL BE OPENED EARLY. 'Öğretmen söyleyince aç!' with 10-year-olds means half the class has opened it before the mission starts. That ruins private twists and the surprise.

DEAD TIME AND UNEVEN PACE. At A1 there is one 'find' goal, so a strong pair finishes in 40 seconds of a 3-minute mission and starts chatting in Turkish or disrupting others. Meanwhile 3-4 pairs are stuck and all raise 'help feathers' at once. Nothing tells the teacher at a glance which pairs are done, and nothing gives early finishers a task.

SCORING BY FINGERS IS UNRELIABLE AND SLOW WITH KIDS. When 0-3 fingers per partner are self-reported, every 11-year-old shows 3. The teacher then has to tap totals for 4-5 squads (about 20 s each), while the software has to know how many pairs each squad has to average them. That comes to about 2 minutes of dead, noisy time per round, and the scores it produces carry little meaning.

TEACHER COGNITIVE LOAD IS TOO HIGH. Walking around with a phone, tapping seat numbers and picking notes while pressing 'Sonraki adım' remotely, answering feathers, watching Türkçe jetonu, triggering the twist and running the silence signal does not fit one person standing in a room of 28. The Walkabout notes will be skipped after the first lesson.

CHAOS TWISTS. With 28 kids, 'Speak like a monkey' or 'Everyone stand up and count to 10' takes 1-2 minutes to settle, not 5 seconds. Whispering twists are fine, but loud physical twists in the middle of a mission destroy the pair focus that just built up.
BACK-TO-BACK SEATING IS UNREALISTIC in Turkish classrooms with fixed paired desks (sıra) and narrow aisles. Rearranging chairs costs 2-3 minutes and adds noise.

THE ADULT CLASS OF 10 GETS LITTLE FROM SQUADS. It is 5 pairs in 2-3 squads, so squad scoring and podiums feel artificial. What adults actually want is new partners and new facts, not a swapped role with the same partner.

FEATURE BLOAT: wager, phrase bingo, Türkçe jetonu, streak x1.5, noise meter, Walkabout, Showtime spinner, stamps, class meter, 'Karışık görev', private twist codes, mishear twists and register twists. Each one is reasonable, but together they mean a long first-time learning curve for the teacher and a build that is L-plus. It also collides with the kids checklist, which should hold to 3 rules plus a whole-class moment.

THE OBSERVER IN A TRIO IS PASSIVE AT KIDS LEVEL. A 10-year-old ticking a 3x3 bingo while two peers talk quickly drifts off-task, and 'rotating a strong student into observing' removes that student's speaking time.

ARENA STREAK SNOWBALLS. Its condition (all pairs in the squad clear at least 2 goals, 3 rounds in a row) usually happens in only one squad, and with only 3 rounds it barely triggers anyway. It adds rule text for almost no effect.

FIRST-LESSON TIME IS UNDERESTIMATED. The rule card, the demo, handing out strips, explaining the colours and forming squads take 8-10 minutes the first time, so the '18-22 min' kids session really runs 30 or more.
fixes: Round 2 must RE-ROLL the fact table. Facts are code-filled, so regenerate the numbers, times, prices and which goal is blocked while keeping the scenario frame and the Useful box. Call it 'Aynı görev, yeni bilgiler'. For adults, make the default 'rotate partner' (Blue moves one seat) plus new facts. Swapping roles with the same facts should be an optional choice only.

Choose the sync model explicitly. Option A: phone mode with no aggregation. Pairs show their stamp on their own phone, and the teacher enters one number per squad ('kaç çift görevi bitirdi?') with a big +/- stepper. Option B: a lightweight Supabase realtime room with a 4-digit code and no login. Either way, delete the claims about auto-verified results reaching the projector unless B is built.

Print as TWO separate half-cards per pair: a Blue slip and an Orange slip, 8 slips per A4, black-and-white safe, with colour shown by a pattern or icon. Kids hold their own slip. Keep the report questions on the projector, not on the paper, so they cannot sit next to the answers. Add a 'reusable' option: laminate the card templates and project the variable facts (only the table number changes).
Remove sealed flaps for kids and Arena. Put the twist on the projector only, as a public twist or 'Turuncular: ekrana bakın, Maviler: gözler kapalı!'. Private paper twists only for adults, if at all.

Add a DONE SIGNAL and an early-finisher layer. When a pair finishes, they flip their card face down or stand it up, so the teacher can see readiness at a glance. The projector shows a 'Bonus görev' early-finisher line ('Ask 2 more questions about...' or 'Swap and retell'). For A levels, give 2 small 'find' goals per card instead of 1, so a mission lasts at least 90 s.

Replace finger scoring for kids with a whole-class SHOW ME report plus teacher-judged squad stamps: the teacher taps a squad and presses +1 stamp for each pair that shows the right picture. Or skip squad scores at Oyun Parkı and keep only the shared class meter, which also fits Nazik better.

Cut the teacher load to one button. The phone Walkabout has 3 preset notes and one tap per note, off by default. The twist fires automatically at the half. The silence signal sits on the same remote. Put the Walkabout, the noise meter and the wager behind 'Gelişmiş'.

Make kids' fun twists whisper or seated only (whisper, robot voice sitting down, speak slowly). No standing up or animal noises in the middle of a mission; put those in the between-round TPR stirrer instead.
Replace back-to-back seating with 'kartı göğsüne yasla / turn your chair 90°' or a 'phone-call hand' gesture, which works with fixed sıra desks. Mention back-to-back only as optional.
Under 12 students (the adult evening class), hide squads and use pair or rotation mode: every round a new partner and new facts, with the Kaçırılanlar sheet at the end. Scores are optional.

Cut the feature set for v1: pairs, one twist, report, SHOW AND CHECK, stamps and a class meter, plus the adult Kaçırılanlar sheet. Defer the wager, bingo, streak, noise meter, 'Karışık görev' and mishear/register twists to v2. Drop the streak from Arena entirely.

Kids trios: make the third student a 'helper' who holds the picture bank and hands out the frame when asked, instead of a bingo observer. Never rotate strong students out of speaking. Rotate who observes by round, on the seat number shown on screen.

Add a 'İlk kez oynuyoruz' mode: a 2-minute animated rule demo, pre-assigned squads by row (skip the emblem and motto choice), and a single round, so the first lesson ends on time. Put a realistic time estimate in the setup summary line (first time: 30 min).

issues: It is the only candidate that makes every student produce spoken English at the same time. That is a big plus for the suite, but it is really a structured communicative task in game clothing. The Oyun Parkı flow has about 9 phases: brief, demo, envelope, prep, mission, twist plus freeze, report, stamps, showtime. The 3-rule card passes on paper, but the procedure itself cannot be explained in 20 s to 9-10 year olds. The procedure is the real rule load, and the kids checklist does not count it.

A1 Genç children who barely read: the picture card helps, but for a Turkish state-school A1 class of 9-year-olds, free pair talk will fall back into Turkish or pointing ('şu kaç?'). There is no mechanism that makes the English turn happen, so the strip gaps can be filled by peeking or by pointing at the picture.

Validator conflict: rule 5 caps an A1 Genç line at 0-4 words, but the printed frames ('How much is the ___?' is 5 tokens, and 'It's ___ coins.') and the report questions ('Which pet?' is fine, 'What time is your table?' is not) already break it. The caps need to say whether frames and questions count.

Validator conflict: rule 2 requires word counts within 20% and asks balanced within ±1, yet levelTuning relies on a 'lighter Orange card (mostly answering)' for weaker students. Both cannot pass validation.

LLM prompt path for kids: a free-text prompt such as 'hastanede randevu' or 'uzay istasyonu' needs pictures for every fact, item and report option at A1/A2 Genç. The LLM cannot invent art, so any prompt outside the sticker library produces a text-only card that A1 kids cannot use. The design does not say how picture keys are constrained.

Built-in content cost is underestimated. 12+ scenarios per audience × 4 levels × roles, goals, blocked goals, twists and report items, each passing the needs[]/blocked validator, means hundreds of hand-checked cards. Without a level-parameterised template this will ship thin.

Paper mode, which is the Genç default, loses almost all verification. The report is a self-held finger count and the teacher taps in squad totals, so 'find' goals are no longer auto-checked. The strongest learning check disappears for exactly the audience that peeks most.

Paper logistics: print mode needs a new strip set per round (the round 3 new scenario, the round 2 new twist flap) and 4 pairs per A4 sheet. For 15 pairs over 3 rounds that means cutting and folding about 12 sheets before class, which is heavy for a teacher on a weekly load.

Report items test listening and recall only. Production quality (the target functions, politeness, past narrative at B1) is only captured by the teacher's anonymous Walkabout notes, which cover maybe 5-6 of 15 pairs. Stamps reward information transfer, not the target language.
Phrase bingo for the observer at A1/A2 Genç means reading 9 phrases while listening. That is too much text for weak readers, and observers in kids classes will disengage.

Adults: the B2 example uses £ rents and the flat/salary negotiation. That fits adults, but in a Turkish adult class a foreign currency with a secret floor can confuse the arithmetic. The adult A1 content ('buy a pet') must not leak into Stüdyo: A1 adults need life tasks (pharmacy, bus ticket), and nothing in the design explicitly stops the kids scenario pool from being offered to them.

B2 Genç conflicting goals plus a secret bottom line plus a register or mishear twist is cognitively dense for 12-13 year olds even at B2. At 9-11 (Oyun Parkı with B2 content) the negotiation frame is too abstract.

Confusable number pairs (13/30, 15/50) at A2 Genç are good. The design does not state that they are OFF at A1 Genç, though levelTuning implies it only for mishear twists; fact tables still get code-filled numbers.

Phone mode QR with the 'no server state' claim: the open code shown on the projector is also in the QR payload, so the seal is trivially bypassable. That is harmless, but the report answers must not ride in the same payload, or phone users can read them.
fixes: Collapse Oyun Parkı to 4 visible phases with pictograms on the projector: LISTEN (choral phrases plus demo) → TALK (sun timer, twist inside) → SHOW ME (whole-class picture report) → STAMP. Drop the envelope code, the separate prep timer and Showtime for 9-11. Count the procedure against the 20 s explanation test.

Add a scaffolded 'turn-taking script' mode for A1 Genç: the strip is a numbered dialogue in which Blue's lines 1-3-5 and Orange's lines 2-4-6 alternate, gaps sit only on the partner's side, and Gogo TTS models each line pair on the projector before the pairs say it. The English turn becomes the move, not optional talk.

Rewrite validator rule 5 so that text caps apply to info and fact lines only, with frames and report stems having their own cap per group (A1 Genç frame ≤6 words, always with TTS). Validate the frames against the grammar whitelist.
Make talk-balance rule 2 a mode rather than a hard rule: 'balanced' (default) or 'light Orange', which permits a 30-50% gap and marks it internally. Remove the contradiction.

For Genç A1/A2, constrain LLM output to the sticker/picture library. Pass the allowed picture keys in the prompt, reject any fact, item or option without a key, and when a teacher prompt is out of library, map it to the nearest built-in scene and warn: 'Bu konu için resim yok: metin kartı olarak üretildi (A2+ önerilir)'.

Build built-in content as level-parameterised scenario templates: one template per scenario with the fact table, then goals, blocked goals and twists toggled by level rules. A1 uses only 'find', A2 adds a blocked 'get', and so on. Ship 8 kid, 8 teen and 10 adult scenarios for v1 instead of fully hand-writing every level.

Paper-mode verification: print report questions as picture MCQs on the ANSWERER's flap and have the class do the report as a whole-class SHOW ME (hold up A/B/C letter cards or fingers per question, read aloud by the projector). The teacher sees accuracy at a glance, and it doubles as the whole-class moment.

Print one A4 per pair that holds all 3 rounds (the round 2 twist flap on the back, round 3 as a second fold), or default Genç rounds 2-3 to the same scenario with a role swap plus a new PUBLIC twist shown only on the projector, so no second print is needed.

Tie stamps to target-language use, not only info transfer. Give each goal one 'must-use' phrase from the Useful box, which the partner ticks on the report ('Did Blue say “Can I…?”'). At B1+ add the typed 'We agreed that…' line, spot-checked by the teacher. Feed the Walkabout notes into a per-function error summary.

Kids observer: replace text bingo with a 3x3 PICTURE bingo (icons for 'please', 'how much', 'thank you', numbers), or assign 9-11 trios a 'Gogo helper' role that only holds the help feather and taps the stamp.

Scenario pools must be filtered by AUDIENCE as well as level. Stüdyo A1 gets adult life tasks only (pharmacy, bus ticket, café order, hotel reception), never the pet shop. Use TL or a neutral currency for adult prices by default, with £/€ as an option for 'travel' scenarios.

Cap B2 Genç at 2 conflicting goals, a single visible budget limit and no secret bottom line. Allow either a register twist or a mishear twist per round, not both. When Oyun Parkı is paired with B2 content, fall back to B1 mission complexity with richer language.
State explicitly: confusable number pairs and mishear twists are OFF for A1 and A1 Genç, and the code fact-filler picks numbers ≤20 with distinct sounds there.

Keep report answers and 'why' lines off the student QR payload. Store them only in the projector session, and let phone clients send an answer index that the projector scores through a lightweight relay, or keep phone reports self-checked by the partner. Treat the wax seal as theatre, not security.

If the suite has another roleplay or speaking-card candidate (Hot Seat, a WYR wheel, Crossroads role-play), reuse this engine's roleplay item and validator for it rather than building a parallel one. This game should own the 'info-gap pair' slot.

reviews.mergeWith: Merge in any separate 'role-play card' or 'speaking card' candidate that uses the roleplay type. This should be the only info-gap pair engine. Keep it separate from Alibi / Kim Yaptı (case frames). They can reuse its shared-fact-table validator.
issues: The architecture contradicts itself. It promises 'no login, no server state; the card travels inside the QR'. It also promises a remote 'Sonraki adım' from the teacher's phone, Walkabout notes that feed the projector's Kaçırılanlar sheet, report answers from phones that roll up into squad totals, and seals that crack for everyone 'at the same moment'. None of those can happen without a realtime channel. In phone mode the projector cannot know any pair's score, so as written phone mode needs manual score entry just like print mode.

The QR payload is too big. A B2 card has 6 info lines, 3 goals, a secret, the hint ladder with 3 levels, report questions, useful phrases, the twist flap and a persona. That is 1.5-3 KB of JSON, which means a version 25-40 QR. A student cannot scan that from row 5 off a projector with glare. The design has no size budget and no encoding plan.

It is really a speaking-activity framework, not a game. For 70% of the round the projector shows a calm progress bar and a phrase box. It risks feeling like a nicely formatted worksheet generator with a timer. Most of the game feel sits on paper (the flap, the token) or on phones in mode 2, and none of it is on the shared screen, which is where Baamboozle and Kahoot put their excitement.

Scoring is too heavy for a paper classroom. Goals count 0-6, plus a twist bonus, bingo lines, a no-Turkish bonus, average × 10, a streak × 1.5, the adult wager and hint costs. In print mode the teacher taps 3-5 squad totals from finger counts that pairs compute themselves. That takes 1.5-2 minutes per round, invites arithmetic arguments, and the × 10 average hides every detail anyway.

An LLM cannot reliably write the semantic validators. Check (3), 'every blocked goal has a reachable compromise', and check (4), 'the twist affects a goal a report checks', are only checkable if the compromise and the twist target are stated as fact ids. As written they are prose, so code cannot verify them. Check (7), teenSafe, is a keyword filter at best. DeepSeek will also drift on {factId} placeholders by inventing ids, hard-coding numbers in text, or leaking the partner's facts into its own card.

The report questions must not come from the LLM. If it writes the options, it will make the distractors guessable or the answer ambiguous. The design wants deliberate confusable pairs (15/50) but lets the LLM write the text around them.

A 'mishear' twist cannot work in text. A fact printed on a card or shown on the projector cannot be misheard. Ambiguity only arises when the partner says it aloud, so the twist has to be delivered as audio or as an instruction to say it, and the design doesn't say this.

Print mode is hard to lay out. Double-sided Blue/Orange strips with a sealed flap, 4 pairs per A4 sheet, depend on duplex alignment. Turkish schools mostly photocopy single-sided in black and white. The private twist flaps and the report strips also freeze the twist at print time, so 'Bu twisti yenile' or 'Gizle' mid-lesson does not match what is on paper. Colour coding also fails on B/W copies.

Kids pictures are the hidden cost. Oyun Parkı needs picture cards, picture report options, picture banks for gaps and scene stickers across 12 categories: 150-250 consistent illustrations. Free-text LLM scenarios for kids will ask for objects that have no sticker, and the design doesn't say what happens then.

TTS is fragile on the actual hardware. Gogo's demo through TTS, auto-read at 0.8×, and 'Gogo reads the question' all rely on the Web Speech API. MEB smartboards (Pardus/Etap, Android boards) often have no decent English voice or none at all, so the kids demo breaks in exactly the classrooms it targets.

The teen mode is shaky at the youngest end. Fifteen simultaneous pairs of 9-10-year-old A1 learners in 30-35-seat Turkish classrooms is realistic only with the dialogue strip. The 'goal/mission' layer adds little there, and noise control carries the whole design. 'Back to back' seating is barely possible with fixed double desks.

There is too much teacher surface for v1: the scenario picker, Karışık görev, inline editing, partial regeneration, pairing, squads, trio/observer, print vs QR, timing, twist type and privacy, gloss, bingo, tokens, silence signal, noise meter, Walkabout, Showtime, wager, and a handout. The size is really XL, not L. With this many options it will ship half-polished.

Some features pull against each other. The adult wager, the streak multiplier, the hint point costs and the Arena podium add competition to a cooperative info-gap task. The streak rule ('ALL pairs clear 2 goals, 3 rounds running') almost never fires, because sessions are only 2-3 rounds long.
fixes: Choose one transport and say it honestly. v1: the projector plus print only, with manual score entry that works fully offline. v2: phone mode through a short-lived Supabase row (a 4-char room code; the row expires after 2 hours and holds no student data) plus Realtime for the remote 'Sonraki adım', Walkabout and the report roll-up. Drop the 'no server state' claim, or limit it to 'no personal data stored'.

If the QR mode stays, the QR should carry a URL with the room code plus a colour, never the card JSON. If it must work offline, deflate and base45 a slimmed card (no hints, generated client-side from the frames) and fail validation above about 800 bytes.

Give the shared screen real game beats. A live Mission Meter (a balloon or rocket) that fills as pairs press 'we're done' on their phones, or as the teacher taps pair numbers in print mode. The twist becomes a full-screen cinematic with sound. SHOW AND CHECK becomes a projector reveal of the model exchange, with the class reading both parts chorally. The stamp storm on the seat grid comes at the end. Budget polish for these 4 moments first.

Cut the score to STAMPS. A pair earns 0-3 stamps: at least one goal each, the twist handled, and optionally English kept. Pairs hold up fingers, and the teacher taps each squad's stamp count, or the count arrives from phones. The squad score is stamps per pair, shown as a bar. Remove the × 10, the streak, the wager and the hint costs in all modes. Arena keeps the podium plus stat awards, computed from the same stamps.

Make every semantic check structural. goal.blocked requires goal.alternatives: [factId] that exist in the fact table. twist.changes or twist.addGoal must name a goalId that has a report question. The LLM writes only prose templates with placeholders. Code rejects any digit, price or time found in the LLM text, any unknown {id}, and any fact value appearing on the wrong card. For teens, use an allowlist of scenario domains and sticker keys, not just a block-list.

Generate report questions entirely in code from the fact table. The question comes from a slot template ('What time…?', 'How much…?'), the answer is the fact value, and the distractors come from the confusable sets and the pre-twist value. That removes a whole class of LLM errors and makes the 'twist handled' check automatic.
Deliver the mishear twist as an instruction to one colour: 'Tell your partner: the price is now £{15}.' The code picks the confusable value, and the report checks it. Keep it B2 only, as designed.

Print design: single-sided, B/W-safe (use role icons ★ and ● as well as colour), a fold-in-half strip where the fold hides the partner's half, and the twist and report printed on a separate teacher-cut 'intel slip' sheet. Once printed, lock the twist in the UI ('Basıldı: twist sabit'). 'Gizle' stays available. Use CSS @page with mm units and a test-print calibration page.

For kids content, limit the LLM to a closed sticker vocabulary. The validator maps every noun to a sticker key or swaps it for the nearest one, and free text for Oyun Parkı can only choose among the 12 built-in scenario frames plus item swaps. Ship with about 120 stickers in one flat style, not 250.

Pre-render audio. At build time, generate MP3s for every built-in Useful phrase, Gogo line and report question with a good neural TTS, and cache them. Fall back to Web Speech only for LLM content, and hide the TTS button when speechSynthesis has no en voice.

For Oyun Parkı, make the A1-A2 unit the dialogue strip plus one picture mission. There are no goal types; the 'mission' is the strip's 3 gaps. The whole-class moment comes every phase: choral phrases, the performed twist, the Show-Me report. Replace back-to-back seating with a 'fold wall' (the card stands as a tent between the partners).
