- Grid 9 or 16; 3-6 rounds.
- Impostor count: 1, or 2 only with 8+ players at B1/B2.
- Switches: Gönüllü kedi, Kedi ikilisi, Gizli Ajan, Soru turu, Nerede?, Zor forbidden words, 1 or 2 clue rounds.
- Timers per phase, with +10 s, T to pause and 'Süresiz'.
- Frames-panel level, with a TR toggle.
- 'Justify to vote' on/off; defence seconds.
- The round's target structure, picked from the unit list.
- Teacher-tap bonuses (Sharp clue, Target structure, Best bluff).

TOWN DIALS
- Role mix, auto-suggested for the number of players.
- Narrator voice on/off and its speed; Turkish script help on the teacher view.
- Day length and trials per day.
- Ghost jobs.
- Newsroom or twin villages.
- Event cards: Green only for kids, Yellow opt-in for Arena, Red off.
- First-language tax (Stüdyo only, off by default).

CREW DIALS
- Impostor ratio.
- Meeting cooldown and emergency buttons.
- The sabotage list.
- Wrong-answer penalty (Stüdyo only, floor 0).
- Phase length.

SECRET TEACHER VIEW
- Shows who is who, only on the teacher remote (a phone joined with the teacher QR) or the printed key. It never appears on the projector.

KEYBOARD
- Space: next phase. T: pause. +: add 10 s. B: blank the projector.
- 1-7: tap the accused letter. R: reveal. V: void the round.
- S: 'Sessiz sıfırla'. It ends the round with a reshuffle and no reveal, for when a student is upset.

PRINT PACK
- Laminated code cards (colour, shape and number, so they are colour-blind safe).
- Role cards with identical backs.
- Persona name tents and A-G letter signs.
- An A3 frames poster for each level.
- The night script, score strips and the teacher key.

The whole setup is saved to the local class profile ('7-B · A2 Genç · Arena').
catalog.delightDetails:
PHONES
- The role card is hold-to-peek, with a 'SHHH' overlay, and auto-hides after 3 s.
- Crew and impostor screens share the same layout, colour and vibration, so a glance or a buzz gives nothing away.

QUICK MODE
- The Topic Grid tiles flip in one by one, and the dice tumble in with a chunky clack.
- 'Point on 3!' shows a giant hand pictogram with a drumroll (a marimba roll for kids).
- The clue strip keeps each seat's clue as a speech bubble that players can quote.

REVEALS
- Kids: the Sneaky Cat pops out of its box ('Miyav! Kedi yakalandı!'), or flies away on a paper plane holding a fish.
- Arena: a 'SIGNAL LOST' glitch.
- Stüdyo: a manila folder stamped CONFIRMED or CLEARED.

GOGO
- He runs the demo round, echoes the grid words with the class and dozes on the pause screen.

CLUE GALLERY
- Turns the best clues into model sentences.

TOWN MYSTERY
- Night falls with the screen dimming, crickets and a rising moon. Morning brings a rooster and a sunrise.
- Evidence cards pin to a cork board with red string.
- The finale is a printable newspaper front page with a generated headline that uses persona names ('MAPLE TIMES: Baker Rosa caught with 12 cookies!'), and the Village Diary as the article.

CREW
- Repair bars fill with a soft tick.
- A meeting sound: a short klaxon in Arena, a bell in Stüdyo. Kids have no Crew mode.
- 'Comet-7 was not the impostor.'

ENDINGS
- Kids: team titles and an album sticker.
- Arena: a podium with stat awards.
- Adults: full scores, Kaçırılanlar and the Clue Gallery.

SOUND AND MOTION
- Every effect is 1 s or shorter and loudness-normalised.
- Reduced motion replaces every effect with a static stamp.
catalog.risks:
PRIVATE INFORMATION
- Phones are banned in many MEB schools, so every mode has a route without phones: code cards, printed roles with identical backs, pass-the-tablet and heads-down.
- Heads-down depends on nobody peeking.
- The code cards carry 4 lookup tables, so memorising one round does not help later.

FEELINGS
- Being accused, or being made the impostor, can hurt, especially at 9-12.
- Protections:
  - Personas, letters and codenames instead of names.
  - A 'Game reasons only' card.
  - Volunteer or paired Cats.
  - Sessiz sıfırla.
  - Children never play hidden-role elimination.
- Students may accuse the quiet kid or a friend out of habit. 'Justify to vote' and frames about clues push them towards evidence.

LANGUAGE
- A1 learners may freeze. Frames, pictures, gesture clues and the Clue helper help.
- Students slip into Turkish in heated discussion. The frames panel helps, and adults can opt into the first-language tax.

IDLE PLAYERS AND BIG CLASSES
- Idle players: Ghosts get jobs in every long mode.
- Big classes: Stage + Jury, parallel tables, the Newsroom, or two ships.

BAD GRIDS
- A grid breaks the game when one word obviously stands out, when synonyms make the clues ambiguous, or when kids get words that can't be pictured.
- Fix: an LLM coherence check, code checks, and a teacher preview with swap and lock.

FIRST PLAY
- Town and Crew take long to explain the first time. Start with the quick mode and use the 2-minute tutorial.

TECHNICAL
- The teacher view must never reach the projector.
- Realtime rooms need Supabase Realtime, clean-up after 24 h, and no free-text names.
- No Among Us crewmates or beans, and no 'The Chameleon' or 'Spyfall' names on screen.

BUILD SIZE
- XL. Ship it in three drops:
  1. Quick mode with print, pass-tablet and heads-down (the biggest classroom value).
  2. Town Mystery plus the kids' case, sharing the case engine with the Kim Yaptı? game.
  3. Crew on Realtime phones.
reviewVerdicts: age-level: keep-with-changes -> Kim Yaptı? (move Town Mystery and 'Kurabiyeleri Kim Aldı?' into its case engine; keep only the quick impostor mode here)

feasibility: keep-with-changes -> Kids' case 'Kurabiyeleri Kim Aldı?' goes to the Kim Yaptı? / Guess-Who deduction game. Crew mode goes to the phone-quiz candidate (Gimkit/Blooket-style), if one exists.

issues: The heads-down route breaks the core secret in Stage format. Stage players sit side by side facing the class. When the narrator says 'Stage players, except the impostor, look!', one head stays down, so every peeking juror and every neighbour on stage knows who the impostor is. The secret cell also glows on the projector for the 22 jurors whose heads are supposed to be down. With 10-12 year-olds, peeking is close to 100%. This route only works when the impostor also lifts their head and sees a decoy, which the design does not do.

Code-card lookup is too heavy for 10-year-olds. They have to read the die roll, find Table III, then the blue star and the 4, map that to a cell and remember it, all in 15-20 s. In practice it takes 60-90 s. A single misread silently creates a second 'impostor', and nobody finds out until the reveal. There is also dealing, collecting and shuffling laminated cards between rounds, done by the teacher or by kids.

The round-time estimate is optimistic. With 7 delegates: grid 10 s, deal 30-90 s, clues 7 x 15 s = 105 s (kids are untimed, so longer), discussion 20-60 s, defence 15 s, vote with tie-break 20-40 s, reveal and last chance 30 s, word moment 20 s, rotate and new delegates 30 s. That is 5-7 min, not 3. The kids' 12-15 min block (demo + 3 rounds + stirrers) realistically fits 2 rounds.

Speaking share is low in Stage + Jury. Over 3 rounds with 5-7 delegates, 15-21 of 28 students give exactly one clue, and the rest give none. Jurors are active listeners, but the productive-speaking goal mostly lands on the delegates. The seat spinner is random, so the same child can come up twice while others never play.

Parallel mode leaks and is unmanaged. Every table gets the same projector roll, so all tables share the secret. A neighbouring table's shouted 'It's cold!' hands the impostor the word. With 10-12 year-olds at 5 tables, the vote, reveal and self-scoring on paper strips run without the teacher. That leads to arguments ('you looked!') and inflated scores that the teacher cannot adjudicate.

Scoring fairness is luck-driven. Being the impostor is worth +3 to one team, while crew points are +2 spread across all the others. With 3-4 rounds and 5-6 teams, some teams never get an impostor turn, so the final ranking mostly shows who drew the Cat. On 3x3 A1 grids with one-word clues ('yellow'), a caught Cat usually guesses the picture, and that pays 2 stars. The Cat therefore scores in almost every outcome and crew teams feel it's pointless.

Keyboard shortcuts (Space, T, R, 1-7, S) are useless at an interactive smart board, where the teacher stands with a finger or pen and no keyboard. Typing each clue into the clue strip on the board mid-round is extra load and creates dead time while 28 kids wait.

The teacher faces too many choices before the first round: 3 modes, 2 formats, 4 deal routes, about 10 switches, per-phase timers, a frames level, a target structure and bonuses. The summary line helps, but a first-time user will still pick a broken combination (Heads-down + Parallel, Code cards + Kids + 16 grid). Nothing blocks invalid combinations.

Kid welfare in Stage format: a child sits at the front facing 27 classmates who all point at them on 3. 'Gönüllü kedi' only helps if a volunteer happens to be among the spinner-chosen delegates. Shy children picked by the spinner freeze in the clue ring. Being untimed stops the pressure, but it also brings the whole room to a halt.

Town Mystery in a 40-min adult evening class of 10 people: the first player eliminated (at night or at trial) becomes a Ghost 8-12 minutes in and spends 25+ minutes with a thin job (one yes/no question a day, double-weight task answers). Paying adults who get eliminated early is a real complaint. At A2 the Mafia discussion collapses into the 2-3 strongest speakers. The teacher is narrator, night tracker, task host and moderator at once.
The 'One thief is sitting on the window side' evidence needs a seat map entered into the app. That is setup the design never budgets for, and it breaks when students move.

Crew mode is likely unusable in the target public-school context: MEB phone bans, and 28 phones on school Wi-Fi. For 10 adults it becomes mostly a quiz on the phone with little speaking. Scan maths ('impostors always come back inconclusive, crew clear half the time') lets players eliminate impostors statistically after a few scans. The impostor win condition 'equal the crew' is rarely reachable, so balance falls back on 'run out the clock'.

Scope: three games in one XL spec, plus a separate kids' Guess-Who case that duplicates the Kim Yaptı? case engine. That dilutes build effort. The quick mode alone holds about 80% of the classroom value.

Small adult class of 10: Stage + Jury (4-7 delegates, 3-6 jurors) feels artificial, and Parallel with 2 tables of 5 is thin. There is no 'everyone plays in one circle' format, even though that is how Spyfall-type games naturally work with 8-10 adults.

Noise: the jury of 22 argues on mini-whiteboards while the stage discusses. Discussion is capped at only 20 s for kids, but the 'Point on 3!' drumroll plus 5 jury teams shouting letters will drown out the defence. There is no built-in quiet signal before the defence and before the reveal.

Tie-break rule: a tied stage gives more clues, votes again, and if still tied the impostor escapes. In practice this adds 1-2 min and usually ends with the impostor escaping. That is frustrating for kids, even though the Jury breaks ties for them.
fixes: Remove heads-down from Stage format, or redesign it so it never leaks. Everyone lifts their head on 'Heads up and look', and the teacher has already told the impostor by a secret shoulder tap. The screen shows the secret only to a stage sub-area (hard on a projector). Better: for no-phone, no-print use, keep heads-down only for Parallel/circle and never with a projected secret. Make pass-the-tablet (or the teacher's phone passed along the stage row) the default no-print route for kids.

Simplify code cards for Oyun Parkı. Deal one pre-printed picture per child from a per-topic printable deck (7 cards: 6 identical + 1 Cat), generated by the app's print pack. The deck is shuffled face down and handed along the stage row. There is no lookup at all. Keep the lookup tables only for Arena and Stüdyo, and add a 5-s 'thumbs up if you found your cell' check.

Retime the design honestly: plan 5 min per round with 5 delegates and 6-7 min with 7. For kids, default to 5 delegates, a 10-s gentle ring (untimed on request) and 2 rounds in 12-15 min. Show a live 'rounds that still fit' estimate from the lesson timer, and use it for the stop decision.

Replace the random seat spinner with a no-repeat rotation. The app tracks which seat numbers in each team have played (as numbers, never names) and cycles through all of them before anyone repeats. Add a 'Pas / helper' option so a delegate can bring a teammate as a whisper-helper.

Increase speaking for jurors: after the stage clue round, each Jury team gives ONE agreed clue guess ('We think it's cold because...') on its whiteboard, and one juror reads it aloud. The team's rotating reader counts as a speaking turn. For kids, the whole-class word echo stays.

Parallel mode: give each table its own roll (Table I for table 1, Table II for table 2, etc., or different grid subsets) so neighbouring tables' clues don't leak. Make Parallel Arena/Stüdyo only, and use Stage for Oyun Parkı. Give tables a printed reveal envelope so disputes can be checked.

Rebalance scoring. Rotate the impostor seat so every team gets the impostor role equally over a session, with the game length rounded to a multiple of the team count, or treat impostor points as a small bonus (+1). Make the jury read (+1 letter, +1 word) the main points source, since every team gets it every round. For kids, a caught Cat that guesses the picture earns 1 star, not 2. For A1 3x3 grids, have the validator ban single-feature giveaways (the only yellow item) or require 2-3 items per colour.

Design the teacher control for touch first. Put one big 'Sonraki' button, a pause button and letter buttons A-G along the bottom edge of the smart board, within reach from standing height. Keep the keyboard shortcuts as a secondary option. Make the clue strip optional and off by default for kids; alternatively, a tap on a pictogram category (colour, size, place) logs the clue type instead of typing.

Offer three presets instead of a setup form: 'Hızlı · Çocuk (Sahne, deste kartları, 3x3)', 'Hızlı · Genç' and 'Hızlı · Yetişkin (Çember, telefon/tablet)'. Show the advanced dials only on request, and hard-block invalid combinations (heads-down with a projected secret, code-card lookup with Oyun Parkı, Parallel with kids).

Kid welfare: choose the Cat from volunteers who put their hands up before the delegates are chosen, then seat the Cat among the delegates. Offer 'Kedi ikilisi' by default for kids so no child is ever alone as the Cat. Put the stage row side-on to the class (a panel) rather than facing it. Show a visible 'Game reasons only' pictogram during every vote.
Add a 'Çember' (circle) format for 6-12 players where everyone plays, with phones or a passed tablet: 1 impostor for 6-8 players, 2 for 9-12. Make it the default for adult classes of 12 or fewer.

Split the scope. Ship the quick mode (Kelime Sahtekarı) as this game. Merge Town Mystery and 'Kurabiyeleri Kim Aldı?' into the Kim Yaptı? case game, which shares its engine. Park or drop Crew mode as a later phone-only addon for adults. If Town stays for adults, make it no-elimination: a 'suspended' player keeps voting and stays in the evidence phase and the discussion, and only loses their secret-role power.
Replace seat-map evidence with evidence built from persona attributes ('One thief's persona works with food'), so the teacher enters nothing.
Add built-in quiet cues: a 3-s 'SHHH' hand pictogram with a chime before the defence and before the reveal. The reveal only plays after the teacher taps it, so the payoff lands in a quiet room.
Tie-break for all audiences: one quick Jury vote (the jury majority decides), or a 10-s rebuttal from each tied player and then the jury. Drop the rule that a tie always lets the impostor escape.
Add a 'Round ends now' button that jumps straight to the reveal and the word moment from any phase, and a 'last round' flag the lesson timer raises, so the teacher can stop cleanly at the bell.

reviews.mergeWith: Kim Yaptı? (move Town Mystery and 'Kurabiyeleri Kim Aldı?' into its case engine; keep only the quick impostor mode here)
issues: Too little language per student in the core Stage mode. Each round, 4-7 delegates each say one clue (1-3 words at A1/A2) in about 3 minutes. The rest of the class (up to 30) only listens and holds up a letter. With 36 students, a given student speaks about once every 5-6 rounds, and the one-word clues at A1 are close to 'just clicking'. Parallel mode fixes the numbers but loses teacher monitoring, and the talk drifts to Turkish.

The Oyun Parkı quick mode is still a hidden-role, accuse-a-classmate game for 9-11 year olds. The kids' version says 'children never play hidden-role elimination', but Sneaky Cat still singles out a real child to be pointed at by the whole class. Most 9-year-olds cannot keep a poker face (they giggle or look at the grid), so rounds are solved by body language, not by language. It is not elimination, but it breaks the spirit of the Nazik mod.

The secret-deal routes cost too much for kids and A1. 'Table III · Blue star · 4' followed by a grid lookup is a non-language cognitive task that 9-year-olds and low-literacy A1 kids will get wrong, and one mis-lookup breaks a round silently (a crew member who thinks they are the impostor). Heads-down depends on nobody peeking, which does not hold with 12-14s. On phones, many MEB schools ban phones.

The impostor's job at A1 is nearly trivial or nearly impossible, with little in between. On a 3x3 picture grid, crew clues like 'red' or 'big' give the word away at once. With only one clue round the impostor has almost no information when they speak, so an A1 clue is either the giveaway or random. Balance depends on grid design that an LLM cannot reliably produce.

Town Mystery at A2 (adults and Arena) asks too much. A 2-minute accusation with a reason, a seconder with a DIFFERENT reason, and a defence is B1+ discourse. At A2, heated social deduction slides into Turkish within seconds, and fixed frames become 'I think it's Rosa because... evet'. Evidence cards such as 'One thief is sitting on the window side' also drive the logic toward seating geometry, not language.

Arena 'Night Shift' still eliminates players ('freeze a player'), which conflicts with Nazik mod being ON in Arena. The Offline Helper role softens it, but the frozen 12-year-old leaves active play, often in the first night and often picked for social reasons.

The content type depends on the prompt. Quick mode needs a coherent, picturable category grid with no near-synonyms and no outlier. A free-text grammar prompt ('present perfect', 'geçmiş zaman düzensiz fiiller', 'comparatives') has no natural category grid. Nothing routes such prompts to Town or Crew task items, or builds a grid of verbs or adjectives with sensible clue frames.

The Gizli Ajan decoy comes from distractors[0] ('the first same-field distractor'). MCQ distractors are chosen to be wrong answers, not near-neighbours, so the decoy may be too far (tea/hammer, trivially exposed) or a synonym (cup/mug, undetectable). The LLM also rarely hits the right semantic distance on its own.

Picture coverage is the real bottleneck for A1/A2 Genç. MEB grade 6-8 units (Public Buildings, The Internet, Tourism) contain many members that can't be pictured with emoji. The rule 'unpicturable members are dropped' can leave fewer than 9 members, and nothing says what happens then.

At B2, topics like freedom, deadline and privacy make weak impostor grids: abstract nouns overlap, so clues are ambiguous by nature and the 'odd one out' is arguable. Forced target structures (second conditional as a clue) produce stilted clues that are easy to fake, which rewards bluffing over accuracy.

Scope is three games in one (Spyfall, Mafia, Among Us) plus a Guess Who kids' case. That doubles the teacher-facing rules and dials (more than 30 toggles). 'Kurabiyeleri Kim Aldı?' is really the Kim Yaptı? deduction game, and Crew mode duplicates a Gimkit-style phone quiz. Explaining any long mode to A2 teens costs 5 minutes or more of class time in Turkish.

Text load in the long modes breaks the dial caps. Persona timeline cards, the newspaper headline, evidence cards and the Journalist's headline easily go past the A2 Genç 8-word and B1 Genç 14-word caps. The design names the caps but does not say who enforces them on code-built evidence strings.
The last-chance guess at A1 kids ('point first, then say it with Gogo') credits pointing, so the speaking outcome can be zero.
fixes: Ship quick mode (Kelime Sahtekarı) as the product. Move the kids' case and Town Mystery into the Kim Yaptı? game (merge the case engine), and cut Crew or make it a skin of an existing phone quiz game. That makes the build L, not XL, and leaves one ruleset to learn.

Make the Oyun Parkı default 'Class vs Cat'. The Sneaky Cat is a cartoon character: Gogo or a puppet gives the fake clues from a scripted bank (for example, a vague clue with a slightly wrong colour). Every team gives one clue in turn, and the whole class finds which cartoon clue-giver is the Cat. Keep the human-Cat version as an opt-in for 10-11s, with volunteers only.

Raise production per round. After the delegates' clues, every Jury team must write one clue of its own for the word it suspects on the mini-whiteboard before the reveal, then read it out. Score the most accurate one. In Parallel mode, add a 'one clue each, whole table' speaking sheet the teacher can spot-check.

Drop the table and shape lookup for kids and A1. Use colour-only cards: 'Everyone with a BLUE card: the secret is the blue-framed picture.' The impostor card is a plain grey card with the cat icon. Or make pass-the-tablet the default for A1/A2 Genç. Add a 'Kontrol et' step where crew silently touch their nose to confirm they got a card, so mis-deals are caught.

Balance A1 grids by code. Pick grid members that share visible features (4 red items, 3 big animals and so on, from attribute tags), so a single colour or size clue never isolates the word. Give the impostor clue position 3 or later automatically, and use two clue rounds at A1 with a strict 1-word clue.

Gate Town Mystery to B1 and up (adults and Arena opt-in). At A2, offer only a narrated listening case with pictured suspects. In the Arena Night Shift, replace 'freeze' with 'swap roles': the tagged player becomes a Detective's Assistant who keeps voting, so there is no exit.

Classify the teacher's prompt before generating. A lexical topic gets a category grid. A grammar point gets a 'structure grid' (for example, 9 irregular verbs that are actable, with clue frames like 'Yesterday I ___ ...'), or the teacher is told to use Town or Crew task items. Show a Turkish explanation when a prompt doesn't suit the quick mode.

Add an explicit decoy field to the category-list (decoyFor: {term, decoy, reason}) and validate its semantic distance with words.js POS and field tags plus an LLM check ('similar function, different object'). Reject synonyms and trivial pairs.

Require at least 12 picturable members for A1/A2 Genç topics. Fall back to the built-in picture-bank categories and warn the teacher in the grid preview when a prompt yields fewer. Restrict Genç topic lists to picture-safe MEB units.

Replace abstract-noun grids at B2 with concrete-but-rich sets (workplace situations, travel problems) and use abstract nouns only in Soru turu. Make the target structure a bonus, never a requirement for a valid clue.

Enforce text caps in code for every generated or computed string (evidence cards, headlines, persona lines). Truncate or replace them with picture plus keyword for Genç, and give a TTS reading for A1/A2 Genç.
For the caught Cat's last chance, award the steal only if the child SAYS the word (Gogo models it first, and the child repeats it). A point earns an effort star only.

reviews.mergeWith: Kids' case 'Kurabiyeleri Kim Aldı?' goes to the Kim Yaptı? / Guess-Who deduction game. Crew mode goes to the phone-quiz candidate (Gimkit/Blooket-style), if one exists.
issues: Scope: this is three games under one name. Quick mode is about M. Town Mystery is L. Crew is L-XL and depends on Realtime. Together they are XL with the highest risk in the suite, and Crew plus Town would soak up effort without making Quick mode any better. 'Ship in three drops' is really 'ship one game, then two more games later'.

Thin software role in the core mode. The secret deal, clues, discussion and vote all happen off-screen, so the app is a grid, a spinner, timers and a scoreboard. Unless the reveal and the moment-to-moment presentation are strong, it will feel like a slide deck with a timer, not a 'proper game'. The polish budget has to go into the grid, the clue strip, the Point-on-3 moment and the reveal, not into extra modes.

The code-card route is too many steps. A die gives a colour and shape, a second die gives a number, the player finds the table, then the cell, then the coordinate on the projected grid. That is 4 lookups under time pressure. Expect 1-2 lookup errors per round, and a single crew member with the wrong cell wrecks the round. For kids (9-11), colour-only cards with Sun/Moon sides and starred mini-grids are the opposite of '20 seconds with pictograms'. Printing and laminating is also a real barrier to first use.

Heads-down is fragile. The secret cell glows on the PUBLIC projector while 16-30 Jury students are meant to keep their heads down. One peek spoils it, and in a class of 13-year-olds someone will peek. The Jury also has to 'never see the secret', and that is enforced only by honour.

The teacher remote needs Realtime. 'Teacher phone joined with the teacher QR' needs the same Supabase Realtime infrastructure as Crew, but drop 1 claims to have no phones. Town night targets and the secret teacher view either need Realtime in drop 2 or fall back to paper.

Scoring is too complex for projector play. Stage mode has 3 impostor outcomes plus jury +1/+1 plus 3 tap bonuses, adults add minus points and a wager, and Arena adds combo multipliers. Teachers will mis-tap under time pressure, and the scoreboard won't read at a glance. Crew-team scoring (+1/+2 split across several teams) is also odd when each team has only one delegate on stage.
Town evidence ('One thief is sitting on the window side') needs a seat map the app does not have. The teacher would have to enter seating before every game, which is friction nobody will accept.

Town Mystery overlaps: the kids' case duplicates the Kim Yaptı? deduction game, and the Town Task items are the generic MCQ quiz. Crew mode overlaps any Gimkit/Blooket phone-quiz candidate (energy, sabotage, answer-to-earn). The candidate absorbs three other suite slots.

Kids fit is weaker than claimed. Hidden-role bluffing is cognitively hard for 9-10-year-olds at A1. The Cat mostly cannot bluff a clue for a word they haven't seen, so rounds turn into 'the Cat said a random colour'. It works better at 11-14. The 3x3 kids grid also makes the Cat's last-chance guess about 1 in 9 minus eliminated options, which is fine, but clues like 'red' at A1 give the word away instantly.

Picture dependency: pictures are required at A1/A2 Genç, so every grid member needs an image key. OS emoji render differently on Windows smartboards (flat Segoe) and Android, and many A1 nouns have no emoji. LLM-generated categories will often drop below 9 picturable members.

LLM validation for the core content is feasible but needs code-side checks. The LLM reliably produces category lists and near-neighbour pairs, but it often puts synonyms or hypernyms in one grid (cup/mug, sofa/couch, bus/vehicle) and trivially odd members. An 'LLM coherence check' by the same model is weak evidence. Town persona timelines with deliberate alibi gaps are the least reliable generation in the whole design.

Assets are heavier than they look: cat-in-box pop and paper-plane animations, the Gogo parrot (demo, sleep, echo states), glitch shader, manila-folder stamps, night/day scene, cork board with string, 8 mascots, about 20 SFX across three sound palettes, TTS for grid words at 0.8x, plus printable PDFs (code cards, tents, letter signs, posters, night script). Three skins times three modes multiplies it.

Smartboard/mobile input: the vote requires the teacher to tap 'the most-pointed letter', which is fine. But the clue strip ('drop each clue in') means typing during play, and that is unrealistic on a smartboard at speed.
Parallel-tables mode is barely supported by the app (paper score strips, a hands-up meta-score). It is really an unplugged activity with a timer.
fixes: Cut the scope to one game. Ship 'Sahtekar Kim?' as QUICK MODE ONLY (Stage + Jury, pass-the-tablet, heads-down), sized M-L. Move the kids' case into Kim Yaptı? (a shared case engine). Treat Town Mystery as a separate later game, or drop it. Merge Crew into the phone-quiz candidate as an 'Impostor' ruleset, or drop it.

Make pass-the-tablet (or a teacher's second device showing a 'secret card' page, no Realtime needed) the default deal. Build it as a separate local window: the teacher opens /sinif-oyunu/sahtekar?kart=1 on a tablet, and it is seeded from the same round seed via a short code the projector shows (e.g. 'Tur kodu: 4K'), so no network sync is needed. This replaces code cards and the teacher remote in drop 1.

If code cards stay, simplify them to ONE lookup: each crew card is a printed 4x4 of symbols, and the app shows 'Look for ★'; the crew see which coordinate holds ★ on their card. Use 4 card sets (I-IV) that rotate. For kids, drop cards entirely: the teacher holds the tablet up to the stage kids while the Cat covers their eyes.
Heads-down: show the secret only on the pass-around device, never on the projector. If the projector must be used, blank it (B key) and let the teacher point to the picture on a printed grid.

Simplify scoring to 3 visible outcomes (Caught / Caught but guessed / Escaped) plus Jury +1. Collapse the tap bonuses into one 'Yıldız' button. Keep the wager and minus points as hidden Stüdyo options, and drop Arena combo multipliers on jury reads.
The clue strip should use one tap per seat on preset chips (the pictogram frames: colour, size, place, action). Keep typing optional, from the teacher device only.

The polish budget should go to the core loop: grid flip-in, seat spinner with an order strip, a per-seat clue ring, a big Point-on-3 drumroll, three distinct reveal animations (cat box, glitch, folder stamp) done really well, and a word-moment echo with TTS. Give Point-on-3 a proper beat: dim, count, and hold 1.5 s on the accused letter before the reveal.

Validation pipeline for the category-list: (1) code checks each member against words.js for the CEFR band and part of speech, with a single-token or known-chunk check; (2) a synonym/hypernym blocklist plus a WordNet-lite table built from words.js definitions (reject a member whose definition contains another member); (3) a picture resolver against a self-hosted OpenMoji/Twemoji SVG map keyed by lemma, rejecting unpicturable members for Genç and requiring at least 12 resolvable members; (4) the teacher preview with swap and lock. Ship 40+ curated built-in grids so the LLM path is optional.
Self-host an icon set (OpenMoji SVG subset, about 400 nouns covering YLE and MEB 5-8 units) and never rely on OS emoji. This also makes kids' pictures consistent on smartboards.

Kids: set a default minimum of A1 Genç with 3x3 grids of same-colour or same-shape members, so that a one-word clue cannot trivially give the word away (the validator checks for a shared dominant colour). Keep 'Kedi ikilisi' and 'Gönüllü kedi', and start with Gogo's demo round. Mark Oyun Parkı as best for ages 10+ in the teacher hint.

Keep Gizli Ajan (near-neighbour decoy) as the adult/B1+ headline variant. It is the most distinctive feature and cheap to build, since it only needs a second secret on the device. Drop Nerede? roles and Zor forbidden words from drop 1.
Parallel mode: provide a printable table kit (grid, score strip) and a projector pacing screen only. Don't build per-table state.

Sounds: one shared 10-sound set with 3 timbre swaps (marimba, synth, woodblock), each 1 s or shorter. Animations should be CSS/SVG only, about 150 KB total for skins, with a reduced-motion static stamp.
Name-safety: keep seat letters and personas only, and no Chameleon/Spyfall/Among Us naming or art. The mechanics themselves are fine to use.

catalog.rankReason: Adults love it (8.3), but it is a hidden-role, accuse-a-classmate game that fits 9-11s badly, and the core round gives little language per student. Keep only the quick 'Kelime Sahtekarı' mode, with 'Class vs Cat' for kids. Town Mystery and the kids' case move to c26; Crew mode is cut.

catalog.name: Tanık! (What's Missing, Eyewitness & Spot the Difference on code-built scenes)
catalog.familiarAs: Kim's Game / What's missing?, Spot the Difference (Farkı bul), Listen and Draw (picture dictation), eyewitness memory quiz
catalog.oneLiner: A scene built by code from the pack's picturable items flashes on screen. Teams recall and describe it, name what vanished or moved, or find the differences between paired A/B sheets, and every answer is checkable because the engine knows where each object is.
catalog.howItPlays: The engine composes a scene: a background (room, kitchen, park, classroom, street, beach, café, airport gate) plus 6-16 stickers taken from the pack, each with a colour, a count and a position relative to landmarks (on, under, next to, between, behind). Questions and answers are computed from this, so nothing is hallucinated. MODE 1 'What's missing?': 6-12 labelled items are shown and read aloud for 20-30 s. The screen goes dark ('Close your eyes!'). One or two items disappear; at higher levels items move, change colour or change count. Every team answers on boards ('The umbrella is missing', or at B 'The cat was under the table; now it's on the chair'). MODE 2 'Eyewitness': a busy scene shows for 20-40 s, then hides. 5-8 computed questions follow: tf 'There were three cups on the table', mcq 'What colour was the man's bag?', qa 'How many birds were there?', and at B1 'What was the woman doing?'. Everyone answers each one, then the scene returns with the relevant object highlighted. MODE 3 'Farkı Bul' (pairs): printed A/B sheets of one scene with 5-7 computed differences. Partners cover their sheets and find the differences only by talking ('In my picture there are two apples.' 'In mine there are three!'). The screen shows a timer, language frames and the circled reveal. A 'Resim Dikte' variant has TTS or the teacher describe the scene while students draw; the reveal comes with a self-check list ('Is there a cat under the table?').
catalog.playerSetup: Modes 1-2: the whole class in 2-6 teams, all answering. Mode 3: the whole class in pairs at the same time.
skills: grammar (there is/are, prepositions, past simple/continuous, quantifiers, deduction modals)
catalog.adultVersion: Stüdyo 'Eyewitness' uses scenes adults recognise (hotel lobby, café, airport gate, shop with prices and signs) in a flat editorial illustration style with a muted palette. A1-A2 do Spot the Difference with prices, times and signs. B1 works on past continuous witness statements. B2 uses deduction modals ('He must have been waiting for someone') and writes a three-sentence 'witness report' that is compared with the scene. The game is co-operative or scored, as the teacher chooses.
catalog.teenVersion: OYUN PARKI 'Gogo's Room / What's missing?' has three rules: look, close your eyes, say what's missing. It shows 6-8 big stickers, with labels read aloud at 0.8x. The whole class points or calls out, then Gogo reveals the item hidden behind his wing ('Gogo took it!'), and everyone repeats 'The ball is missing!' twice. Stars are never lost. Spot the Difference in pairs has 3-5 differences, supported by an 'In my picture...' pictogram frame. ARENA 'Recon' is a dark HUD with a 'scan' sweep across the scene for 20 s. Questions come as 'intel checks', perfect recall builds a streak, and a 'Moved or missing?' hard mode is available. The end award is 'Sharpest eyes'.
catalog.levelTuning: A1T: 6 items, 1 missing, nouns, colours and numbers. A2T: 8-10 items, there is/are, prepositions, 2 changes. B1T: 12 items, past simple and continuous questions, changes of position and colour. B2T: 14-16 items, comparative and relative-clause questions ('the girl who was holding...'). A1: shop or café scene with prices and there is/are. A2: 'Was there...?' in past simple. B1: past continuous witness reports. B2: deduction modals, a written report, and 7 subtle differences (a few vs a lot of).
catalog.sessionMinutes: 5-10 (What's Missing warmer); 10-20 (Eyewitness or Spot the Difference)
catalog.contentShape: A new computed 'scene' frame: {bg, objects[{imageKey, vocabId, colour, count, anchor, relation}], variants{A,B,diffs[]}, questions[] (computed tf/mcq/qa)}. It draws on vocab items with media.img and concrete=true. Placement rules keep scenes sensible (cups on tables, birds in trees). A grammar-only pack falls back to a generic scene, with the grammar carried by the question templates.
catalog.delightDetails: A soft 'camera flash' opens each look. The reveal zooms onto the answer. A/B sheets print with a fold line and big A and B labels so partners can't peek. The self-check list for picture dictation is generated automatically. A 'class memory record' carries over between lessons. A colour question is never the only cue, for colour-blind students.
catalog.teacherControls: Look time, number of objects, number and type of changes (missing, moved, colour, count), question templates, background, print A/B sheets, re-show key, colour-question toggle, a 2 s 'peek' hint in Nazik mode.
catalog.risks: The whole game depends on a large, consistent sticker set (words.js has no image fields), and scene quality makes or breaks it. Abstract topics can't be pictured, so the game falls back to generic scenes. Memory games can frustrate weaker learners, which the peek hint and team answers soften. Public schools may not be able to print, so Mode 3 can also run half-screen on the projector with one partner facing away.
sources: C:/lg/docs/classroom-games-roadmap.md G02 (information-gap chart) and G14 (Dinleyici çizimi), both missing from the clusters
Raw idea 34 'What's Missing', lost in the c11 merge

issues: The build is too big for what it is. A code-composed scene engine (backgrounds, placement rules, relations, colour/count variants, A/B diffs, computed questions) plus a consistent sticker library does not exist yet (words.js has no images). It is an L build whose weakest classroom mode (Mode 3) is the most expensive part. If the stickers look cheap, the whole game fails in front of 28 kids.

Mode 3 does not work in a Turkish public school. Printing A/B sheets for 14 pairs needs a photocopier the day before, which kills 'pick a topic and play now'. The half-screen fallback ('one partner faces away') becomes 28 chairs turning around, and the facing-away partner has nothing to do but listen. That is noise and chaos, with no information gap for half the room.

The 'Close your eyes!' moment is a cheat magnet with 10-12 year-olds. Some peek, and the teacher must also blank the board without students seeing the change. If the change happens on a visible frame or the animation hints at the location, the game is spoiled. The blackout has to be a full-screen cover with a random delay.

Calling out answers collapses the teams. In Oyun Parkı 'the whole class points or calls out', so the 3 fastest children answer every round and the rest echo them. That breaks both the 'team answers on boards' promise and fairness. Nothing enforces simultaneous commitment, e.g. writing on boards and showing them at a signal.

Mini whiteboards are assumed. Many public classrooms have none, so 'every team answers on boards' becomes shouting. There is no no-board fallback, such as holding up fingers for MCQ options A-D, standing or sitting for T/F, or a team spokesperson with a rotation token.

Scoring 2-6 teams on a smart board is heavy for the teacher. Tapping each team correct or incorrect after every one of 5-8 Eyewitness questions means 6 teams × 8 questions = 48 taps per round. There is no one-tap 'all correct except…' control.

The Eyewitness question load is uneven. At B1T a question like 'What was the woman doing?' is open qa, and the teacher must judge free-form answers from 6 teams about a scene they themselves barely looked at. The expected answer plus acceptable variants must show on the teacher's view only. On a single projector it is unclear where that goes without spoiling the answer.

Dead time and pacing. 20-40 s of silent looking plus a blackout plus answer collection is fine once. But What's Missing loses energy quickly after 4-5 rounds in the same background. Kids ask for 'again!', but they are really asking for a new scene, which depends on how rich the sticker set is.

Memory ability is the hidden skill being ranked, not English. In an adult evening class, a tired 50-year-old learner loses to a 22-year-old on recall, not language. That is demotivating and makes the adult 'scored' mode unfair. The language demand in What's Missing at A1 is one noun.

Adults may find it childish. What's Missing and Spot the Difference read as kids' activities to a 10-person evening class unless the framing is truly 'Eyewitness/witness report'. At 10 adults, 2-3 teams of 3-5 is fine, but the B2 written-report comparison has no checking tool beyond the teacher reading reports aloud.
Picture dictation (Resim Dikte) with 28 kids drawing means 5+ minutes of silent drawing with fast finishers idle, and self-checking against a list is unreliable. It is a different activity bolted on.

Abstract or grammar-only packs fall back to a generic scene. So the 'content is swappable, including LLM prompt' promise is only half-true here, and teachers will type 'present perfect' and get a kitchen.

The colour-blind rule 'a colour question is never the only cue' conflicts with colour-change modes at A2T/B1T. The design does not say how colour changes are made distinguishable (pattern or shape overlays).
Stopping at any moment is fine for Modes 1-2 (short rounds), but the 'class memory record' carried between lessons invites one class comparing itself with another. It needs a per-class-profile scope.
fixes: Ship Modes 1-2 first (What's Missing plus Eyewitness), on screen only. Make Mode 3 a later add-on, or cut it to an on-screen 'Farkı Bul' where the two scenes appear side by side and teams take turns tapping differences. Drop Resim Dikte, or make it a teacher-led variant with no scoring.

Scope the art: 6 backgrounds, about 120 curated concrete stickers covering A1-A2 nouns (food, animals, clothes, classroom, household, transport) in one consistent flat style. Include a pattern overlay for colour variants (stripes or dots) so colour is never the only cue. Map vocab ids to stickers explicitly rather than trying to picture words.js.

Implement the blackout properly: a full-screen opaque cover (Gogo's wing, or a 'shutter' in Arena), a 3-2-1 countdown, the change applied while covered, and a random 2-4 s dark period. The cover is also the 'close your eyes' pictogram, so peeking gains nothing because the changed state only appears after the reveal.

Add a 'commit then show' rhythm. Answer time ends with a 3-2-1 'Göster!' (show!), and all teams reveal at once: a board, fingers (A-D appear as 1-4 fingers on screen), or stand/sit for T/F. Add a rotating 'spokesperson' marker per team on screen (the mascot passes a microphone) so a different child speaks each round.

One-tap scoring: after each question, all teams start as correct and the teacher taps only the wrong ones. Also offer 'whole-class mode' with no team scoring: one class star meter that fills when most of the class gets it right. Make that the default in Oyun Parkı.

Keep open qa out of kids' and scored modes. Convert 'What was the woman doing?' into an MCQ with 3 picture or verb options. For adults keep open questions but show model answers only at the reveal, and let the teacher accept or reject with one tap.

Add pacing variety: each round auto-rotates the background and the change type (missing → moved → colour → count), and a 'Hızlı tur' (quick round) with a 10 s look. Suggest a 6-round cap with an end screen (Sharpest eyes / class star total), so it fits a 5-10 minute warmer.

Make language count as much as memory: award the point for the full sentence frame ('The cat was under the table'), and give a bonus for the correct preposition or tense even if the item is wrong. For adults, default to co-operative mode (the class vs the witness report) so weaker memories aren't ranked. Adult Eyewitness should involve reading details (price tags, signs, times), not only recall.

Honest fallback for abstract packs: if under 6 picturable items, the game says 'Bu paket resimli sahne için uygun değil' (this pack isn't suited to a picture scene) and offers a built-in scene topic with the pack's grammar templates. Don't silently put a kitchen in a present perfect lesson. Mark the game in the picker as 'best with concrete vocabulary'.

The 2 s peek button should be one visible teacher control (keyboard P or a big on-screen button). Keep the teacher panel to 4 controls while standing at the board: Başla (start), Göster (reveal), Tekrar göster (re-show), Sonraki (next). Everything else lives in the setup screen.
Scope the class memory record to the local class profile, and never show other classes' records.

issues: Content-source mismatch: words.js has no images, and an LLM prompt cannot produce pictures. Free-text prompts like 'jobs', 'feelings', 'environment' or 'present perfect' only work if every returned word maps to a sticker that already exists. As written, the 'LLM-generated content' requirement is met in name only for most prompts.

The grammar claims go beyond what a static sticker scene can compute. Past continuous questions ('What was the woman doing?') need people drawn doing actions. B2 deduction modals ('He must have been waiting for someone') need narrative clues such as a clock, luggage or a ringing phone, and inferential answers. Neither can be checked by an engine that only knows positions, colours and counts. So B1/B2 adults and B2T fall back to noun/colour/count recall, which is below their level.

Memory can crowd out language. In Mode 1 an A1 team can win by shouting 'umbrella', and a B2 team wins by having the best memoriser, not the best English. Scoring rewards recall, not the target structure, so learning at B levels is shallow unless answers are scored on the sentence.

The adult fit is uneven. 'What's missing?' with 6-8 stickers feels like a kids' game to B1/B2 adults. The Stüdyo skin helps, but the mechanic is still Kim's Game. Eyewitness and Spot the Difference suit adults; Mode 1 mostly doesn't beyond A2.

B2T 'relative-clause questions' and B2 '7 subtle differences (a few vs a lot of)' need visually distinguishable quantities and many human figures with attributes, which again multiplies the art demand.

A1 kids who can't read: Mode 1 works (pictures plus TTS). The Eyewitness tf/mcq questions are written text, and 5-8 read questions are too much text for A1T/A2T unless everything is read aloud and the options are pictures.
Colour questions clash with the colour-blind promise. If colour is a tested attribute, a colour-blind student is disadvantaged on exactly those items. The toggle exists, but the default isn't stated.

Mode 3 printing: many Turkish public schools can't print per lesson. The half-screen fallback with a partner turned away is awkward for 30+ pairs, and the 'talk only' information gap collapses when the answer is visible to half the class.
Production is thin at A1-A2 adult and A1T-A2T: the output is mostly 'The X is missing' repeated. That's fine as a warmer, but with no escalation it isn't a 10-20 min lesson.

Build size L, and quality depends on art: a scene engine with placement rules, 8 backgrounds and hundreds of consistent stickers in 3 skins (kid, Arena HUD, editorial adult) is the single biggest asset cost in the suite.
fixes: Ship a closed, curated sticker library (about 250-400 concrete nouns tagged by CEFR band and topic: food, animals, classroom, clothes, house, town, travel, shop) with one art style that the skins recolour or frame, rather than three art sets. The LLM step must pick only from library ids (constrained JSON output, validated server-side) and may only choose a background, a topic and question templates. Words outside the library are shown to the teacher as 'resimlenemez' (can't be pictured) and dropped, never silently replaced.

Replace free placement with hand-authored background templates that have named slots (table-top, under-table, shelf, tree, bench, window, counter). 'On/under/next to/between' then come from the slot graph and are always sensible and checkable.

Add a small set of about 12-16 people sprites with action poses (reading, eating, running, talking on the phone, waiting, carrying a bag, sleeping...) plus attributes (hat, glasses, bag colour). That makes past continuous, 'the girl who was holding...' and comparatives computable. Cap the B2 deduction content at authored 'clue props' with fixed accepted inferences (a suitcase gives 'must be travelling'), or drop modals from the promised grammar.

Score the language, not only the memory. Points depend on the level frame: A1 accepts the noun, A2 requires 'There was/were...' or a preposition, B1 requires a past continuous sentence, B2 requires a two-clause statement. The teacher confirms with a quick tick. Add a 'Describe it before it hides' phase in which teams must say N sentences while the scene is visible, so production happens even for weak memorisers.

Restrict Mode 1 to A1-A2 (all groups) and B1T as a warmer. For B1/B2 adults, open with Eyewitness or Picture Dictation, and add a 'witness vs witness' twist: two teams give conflicting statements and the class argues which is right, using modals and past forms.
For A1T/A2T Eyewitness, read every question aloud automatically, use picture answer options (tap the red bag or the blue bag), use tf with thumbs up/down, and allow at most 3-4 questions per round.
Default colour questions to paired cues (colour plus pattern or position) and keep them out of B levels unless the toggle is on. Never make a whole round depend on colour.

Mode 3 without printing: generate A/B as two phone-free projector halves shown one after another (Team A looks for 10 s, then Team B), then the teams question each other. Also offer a one-page PDF with 2-4 pairs per A4 sheet to cut print cost.
Give the teacher a 'Topic → scene' preview before class that shows which pack items were pictured and which were dropped, so a failed LLM prompt is caught before it reaches the projector.

Stage the build: v1 is Mode 1 plus Eyewitness with nouns, colours, counts, prepositions and there is/are (covers A1-A2 all groups and B1T well). v2 adds people and action poses for past continuous and relative clauses. v3 adds the A/B print and picture dictation. Don't advertise B2 modals until v2 or later.

issues: The art is the real build cost, not the code. The code is an M; the art is an XL. It needs a consistent, recolourable sticker set of about 120-200 objects, 6-8 backgrounds with anchor slots, and people in action poses for 'What was the woman doing?'. The adult 'flat editorial muted' style and the kids 'big rounded' style double that again if they are drawn separately. words.js has no images, so nothing exists today.

Content swapping only partly meets the hard requirement. A free-text prompt like 'present perfect' or 'feelings and opinions' cannot be pictured, and the 'generic scene' fallback turns the game into the same room every time. It is honest only for concrete-noun topics such as house, food, classroom, town, clothes, animals, travel and shopping.

Letting the LLM invent picturable items fails, because it will name things with no sticker. The LLM can only choose from the fixed sticker lexicon. Every out-of-lexicon item has to be dropped silently or mapped to a synonym, and the teacher needs to be told how many were kept.

Some computed relations don't render readably in 2D 3/4 art. 'Behind' gets occluded or looks like 'next to'. 'Between' needs exact triple alignment. Count changes of small items (5 vs 6 grapes) are unreadable on a washed-out classroom projector, and colour changes on small stickers vanish too.

Referring expressions become ambiguous. If there are two cups, 'What colour was the cup?' has no single answer. Without a uniqueness solver, the computed questions will produce disputed answers in class, which is the one thing this game promises never happens.

B1 'What was she doing?' and B2 deduction modals ('He must have been waiting') cannot be computed. The first needs action-pose art tagged with verbs. The second has no checkable answer, so the B2 layer is teacher-judged writing bolted onto a memory game. For B2 adults the game risks feeling like a children's warmer.

Mode 3 without printing falls apart. 'Half-screen with one partner facing away' is clumsy with 30 students and one projector: everyone sees both halves. In practice a projector-only Spot the Difference is the same as Mode 1 (show A, hide, show B, 'what changed?').
Three modes, a picture dictation variant, print A/B sheets, and a cross-lesson memory record is too much scope for one game. Risk: a shallow version of each instead of one polished loop.

Colour-blind safety conflicts with the core mechanic, since colour changes and colour questions are central. The 'never the only cue' rule needs a concrete design, or colour diffs should be off by default.

TTS at 0.8x through the Web Speech API is unreliable on school Windows PCs and smartboards (robotic or missing en-GB/en-US voices, offline boards). For children the labels are the listening input, so bad TTS is a real quality hit.

Mode 1 has no whole-class answer input beyond calling out, and team boards are paper. On a smartboard, the reveal and the 'which one?' interaction need large tap targets. Distinguishing tap-to-circle from accidental taps on IR boards is fiddly.
fixes: Build art first, and once. Make one sticker style (clean flat SVG, thick rounded outline, one recolourable 'main' fill via a CSS variable plus an optional pattern layer) and use it in all three skins. Skins change only the frame, background treatment, HUD, mascot and typography. Arena gets the scan sweep and HUD over the same stickers; Stüdyo gets a muted background, a thinner frame and price or sign labels. This keeps the art to a single set.

v1 scope: a curated picturable lexicon of about 120 A1-A2 concrete nouns, mapped to words.js ids and tagged with CEFR band, size class (S/M/L), affordances (onSurface, floor, wall, sky, tree, inContainer), recolourable yes/no and max count. Backgrounds: room, kitchen, classroom, park, street, café. Add airport gate and beach later.

Replace free-form placement with anchor slots. Each background defines named slots ('table.top[0..3]', 'table.under', 'chair.seat', 'shelf.top', 'tree.branch', 'floor.left'), and each slot lists the relations it supports. Supported relations: on, under, next to, in, between (only on pre-built triple slots). Drop 'behind'. Keep one seeded RNG so a scene can be re-shown and reprinted identically.

Add a scene validator that runs before any scene is shown. Every question's target must be uniquely referable (unique noun, or noun plus colour, or noun plus location). Changed items must be at least S+ size and at least N px apart. Colour changes only on M/L items, between hue-distant pairs, and paired with a pattern or shape cue. Kids get counts of 5 or fewer, and count changes of at least 2 at A1-A2. Regenerate if any check fails.

LLM contract: send the lexicon list (ids plus English words) and the teacher's prompt (Turkish is fine). The LLM returns only {bg, itemIds[]} and an optional theme title. Validate against the whitelist and the background's affordances, and show 'Bu konu resimlenemiyor; en yakın sahne: Mutfak' with a count of dropped items. Questions are never LLM-generated; they are always computed from templates.

Gate the game by topic. In the game picker, show Tanık! only for packs with at least 6 concrete, picturable vocab items. For grammar-only packs, offer a template-driven scene (there is/are, prepositions, past simple 'Was there...?') instead of pretending any topic works.

Split the build into phases. P1: Mode 1 'What's missing / What changed' with change types missing, moved and colour/count, plus the full reveal choreography. P2: Mode 2 Eyewitness, with computed tf/mcq/qa templates per level and a highlight-zoom reveal. P3: print A/B sheets (print CSS with a fold line and A/B labels, plus an auto answer key). Drop the half-screen projector version of Mode 3; without printing, point teachers to Mode 1 'What changed?'. Picture dictation is P3, reusing the print path.

Action verbs for B1: author about 12 person stickers in action poses (reading, eating, talking on the phone, waiting, running, sleeping), each tagged with a verb, so 'What was the man doing?' is computable. For B2, make the witness report and modals an optional teacher-scored 'Rapor' round with a model answer generated from the scene facts. Don't advertise it as auto-checked. Position B2 adult use as a 5-minute warmer.

Audio: pre-record or pre-generate (once, offline, human-quality TTS) mp3/ogg for each lexicon word and the fixed kids phrases ('The ball is missing!', 'Close your eyes!'). Use Web Speech only as a fallback. SFX, 8 in total and all under 20 KB: camera flash, shutter click, dark whoosh, pop-out, reveal chime, streak ding, scan sweep (Arena), soft 'oops' (never a buzzer).

Input: presenter controls by keyboard or clicker (Space next, R re-show, P 2 s peek, H hint). Reveal items are tapped on the board with hit areas of at least 64 px and a confirmation ring. Answers come from paper or mini whiteboards, with an optional per-team correct/incorrect tally the teacher taps. No student devices needed.

Polish that makes it feel like a game rather than a quiz: the flash plus a 3-2-1 look timer bar, the dark screen with the mascot covering its eyes (Gogo) or a 'signal lost' glitch (Arena), items fading out with a small dust puff (not an explosion), and a reveal that zooms on the change with a ghost outline at the old position and an arrow for moved items. Also a 'Sharpest eyes' / 'Keskin Göz' end card, and a class memory record kept in a local class profile.
Accessibility: colour changes are off by default in Oyun Parkı. Every colour question also accepts or shows position, a colour name label on reveal, and an optional pattern-fill toggle.

Budget honestly. Code M (about 1.5-2k LOC: scene composer, validator, question templates, three skins, print). Art L-XL. Plan the art as the critical path, and ship with 60 stickers and 3 backgrounds if needed rather than a thin set spread over 8 backgrounds.

catalog.rankReason: Kim's game / Spot the difference (teen 8.7), the natural home for there is/are and prepositions. The art is an XL, though: a sticker library plus slot-based background templates. Build it after the shared picture layer exists, with Modes 1-2 on screen only.

catalog.name: Dedektif Dosyası (Detective Mystery)
catalog.familiarAs: Cluedo / murder-mystery party / Guess Who? (the classic ESL 'Alibi' lesson)
catalog.oneLiner: Something has gone missing. Detective teams question on-screen suspects in correct English, search locations and pass 'lab tests' (language items) to unlock clues. They cross off who, where and how on a deduction grid, then back their accusation with evidence. Code guarantees that exactly one answer fits; the LLM only writes the case in the target grammar.
catalog.howItPlays:
0) SETUP (teacher, about 1 min, before class). Pick a CASE: from the built-in library, filtered by audience and level, or by typing a prompt, in Turkish if you like ('uzay istasyonunda kaybolan robot köpek, geçmiş zaman'). Separately, pick the LAB CONTENT. By default it is built from the case vocabulary plus the target grammar; it can also be any built-in grammar unit or vocab category, or another prompt. Then pick the lesson length, and the lesson-fit timer sizes the number of suspects and rounds. The setup shows one summary line, for example 'B1 · Stüdyo · Standart · 40 dk · 5 şüpheli · 1 yalancı', with a 'Değiştir' link. The print pack is optional but recommended: notebook grids, suspect cards, numbered clue envelopes, accusation slips with frames, the teacher cheat sheet and badges. 'Önizle' shows the whole case and the solver proof before class.

1) BRIEFING (2 min). A TOP SECRET folder slides in and the case intro plays at level (TTS or the teacher reads it; A1 Genç gets a 3-panel picture strip with captions of 0-4 words). Then the line-up: 4-6 suspect portraits, each with attribute icons and a one-line bio. Then the map of 4-6 locations (3/4 top-down floor plan), plus the list of objects or methods at B levels. Each team fills its own grid, which is mirrored as an empty template on screen. Kids first play Gogo's unscored 30-s practice case, 'Who took Gogo's cracker?' (2 suspects, 1 clue).

2) INVESTIGATION (2-5 rounds, default 3, about 4-6 min each). In every round each team takes ONE turn. With Comeback set to Light, the trailing team picks first. A turn is: huddle ('Team talk', 10/15/20 s), 'Boards up!', then one action. The seat-number spinner chooses who speaks; nobody is picked by name.
 a) INTERVIEW. The team picks a suspect and ASKS. At A levels the question is built from chips: a template plus a slot, e.g. 'Where were you at ___?', 'Were you in the ___?', 'Have you got a ___?', 'What were you doing at ___?'. If the word order is wrong, the misplaced chip wobbles and the team gets one retry. At B levels teams ask freely. The teacher taps ✓ (grammatical and on topic) plus the matching template button, or taps ✗; ✗ refunds the token and logs the correction to 'Kaçırılanlar'. The suspect answers from the fact table in a TTS voice preset, or the teacher reads it. Answers are PUBLIC, so every team listens and takes notes. At B levels the answer text stays hidden until the second listen. An off-topic question gets 'I don't remember.' Everyone tells the truth except the liar or liars, who lie about exactly ONE fact that a document later contradicts.
 b) SEARCH. The team taps a location and a short document appears: a receipt, diary page, bus ticket, CCTV log, chat message or school notice (for kids, a picture scene). The document is public. One quick tf or mcq on it (textRef) earns the searching team points or stars.
 c) LAB TEST. The team gets a language item from the lab pack, dressed as forensics: fingerprint analysis = fix the error sentence; decode the note = unjumble; chemical test = gap; witness sketch = picture vocab; audio tape = listening tf. The options delay follows the mode. A correct answer gives a CLEAR private clue ('Team Wave: open envelope 4'). A wrong answer gives a BLURRY clue with one key word masked ('The person had a ██ bag'); a later lab test sharpens it. With Arena's opt-in Intercept, after a miss another unit may answer to take the clue, and the first unit loses nothing.
 PRIVATE CHANNELS: printed numbered envelopes (the best option), 'Heads down!' (every other team puts their heads down while the clue flashes for 5 s), or the team phone via QR (hybrid).
 EXTRA TOKENS: each team has 3 per game. A token buys one extra interview question during the team's turn. Unused tokens score at the end.
 END OF ROUND: a PUBLIC CLUE CARD is pinned to the cork board. Code schedules these so the number of possible suspects drops each round (e.g. 6→4→2). During play, red string only links clues that are about the same thing (the CCTV log and the receipt both say 8:15). Eliminations are never drawn until the reveal.

3) TWIST (after the middle round; can be switched off). A pre-planned clue from the logic plan: a CCTV still, a hidden message in capital letters, a new witness, or the object found somewhere else. Kids get a trail of crumbs or paw prints. The optional 'Sürpriz son' makes the family pet the culprit, but only if the pet was already in the line-up, so the logic still holds.

4) ACCUSATION (4-6 min). Each team secretly fills a slip or mini-whiteboard with WHO, plus WHERE, HOW and WHEN depending on level, and 1-2 reasons written with the level frames. On 'Boards up!' all teams show at once (or submit by phone). Each Speaker reads theirs aloud. The teacher ticks each valid reason: the facts must match the cheat sheet, and at B2 the reason must use a modal of deduction. Stüdyo extras: an 'Early call' is allowed from round 2, and there is a confidence wager before 'Boards up!'. Kids: on '3-2-1, point!' the whole class points at a face or holds up a suspect number card, then says one sentence in chorus ('It's Zip! He has got a red cap!').

5) REVEAL (2-3 min). The lights dim, a drumroll plays, the culprit's card flips and the CASE CLOSED stamp lands. Then the timeline replays on the map: little figures walk between rooms minute by minute. Each lie flashes 'LIE' next to the document that exposed it. Red strings are drawn from every clue to the options it ruled out. The culprit confesses at level. At B2 a short must have / can't have teaching moment follows, built from this case.

SCORING (no speed points in any mode).
- Oyun Parkı: stars, and a score never goes down. For every whole-class answer, each team showing the right card gets a star (2 on the first try, 1 on the second). Effort stars go to the class album. Every team that points at the right suspect gets a gold stamp.
- Arena: lab test 10 (combo x1.5 at 3 correct in a row, x2 at 5, accuracy only); search question 5; WHO 30, WHERE 15, HOW 15; each valid reason +10 (max 2); each unused token +5; Sharpest Question +10 (the teacher's pick). A hint costs 5, which is the dial's 1-2 points on this game's ×5 scale. The floor is 0.
- Stüdyo: Arena's base points without the combo, plus WHEN 10 at B2. Optional negatives: hint -5 and wrong Early call -20; with negatives off, a wrong Early call costs the team its next turn instead. A right Early call earns +15. The confidence wager is 0-30.
catalog.playerSetup: One screen (projector or smartboard) run by the teacher, who acts as narrator and judge. Oyun Parkı: 4-6 animal-mascot teams of 3-6 who all share ONE case, so the class is one detective agency. Teams compete only for stars, and every turn has a whole-class response on printed A-D cards or TPR. Arena: 3-6 'units' of 3-5. In 10 s each unit picks an emblem, a colour and a 3-word motto, and gets private intel through envelopes. Stüdyo: 3-6 agencies of 3-5 named from the dial pool ('The Modal Detectives', 'Flat White', 'Kadıköy'); pairs consult during the huddle. Team roles rotate every round on pictogram cards. In Oyun Parkı and Stüdyo they are Reader, Note-taker, Questioner and Speaker; in Arena they are Analyst, Recorder, Interrogator and Spokesperson. Weaker readers always have a real job. Optional LIVE MODE (B1+, Arena and Stüdyo): 4-6 VOLUNTEERS play suspects from printed role cards and the rest interrogate them. Every card has the same layout and length, and every card has a 'secret' box. At B1 an innocent's box says 'Tell the truth'; at B2 it may hold a harmless secret. So nobody can spot the culprit card by its look, and the culprit card never appears on screen. Card rule: 'If it is not on your card, say: I don't remember.'
catalog.contentShape:
Pack = pack.frames.case (the 'case' type, extended) + suspects as 'character' items + documents as 'text' items + lab items.

frames.case fields:
- theme, setting.
- incident, from a whitelist per audience. Genç: ate, took, hid, moved, lost, painted, unplugged, wiped. Stüdyo adds: stole, sabotaged, leaked. A non-graphic murder is possible only with mature=true, adult B only, off by default.
- caseIntro, mature.
- dims {who[], where[], how[]?, when[]?}.
- suspects[4-6] {id, name (fictional, from the name pool; never a real student), avatar (layered sticker key: base + hat/scarf/glasses/bag + colour, so every attribute is visible and printable), role, bio, attrs {look, item, place, time, activity}, liesOn? {templateId, saidValue, exposedByClueId}, secret? (B2 innocent liar)}.
- locations[] {id, label, imageKey}; methods[] {id, label, imageKey}.
- culpritId; solution {who, where, how?, when?}.
- clues[] {id, attrRef (a predicate such as 'look=red cap' or 'place@8:15!=garden'), round, channel ('public'|'envelope'|'doc'|'interview'|'twist'), text, blurText (one key word masked), eliminates[] (computed), links[] (board strings)}.
- answers {suspectId: {templateId: text}}. Each answer is a code sentence template, guaranteed accurate, plus an optional LLM flavour tail.
- Template ids: yes/no (has_got, is_wearing, was_in, can) and wh- (where_at, doing_at, with_whom, saw, item, last_seen, relation, motive at B2).
- witnessLines[] (B1+; reported speech at B2), twist, confession, timeline[{time, suspectId, locationId}], envelopes[{n, clueId}], solverProof {candidatesAfterRound[], unique: true}.
- The 'text' items (receipt, CCTV log, diary…) carry textRef tf/mcq questions. The 'character' items also print as live-mode role cards.
- Lab tests draw from mcq, gap, error, order, vocab, sound, tf and qa items.

PIPELINE:
(1) The LLM proposes the theme vocabulary as JSON (places, objects, looks, activities, names from the pool). Code checks the words.js band for the level and the Kolay/Orta/Zor mix, runs teenSafe, and maps imageKeys. Kids' packs drop anything without a picture.
(2) CODE builds the fact table and picks the culprit with a seed. Values repeat across 2-3 suspects so that clues partition, Guess-Who style. Code then enumerates the candidate predicates and brute-forces the clue plan, which must meet all of these:
- Exactly one (who, where, how, when) fits all clues plus the truthful answers.
- Every wrong option is eliminated by at least one clue a team is guaranteed to see, and at B levels also by a second route (interview or document), so a missed envelope never makes the case unsolvable.
- No clue contradicts the solution, no clue is a pure duplicate, and no single clue solves the case.
- Public clues alone leave at most 2 suspects (kids: exactly 1).
- Each lie is exposed by exactly one document.
- The B2 red herring is true but eliminates nothing.
- The candidate count drops every round.
(3) The LLM writes ONLY text from the fact table: intro, bios, flavour tails, documents, clue sentences, witness lines, twist, confession.
(4) VALIDATOR:
- Every text contains its own exact attribute strings and never another suspect's.
- Word caps per group are respected (a long document is split into 2 cards).
- The grammar target appears (regex: was/were + -ing; must/can't/might have + past participle; 'said (that) … had').
- Genç texts pass the teenSafe lexicon ('took/hid'; never steal, crime, kill, blood).
- Names come only from the pool.
- On failure: two retries, then code-template text. There is one generation per case, cached by prompt hash, through the Material Maker endpoint with its rate limit.
'Aynı dava, yeni suçlu' re-runs steps 2 and 4 with templates only, so the same case can be replayed with no LLM call. Built-in cases are hand-checked JSON in src/data, per audience × level.
catalog.adultVersion:
STÜDYO 'Case File'. The look is an editorial noir quiz night: cream paper or the dark 'Karartılmış sınıf' theme, a typewriter serif for documents, system sans for the UI, no mascot and no voice lines. There is an optional 'Noir anlatım' radio filter on the TTS narration only, off by default.

CASE LIBRARY:
- A1: 'Who Ate the Manager's Birthday Cake?' (WHO + WHERE; there was, was in, has got; adult humour, never childish).
- A2: 'Sabotage at the Office Coffee Machine' (humour); 'The Missing Laptop'.
- B1: 'The Leaked Exam'; 'The Vanishing Influencer'; 'Sabotage at the Bakery Competition'.
- B2: 'Midnight at the Grand Hotel' (a stolen painting); 'The Hotel Jewellery Mix-up'; 'Death on the Istanbul Ferry' (a classic whodunit, only behind the mature toggle, non-graphic).
Suspects have jobs, relationships and motives. Documents are emails, receipts, hotel key-card logs, ferry tickets, CCTV timestamps and chat screenshots.

LANGUAGE: question forms, past simple and past continuous alibis with exact times, modals of deduction in the accusation, and reported speech in witness lines and the final report ('She said she had been in the spa').

RULES: 20-s huddle with pair consultation and a rotating spokesperson. Free questions at B levels, with the teacher's ✓/✗ and a token refund. Early call from round 2. A confidence wager before 'Boards up!'. Optional negatives. Red Harshness is not used, because luck would break the deduction. Live mode with volunteer suspects is recommended at B1-B2.

ENDING: full scores, then a newspaper front page ('GRAND HOTEL PAINTING THIEF CAUGHT') quoting the winning team's accusation sentence with any errors corrected, then the 'Kaçırılanlar' review list. That list holds the rejected questions with their corrections ('Where you were at 8? → Where were you at 8?'), the missed lab items with a one-line why, and the reasons that were not accepted.
catalog.teenVersion:
Two stripped rule packs, not one re-coloured game. Both are teenSafe: incidents are only took, hid, ate, moved, painted, unplugged or wiped, with no violence, horror, brands or dating.

OYUN PARKI, 9-11 (default for A1 Genç and A2 Genç): 'Junior Detectives'.
- Visuals: warm and bright on cream, rounded shapes, big pictures, the Andika-type font.
- Suspects are cartoon animals or robots: Mimi the cat, Bobo the hippo, Zip the mouse, Rex the dog, Bolt the robot. They NEVER use the 8 team-mascot species, so no team feels accused.
- Host: Gogo the parrot in a tiny deerstalker. He demos the practice case, parrots the key question for choral repetition, says the answer after a second miss and sleeps on the pause screen.
- Cases: 'Who Ate the Birthday Cake?'; 'Who Took the Class Hamster?' (it is safe; someone took it home to play); 'Who Painted the School Wall Green?'; 'The Missing Dinosaur Egg at the Museum'; 'Who Took the Golden Trophy?'.
- Rules card, 3 rules with pictograms, read aloud from the Turkish card in about 20 s: 1) 🗨️/🔍 Ask a suspect or look in a place. 2) ✋ Everyone answers together → we win a clue. 3) ❌ Cross out who doesn't match; at the end, point!
- Student strings: 'Your turn!', 'Ask!', 'Look!', 'Clue!', 'Who is it?'.
- Everything is public and shared, and nobody lies.
- Questions are picture chips, yes/no only ('Has he got a 🧢?'). The class repeats the question chorally before the suspect answers 'Yes, I have!' or 'No, I haven't!' with a picture pop.
- Every clue sits behind one whole-class item on A-D cards or TPR. A wrong answer gets a soft boing, a hint and a second try. If it is still wrong, Gogo says the answer, the class repeats it twice, and the clue is given anyway with an effort star, so the case never stalls.
- The picture grid lets students cross out faces.
- Pacing: 3 rounds of 3-4 turns (about 70 s each). Between rounds there is a 45-s 'Detective Freeze' TPR stirrer or a 60-s spot-the-difference settler. The timer is off by default. 20-25 min in total.
- Ending: a kind confession. The culprit says 'I was SO hungry! Sorry!' and shares a new cake. Every team gets a title (Sharpest Eyes, Best Listeners, Bravest Askers, Super Helpers). Everyone gets a printable Junior Detective badge; teams that pointed right get a gold stamp on theirs. The class album gets the case sticker.

ARENA, 12-14 (default for B1 Genç and B2 Genç; suggested for any Genç group in grade 6+ or when 'Bu sınıf çocuksu görsellerden hoşlanmıyor' is ticked): 'Mystery Academy: Cold Case #047'.
- Visuals: dark navy with neon in the unit colours, a condensed display font, geometric emblems.
- No talking mascot and no pastels, just a commentator strip ('CLUE SECURED', 'COMBO x3', 'INTERCEPTED!') at most once per turn.
- Suspects are illustrated human characters or androids: a coach, a lab assistant, the student-council president, a caretaker, a maintenance robot.
- Cases: 'The Missing Trophy'; 'The Robot Who Lost Its Memory'; 'Space Station Blackout'; 'Science Fair Sabotage'; 'The Locked Locker' (codes and fingerprints).
- Rules card in English with a TR toggle: 1) One action per turn: Interview, Search or Lab. 2) Lab = private intel for your unit. 3) Accuse with evidence; points for who, where, how and reasons. Optional 4) Intercept (mild steal, opt-in).
- A UV lamp makes the fingerprint glow during a lab test. Streaks and combos are on, with a floor at 0. Mini-whiteboards come up on 'Boards up!'. Live mode is available with volunteers only, and role cards are dealt face down so a shy student is never forced into the culprit role.
- Rounds of 5-7 min, 30-40 min in total.
- Ending: a podium plus stat awards (Sharpest Question, Longest streak, Clean sheet, Best Evidence, Comeback), then 'All units: case closed'. Never a last place. Printable Agent ID cards with emblem and motto.
catalog.levelTuning:
A1 (A1 Genç / A1):
- Size: 4 suspects (3 on Kolay). WHO only; adults get WHO + WHERE.
- Attributes: 3 visual ones: colour, clothes, and a body feature or 'can fly'.
- Grammar: have got, is wearing, there is, can; adults also get was/were in as a chunk. Questions are yes/no, from chips only.
- No liars and no clock times. Clues are pictures plus 0-4 words (Genç) or 10 or fewer words (adults), and public clues alone solve the case.
- Lab items: picture vocab, sound, gap with a word bank.
- Accusation frame: 'It's ___. He/She has got a ___.'

A2:
- Size: 4-5 suspects × 4 places (WHO + WHERE).
- Grammar: past simple and was/were. Wh- questions (where, when, what, who with) from chips. On-the-hour and half-past times.
- Liar off by default; optionally the culprit lies once.
- Documents: tickets, receipts, notes of 15 words or fewer (8 for A2 Genç).
- Lab items: past-simple irregular gaps and MCQs, unjumble.
- Accusation frame: 'It was ___ because he was in the ___ at ___.'

B1:
- Size: 5 suspects × 5 places × 4 methods (WHO + WHERE + HOW).
- Grammar: past continuous alibis with exact times (8:10, 8:25), interrupted by past simple.
- Exactly one liar (the culprit), exposed by a document. One witness statement per round.
- Free questions, with the builder as an option.
- Documents: 25 words or fewer (14 for B1 Genç), otherwise split into two cards.
- Lab items: error correction, unjumble, context MCQs.
- Accusation frames: 'It was ___ in the ___ with the ___ because…' and 'She couldn't have done it because she was …ing at…'.
- Live mode is suggested.

B2:
- Size: 6 × 6 × 5 plus WHEN.
- Grammar: modals of deduction are required in the accusation (must have, can't have, might have). Reported speech in witness lines and the final report.
- Two liars (the culprit plus an innocent hiding a harmless secret), one red herring, and two witnesses who contradict each other.
- Free questions only. Indirect questions ('Could you tell me where you were…?') are eligible for Sharpest Question.
- Documents: 40 words or fewer (20 for B2 Genç: richer language on concrete topics, never abstract debate).
- Lab items: error sentences with reported speech and modals, plus whyEn.
- The reveal adds the must have / can't have teaching moment.
