Accepted-form rules are brittle. A first-letter lock breaks on accepted forms like 'an apple' vs 'apple', British vs American spelling, or multi-word chunks. The normalisation rules must be exact, or valid answers will produce wrong codes. Students who answer correctly and still get ACCESS DENIED is the worst possible failure for an escape room.

The blind-solve second call roughly doubles LLM cost and latency per room. With 3-7 locks and a reading note, generation could take 30-60 s. That is acceptable only if it happens before class with ÖNİZLEME, not live.
fixes: Split it. Ship 'Kaçış Odası' as Kilit Modu only (co-op and race). Move Komut Modu into its own later game, or merge it into the RPG/Treasure Map candidate, where command-driven exploration fits. Drop Tam Macera from v1.

Launch with 6 lock kinds that derive robustly from any content: NUMBER (MCQ option positions, set by the engine), SORT (count to digit), ORDER (numbered tiles), FUSE (tf to direction), PICTURE/COLOUR (kids, with shape and label), and READING NOTE. Add WORD, ERROR, SOUND, MAP, RIDDLE and CIPHER in v2, each behind a feature flag.

Invert word-lock derivation for prompt mode. The engine takes the first letters of validated answers as they are and uses them as a letter code, reordering the wheels if needed to avoid the blocklist. It does not need to be a real word. Keep the 'real word first' method only for built-in words.js packs. Use a real word only for the master-door fragment, and let the engine choose it from the pack's own vocab.

Make every lock's code a pure function: code = f(items, seed). The race variants, the answer sheet and ÖNİZLEME then all come from the same seed. Add unit tests that auto-solve every bank lock at every level on CI.

Normalise answers before any derivation: lowercase, strip articles and punctuation, fold British and American spellings. Reject an item if any accepted form yields a different code character. Show the normalised answer on the teacher sheet.

LLM scope for prompt mode: generate flat item arrays only (mcq/gap/tf/order/category-list/text), which already have validators in the Material Maker. The engine assigns items to locks. Rooms, skins and story wrappers come from a hand-authored library (3-4 rooms per audience), with slots for intro and outro text that the LLM may fill within the text caps.

Bound the art to 3 skins x 3 rooms at launch. Use SVG layered scenes where a colour or brightness filter per layer gives the 'room lights up' effect cheaply. Build one lock-wheel component, themed through CSS variables, instead of per-skin art. Gogo needs 4 poses at most.

Device mode v1: 'screen-only zoomable cards plus print' needs no backend at all. Presenter view on the same laptop via BroadcastChannel and a second window. Add the QR team devices and the phone remote in v2 on Supabase Realtime, with a join code and reconnect handling. Autosave to localStorage, keyed by class profile.
Print through a print-CSS HTML page (window.print, A4, dashed cut lines, inline SVG QR), not jsPDF. Replace emoji with SVG pictograms so print output is reliable.

Kids (Oyun Parkı) default to screen-only co-op: one lock at a time on the projector, the whole class solving, teams taking turns to answer items, no paper cutting. Use Adım adım wheels (one wheel lights per correct item) so there is partial feedback by design. Ship the jigsaw paper packs for Arena and Stüdyo only.
Wheels: large tap up/down arrows plus a direct letter or number keypad. No drag. The paper-mode kiosk shows only a 'Takım X kodu giriyor' overlay, and the teacher phone or laptop is the masked input.
Drop the paper-mode CHECK hint. Replace it with an engine-side 'which wheel is wrong' reveal as the 2nd hint rung, which is also what Gogo does for kids.

Generate and blind-solve at setup with a visible progress bar and ÖNİZLEME. Cache finished rooms per teacher so a room is generated once and reused. Treat 'yedek' swaps as normal and label them in the preview.

catalog.rankReason: Escape room (adult 8.3), but XL: 14 lock kinds and hardware assumptions that break in state schools. Later, as Kilit Modu only, with 6 robust lock kinds, a 'Tek ekran' profile and no-cut folded A4 packs. Komut Modu goes to c04.

catalog.name: Harf Havuzu (Bir Kelime-style Letters, Boggle Grid & Anagram)
catalog.familiarAs: Bir Kelime Bir İşlem (word round), Countdown letters, Boggle, anagram / Scrabble-like word building
catalog.oneLiner: Letter tiles are drawn, and teams race to build the longest or the most real English words. Each word is checked instantly against the word bank; kids unscramble a picture word from big tiles instead.
catalog.howItPlays: MODE 1 'Bir Kelime' (default for adults): (1) A captain calls 'vowel' or 'consonant' eight times; the engine guarantees at least 3 vowels. The tiles flip, and the 9th tile is a joker '?'. The pool is always seeded from one pack word, so a topic word is always hidden in it. (2) Teams think for 30 s (45 s in Nazik) to a soft ticking loop. (3) 'Boards up': every team shows its longest word on a mini-whiteboard. (4) The teacher types two letters and taps each team's word from autocomplete. The engine checks that the letters are available and that the word is real (lemmas plus generated inflections), then shows its level badge and Turkish meaning. Scoring uses the TV table: 3→3, 4→4, 5→5, 6→7, 7→9, 8→11, 9→15. On equal length, the word without the joker wins, as on the show. (5) Reveal: 'Did you see this?' shows the hidden topic word and the longest word possible at the group's level. A team earns +2 for using its word in a sentence (teacher judge). MODE 2 'Kelime Avı' (Boggle): a 4x4 grid, seeded so it holds at least N topic words; teams list words for 2 minutes; a word no other team found scores double, as in İsim-Şehir. MODE 3 'Karışık Harfler' (anagram / conundrum): a scrambled pack word with a clue ladder (picture, then defEasy, then Turkish). Everyone answers on boards.
catalog.playerSetup: 2-6 teams of 3-6, one mini-whiteboard per team. Kids play whole class. Pairs can play a quiet mode.
catalog.adultVersion: Stüdyo quiz-night letter tiles (a generic look that does not copy the TRT show). The TV scoring table and joker apply, with 30 s per round. B1-B2 get a 'Word family' bonus: say another form of your word (decide → decision). The final round is a 9-letter conundrum of a topic word; hands-up buzzing, one attempt per team. Kaçırılanlar lists the best words the class missed, with their meanings. No wagering.
catalog.teenVersion: OYUN PARKI 'Gogo's Letter Soup' has three rules: look at the picture, say the letters, build the word. A big picture (a cat) sits beside large lowercase tiles (Andika-type font, single-storey a). The whole class spells aloud together while the active team's seat-picked student taps the tiles in order on the board. Every tile sounds out its phonics sound and its letter name. Then comes 'How many words can we make from ELEPHANT?': a whole-class brainstorm where every valid word adds a sticker to the class jar. There is no longest-word race, no losing, and every turn has a response from the whole class. ARENA 'Word Forge' has dark tiles that glow in the team colour, a 30 s forge per round and a streak for a valid word every round. A 'Legendary word' (7+ letters) gets a 1.2 s sting. The Boggle mode becomes 'Grid Raid' (90 s, unique words double). Team stats at the end: Longest word, Most words.
catalog.levelTuning: Anagrams for kids: A1T 3-4 letters, A2T 4-6, B1T 5-7, B2T 6-8, always with a picture. Letter pools for adults: A1 has 7 letters and 3 vowels, words of 3+ letters, and a picture or TR clue for the seeded word. A2 has 8 letters and bonus stars for A1-A2 band words. B1 has 9 letters plus a joker, 45→30 s and the word-family bonus. B2 has 9 letters plus a joker, 30 s, a bonus for C1+ words, and a 'use it with a collocation' sentence. Any real word counts at every level; the level only changes the bonuses.
catalog.sessionMinutes: 5-15 (one round takes about 90 s; 6-8 rounds make a 12-minute block)
catalog.contentShape: The pool frame is computed by code, never by the LLM: {letters[8], joker, seedWord (a pack vocab term), solutions[] (computed), bestAtLevel[] (computed)}. Validation uses words.js lemmas plus an inflection generator and an irregular-forms table, plus the pack terms. Proper nouns are off. An offensive and teen-unsafe blocklist applies to both solutions and displayed words. Anagram mode uses vocab.term, media, defEasy and defTr. Both content doors work, because the LLM or the built-in topic only supplies the topic words.
catalog.delightDetails: Each tile flips with a marimba note pitched by its position. The letter bag follows English letter frequency. The captain's vowel/consonant call gives the team ownership. Input is normalised for the Turkish keyboard (ı→i, İ→I) so a typed answer isn't rejected. Near-miss spellings ('recieve') trigger a spelling tip and go into the Hata defteri. The 'Did you see this?' reveal is the moment that teaches.
catalog.teacherControls: Vowel/consonant balance, timer, joker on/off, minimum word length, dictionary strictness (lemmas only or with inflections), an 'accept anyway' key that saves to accepted-answer memory, topic seeding on/off, bonus-level band, and the mode selector.
catalog.risks: Dictionary coverage: words.js has no inflected forms, so the inflection table and 'accept anyway' are required. Random letters can form rude words, so the blocklist filters solutions and displays. Typing on a smartboard is slow, so the teacher uses two letters plus autocomplete. Weak teams only find 3-letter words, so Nazik mode counts all valid words together as a class total. Do not use the TV show's name or logo as the title: use 'Harf Havuzu' and describe it as 'Bir Kelime tarzı'.
sources: https://atatepeticaretmtal.meb.k12.tr/icerikler/birkelimebirislem_16977899.html (8 letters plus a joker; scoring table)

issues: The '90 s per round' estimate ignores checking. With 6 teams, the teacher types two letters, finds the word in autocomplete, taps it and reads the badge. That is 10-15 s per team, plus disputes and the reveal. Real rounds take 2.5-3.5 minutes, so 6-8 rounds fill 20+ minutes, not 12.

Checking every team puts one teacher at the board, back to the class, typing on an on-screen keyboard while 28 kids wait. This is the main source of dead time and noise. Students go off-task after about 20 s without a job.

Boggle mode ('Kelime Avı' / 'Grid Raid') cannot be checked in class. After 2 minutes, 4-6 teams hold 10-25 words each. Typing them all, and working out which words are unique so they score double, is impossible from one teacher's input.
The 8 vowel/consonant calls take 20-40 s per round. With 28 kids, every call starts a shouting argument over who is captain and what to pick. By round 4 the novelty is gone and it is just dead time.

Too few students are active. In each team one confident speller holds the marker and the rest watch. In Oyun Parkı, one seat-picked child taps the tiles while the others chant, and weak spellers can lip-sync without retrieving anything.

The longest-word race plus a steep scoring table (9 letters = 15 points against 3 for 3 letters) lets a strong team pull away fast. After round 3 the weakest team knows it cannot win. Nazik mode's class total fixes this only for kids, not for Arena or Stüdyo.
Mini-whiteboards: many Turkish public schools have no set of 6 boards with working markers, and handing out and collecting them costs 2-3 minutes. The setup section never mentions a fallback.

Kids' letter-pool brainstorm ('How many words from ELEPHANT?'): 28 kids shout words at once. The teacher has to hear each one, judge it, type it and add a sticker. It is chaos, and the loudest 5 kids produce every word.

Each tile plays both its phonics sound and its letter name. That doubles the audio, clashes with the whole-class chant and confuses 9-year-olds, who in Turkish schools usually learn letter names first.
Letter-pool spelling suits A1 Genç learners badly. Turkish 4th-5th graders barely spell 4-letter words, so the free-building part gives near-empty results unless the pool is heavily scaffolded.

Bonuses judged by the teacher (+2 for a sentence, a word-family form, a collocation) add a 20-30 s judgment per team per round, and each one invites a fairness argument over who judged which team more leniently.
The hands-up buzz in the conundrum finale fails on one shared screen. Who was first? Adults dispute it, and kids fight over it.

Dictionary disputes: words.js lemmas plus a generated inflection list will reject valid words and accept odd ones, and British and American spellings differ (colour/color). Every rejection of a word the team is sure of stops the game while the teacher argues or presses 'accept anyway'.

The seeded topic word gives little topic practice. With random filler letters, most words found have nothing to do with the topic, so a teacher who picked 'Food' may see 20 minutes of 'tone, rent, stare'.
fixes: Check words the Countdown way. Each team calls out only the LENGTH it claims. The teacher checks only the longest claim or claims (2-3 entries at most), and every other team with a real word gets a flat point on a single 'Evet' tap. Add a 'Hepsini doğrula' option for small adult groups only.

Add an 'Otomatik dağıt' button, the default for kids and Arena, that deals a balanced pool in one tap. Keep captain calls as an optional adult ritual. Captaincy rotates on screen by seat or name, and the screen shows who calls.

Rebuild Boggle checking. Each team circles its best 5 words. Teams take turns reading them aloud, İsim-Şehir style, and the others cross off shared words. The teacher types only disputed words. Or drop Boggle from the class build and keep it for pairs and homework.

Rotate the scribe every round, shown on screen as 'Kalem: 2 numara'. Add a rule that the scribe may not suggest the word, so the others have to dictate the spelling. That doubles the spelling talk and stops one student dominating.

Change adult and Arena scoring. Every valid word earns 1 base point, a length bonus goes to the longest word, and a 'personal best' point goes to any team that beats its own previous length. Cap the table so a 9-letter word scores at most 3 times a 4-letter word. Show a round-by-round catch-up round with double points in the last round.
Add a no-whiteboard mode: A4 paper in a plastic sleeve, or just paper and a marker. The setup screen should say 'Kâğıt da olur'.

Structure the kids' brainstorm. Teams go in turn, and each team has 15 s to give one word through one spokesperson. Or a child comes to the board and taps the tiles to spell the word, so the board checks it with no teacher typing. The class checks each word with a thumbs up or down, which is the response moment for the whole class.
Play only the letter name by default, with a phonics option. Mute the tile audio while the class chants.

For A1 and A2 Genç, keep 'Letter Soup' picture unscrambling as the core game. Show the ELEPHANT brainstorm only with a 'hint ghost' (the first letter and length of hidden words) and at most 3-4 findable words.
Give bonuses only to the round winner, or make the sentence bonus a pair task: each team writes one sentence and the teacher spot-checks 2 at random. Always show a 'no bonus' toggle.
Replace the buzz with turn order: a team writes its answer secretly and flips its board on 'Göster!'. Every correct board scores, and a speed bonus goes only to the team the teacher taps first.

Accept both British and American spellings, and pre-compute the solutions for each pool so the teacher sees the full valid list in advance on a teacher view or phone. Make 'accept anyway' one tap with no typing.
Let the pool contain 2 topic words and lean the filler letters toward topic words' letters. In the reveal, show 3 topic words and ask 'Kim bunları kullanabilir?' as the topic practice moment.
Budget time honestly in the UI: a round takes about 3 minutes. Offer 5/10/15-minute blocks that auto-set the round count, and let the teacher end cleanly on any reveal screen with a final scoreboard.

issues: The topic pack barely matters in Mode 1. Only one seeded word links the round to the topic, and 'any real word counts', so the LLM or teacher-prompt door is mostly decorative. A class that asks for 'airport vocabulary' gets a generic letters game. This weakens the 'content is swappable' requirement for the default adult mode.

The longest-word race measures lexical breadth and spelling of words students already know, not the target language. At A1-A2 (adults and Arena teens), the same one or two strong students find the 6-7 letter word every round, while everyone else writes CAT/TEA. The level profile does not control the demand here. It only changes bonuses, so an A1 class and a B2 class face the same open-ended task.

There is no meaning check. A team can win with a string it found by permuting letters without knowing what it means. This is clicking and guessing, not learning. The +2 sentence is optional and judged by the teacher, so production is a side bonus instead of the core.

The A2 rule 'bonus stars for A1-A2 band words' rewards easier words, which works against stretch. The B2 'bonus for C1+ words' rewards obscure words that the bank may contain but the class cannot use.

Mode 2 (Boggle) is the weakest fit for EFL at every level below B2. Adjacency search in a 4x4 grid under time pressure is a native-speaker skill. A1/A2 groups find almost nothing, and 'unique words double' rewards rare, low-value words. It also costs the teacher heavy input time for 2-6 teams of lists.

The Oyun Parkı phonics claim is risky. English letters do not map one-to-one to sounds, so a tile saying /k/ for c or /e/ for e teaches wrong rules for CAKE, CITY and so on. TTS also cannot produce clean isolated phonemes. Letter names are the real Turkish-child trap (e/i, a/e, g/j, i/ay), and the design does not target it.

In 'How many words can we make from ELEPHANT?', A1 kids aged 9-11 can produce very few valid words (pen, hen, ant, help, plan, then). The brainstorm depends on the teacher and on 2-3 readers, so the whole-class response is mostly silence or noise. The pre-literate kids the lens asks about (A1 kids who barely read) can take part only in the choral spelling part.

Anagram lengths for young learners (B1T 5-7, B2T 6-8) are fine, but the kids variant drops Mode 1 entirely while Arena keeps the adult open race. So 12-14-year-old A1/A2 Arena classes get the most exposing, most elitist version.
Teacher input load: 2-6 teams × typing plus autocomplete × 6-8 rounds within about 90 s per round is unrealistic on a smartboard. With 6 teams, each round overruns to 2-3 minutes.
The joker '?' and the TV tie-breaking rule add rules without adding language value. They are acceptable for Stüdyo but confusing for A1 adults unfamiliar with the show.

Content-type list: category-list and riddle are declared but hardly used. Riddle could drive the conundrum clues, and category-list could seed several topic words, but neither is specified. Validation depends on words.js coverage. A valid common word missing from Oxford 5000 (or a plural or -ing form the generator misses) gets rejected in front of the class, which causes arguments and loses trust.
Overlap: Mode 3 anagram with a clue ladder is essentially a spelling/Hangman sibling. It is the pedagogically strongest part, but it is buried as the third mode.
fixes: Make the pack central. Seed the pool or grid from 2-3 pack words, not one. Score the pack words highest ('Topic word ×2'), and show the topic word's picture or TR clue as a silhouette hint after 15 s. Replace the level-band bonuses with 'topic-word bonus' plus 'stretch-word bonus' (one CEFR band above the group, never C1+ at B2 unless the teacher opts in).

Add a mandatory 'Anlamı?' gate. To score, a team must give the Turkish meaning (A1-A2) or an English definition or example (B1-B2) of its word. The engine shows words.js defTr so the teacher can judge in one tap. Make the sentence the core step at B1-B2 (score = length points only if it is used correctly), not a +2 extra.

Differentiate per level with more than bonuses. A1 adults and A1/A2 Arena default to Mode 3 anagram, plus a 'build any 3-4 letter word' warm-up. A2 uses 7-8 letters and a minimum of 3. B1 uses 9 letters plus the word-family bonus. B2 uses 9 letters, a 4-letter minimum and a collocation sentence. Use the class-total Nazik scoring for Arena as well when the group is A1/A2.

Catch-up mechanic against the one-strong-student effect: each team member writes one word and a different student shows the board each round (seat-picker). Or score the sum of the team's 3 best distinct words instead of the single longest one.

Cut Mode 2 (Boggle) for A1-B1 and all Oyun Parkı groups, or turn it into 'Kelime Avı' with straight lines only (a word-search style grid of pack words), which works from both content doors and suits kids. Keep true Boggle as a B2/Stüdyo option only, with 'unique double' restricted to words at or below the group band plus one.

Oyun Parkı audio: use recorded English letter NAMES, with the whole-word pronunciation at the end, instead of isolated phonemes. Add a 'tricky letters' focus (e/i, a/e, g/j, i/y) that Turkish kids mix up, with a visual mouth cue. Offer phonemes only for a curated CVC word set (cat, dog, sun) where they are regular.

Replace the open ELEPHANT brainstorm for A1T/A2T with a guided find. The engine shows 4-6 hidden target words as picture slots (pen, hen, ant, hat...), the class hunts for them, and each found picture fills a slot and adds a jar sticker. This works for weak readers because the pictures carry the meaning.

Reduce teacher typing. Teams show boards, and the teacher only enters the top claim per round ('Longest board?'). Or the teacher taps the letters from the pool, since the engine knows the pool (tap tiles instead of typing), with autocomplete limited to words the pool can build. Cap Mode 1 at 4 teams, or use a whole-class tally for 5-6 teams.
Hide the joker and the tie-break rule below B1 and in all young-learner skins. Keep them for Stüdyo B1-B2 only.

Use riddle items as the conundrum and anagram clue ladder (picture, then riddle, then defEasy, then TR). Use category-list to seed a themed grid or pool. Specify how the LLM output maps to these so the teacher-prompt door is real. Pre-compute solutions at pack build and show the teacher any common words missing from the bank before play, with a one-tap whitelist, so no word is rejected live.

Promote Mode 3 ('Karışık Harfler' with the clue ladder) to the default mode for every group except B1-B2 adults, and cross-link it with Hangman so the two spelling games do not duplicate skins and rules. If the suite needs trimming, merge the anagram mode into the Hangman family and keep Harf Havuzu as the adult 'Bir Kelime tarzı' quiz-night round.

issues: It is three games under one name. Bir Kelime letters, a Boggle grid and an anagram with a clue ladder each need their own generator, input flow, scoring and results screen. Called 'M' it is really L, and the Boggle mode carries most of the risk.

The dictionary is too small to judge fairly. Oxford 3000/5000 plus C1/C2 is about 6-7k lemmas, while adult teams will produce valid words outside it (tan, rein, stead, ore, lint). Each 'not a word' ruling in front of the class damages trust, so 'accept anyway' ends up as the main path rather than a fallback.

A runtime inflection generator is fragile: doubling (stop→stopped, but not visit→visitted), y→ies/ied, silent-e, irregulars, and comparatives like 'bigger'. It will both over-accept (runned) and under-accept.

Seeding and the captain's calls contradict each other. If the pool must contain a pack word, the captain's vowel/consonant choices are either fake or can break the seed. For example, 'elephant' needs 3 vowels and 5 consonants in exactly those counts, so a captain calling 6 consonants makes the seed impossible.

Many pack items can't be used as seeds: phrasal verbs, idioms, chunks, collocations, hyphenated words and anything over 9 letters. A theme like 'Travel phrases' generated by the LLM may leave zero usable seeds.

Boggle validation doesn't scale. Six teams writing 10-20 words each means the teacher enters 60-120 words, and the 'unique word doubles' rule needs all of them entered. That is 5+ minutes of dead classroom time per 2-minute round.
Placing N topic words on paths in a 4x4 grid needs a backtracking placer with retries and a fallback. It is solvable, but it is a testing burden on top of Qu handling and path validation.

Kids-mode audio needs recorded assets. Letter names and especially phonics sounds cannot come from speechSynthesis: TTS reads 'a' as the article and can't produce /æ/ in isolation. That means about 26 letter-name clips plus about 44 phoneme clips, which costs recording time and needs QA.
Kids mode requires a picture for every word, but LLM content and built-in categories have no guaranteed images. Abstract topic words have no picture at all, and the checklist fails without one.

Letter-name confusion with Turkish: children spell aloud with Turkish letter values (e as /e/, i as /i/, a as /a/). A whole-class spelling chorus reinforces the wrong names unless the audio models them.

Much of it overlaps with other candidates: the anagram with a clue ladder duplicates Kelime Oyunu (letter-reveal clue-answer) and Hangman, both of which also practise spelling pack words. The Bir Kelime letters mode is the part that is actually new: open-ended word production from constraints.

Offensive words: the blocklist can filter displayed solutions and 'best word', but students will still say rude words that the pool allows. The teacher needs a silent 'hide' key, and the pool generator should reject pools whose solutions include blocklisted words in Genç groups.
Adult A1 can't do much with 7-9 random letters (the longest words are 3-4 letters), so rounds feel flat. Level tuning only changes bonuses, not how solvable the pool is.
The adult flow has a dead step: teams wait while the teacher types two letters and picks from autocomplete for each team. Pleasant at 3 teams, slow at 6.
fixes: Scope v1 to two modes: 'Harf Havuzu' (letters) for Stüdyo and Arena, and 'Harf Çorbası' (picture anagram plus whole-class 'how many words from X') for Oyun Parkı. Put Boggle/Grid Raid in v2 behind a flag, or cut it.

Precompute a validation list at build time instead of at runtime: a curated ~40-60k common-English list (SCOWL size 35-50, or ENABLE filtered by frequency) with inflections already included. Minus the blocklist and proper nouns, it ships as a lazily loaded ~150-250 KB gz JSON loaded only by this game. Use words.js only to decorate matches with the level badge, Turkish meaning and IPA. Drop the runtime inflection generator.

Make validation three-tier: 'Bank word' (has a badge and a TR meaning), 'Valid English' (in the big list, no badge, full points) and 'Teacher accepted' (saved to accepted-answer memory per class profile). Show which tier applied so a ruling never looks arbitrary.

Fix seeding: pick the seed first (4-7 letters for A1-A2, up to 9 for B1-B2), then set the captain's call sequence so it matches the seed's vowel/consonant counts and fill the remaining slots randomly. Or pre-flip the seed's letters shuffled and let the captain call only the extra tiles. Show 'Konu harfleri gizli' so the ownership stays honest.

Filter seeds: keep single tokens matching /^[a-z]{3,9}$/ and drop multiword, hyphenated and proper-noun items. Ask the LLM prompt for single words with a length range and validate each against the big list. If fewer than 6 seeds survive, top up from the words.js band for that topic, or show 'Bu konu harf oyununa uygun değil'.

Guarantee pool quality in code: reject and redraw any pool whose best word at the group's level is shorter than a target (A1 ≥ 5, B2 ≥ 7) or that has fewer than 8 solutions. Generation runs in under 10 ms, so up to 200 retries cost nothing.

Speed up adult input: autocomplete only from words the pool can make, and a 'same as' chip for duplicate answers across teams. Add an optional 'one word per team, reveal in order from shortest' flow so the table reads as suspense instead of admin.

If Boggle is kept, make it a whole-class hunt with no per-team lists. Students call out a word, the teacher (or a student at the smartboard) traces its path on the grid by drag, and it lights up in the calling team's colour. First team to call a word claims it. Drop the 'unique doubles' rule.

Kids audio: record 26 letter names (English) and only the ~26 single-letter default phonics sounds, as short Opus/MP3 clips of about 5 KB each. Play the word itself from a recording or neural TTS. Budget one recording session and QA it.

Kids pictures: allow only words that have an image in a curated icon/emoji map (about 600 concrete nouns and verbs). In Oyun Parkı, filter LLM and category content to imageable words and show the teacher a 'resimsiz kelimeler atlandı' notice.
Differentiate from Hangman and Kelime Oyunu: drop the adult anagram 'clue ladder' mode (Kelime Oyunu covers it) and keep only the final 9-letter conundrum as a round type inside Harf Havuzu.

Polish list (the minimum for it to feel like a proper game): tile flip with a WebAudio marimba pitched by slot, a letter bag weighted by English frequency, a ticking loop, a board-reveal sequence that sorts answers by length with the table scores popping, a 'Did you see this?' reveal animating the best word's tiles into place, a Kaçırılanlar screen, and team colours. All of it is synthesisable except the font; no art assets beyond icons.
Input normalisation: fold ı/İ/ş/ğ/ü/ö/ç to ASCII, trim spaces, lowercase. Near-miss detection by Levenshtein 1 against the big list feeds the Hata defteri.
Nazik and Genç safety: regenerate any pool whose solution set intersects the blocklist, and give the teacher a hide key that removes a word from the screen without comment.

catalog.rankReason: The Bir Kelime letters round (adult 7.7, kids 5.7). It needs a 40-60k validation list and an 'Anlamı?' meaning gate so it tests the topic rather than general word breadth. Later, with two modes (Harf Havuzu, and Harf Çorbası for kids); Boggle is cut.

catalog.name: Sınıfı Dolaş (Find Someone Who, Find Your Partner & Card Swap)
catalog.familiarAs: Find Someone Who / human bingo, mingle 'find your partner' cards, Go Fish-style 'Do you have...?' card swap
catalog.oneLiner: Every student holds a printed card and asks classmates questions in English to find the person who matches, fill a grid, or complete a set; the screen runs the timer, the question frames, pair checks and the debrief.
catalog.howItPlays: MODE 1 'Eşini Bul' (mingle match): the engine prints exactly as many card halves as there are students (odd numbers get a teacher card). Halves are pair items: picture/word, word/definition, question/answer, sentence halves, present/past, idiom/meaning. The one rule is never to show your card: ask and answer instead ('Have you got something you wear on your head?'). Matched pairs stand together. The teacher types the two tiny card codes, the screen confirms, and each pair reads out its match. The pairs then become the teams for the next game (team-maker hook). MODE 2 'Kimde Var?' (Find someone who): a printable grid (3x3 for kids, 4x4 for adults) of 'Find someone who can swim / has been to Ankara'. Genç groups use fictional role cards by default for privacy. A student needs a follow-up answer before writing a name. A line counts as 'Bingo!'. In the debrief the teacher taps hand counts per square, which gives a class chart and report sentences ('Twelve of us can swim') and can feed c21. MODE 3 'Takas' (seated, groups of 4): collect sets of four (for example 4 animals from one habitat) by asking 'Do you have a...?'. It is calm and works at fixed desks.
catalog.playerSetup: Whole class at once (up to 40). 'Row mingle' means asking only your row and the row behind, for fixed desks. Mode 3 runs in groups of 4.
catalog.adultVersion: Stüdyo 'Networking Mixer' is the first-day icebreaker for a course. Students get fictional business profiles (character items: 'Find the person who works in İzmir and needs a supplier'), or real but safe 'Find someone who has ever...' prompts. A follow-up question is required before a name counts. B2 adds a needs/haves negotiation mingle: each person trades to fulfil a need. There are no scores, so it suits adults who dislike competition. The debrief asks 'What surprised you?'.
catalog.teenVersion: OYUN PARKI 'Find Your Friend!' has three rules: ask, answer, find your friend. A1T uses identical picture pairs ('Have you got a panda?' 'Yes, I have! / No, I haven't.'), and Gogo models the frame on screen. In the seated option, cards pass along the rows. Everyone ends up with a friend, nobody is left out, and there are no scores. ARENA 'Duo Hunt / Squad Draft' shows a timer and a counter of duos found. The Find Someone Who prompts suit this age (has a game high score, can do a handstand, has been to Kapadokya). The resulting duos become the squads for the next Challenge, which gives the students ownership.
catalog.levelTuning: A1T: identical picture pairs, 'Have you got...?'. A2T: picture/word, 'Do you like...?' and 'Can you...?'. B1T: sentence halves, question/answer, 'Have you ever...?'. B2T: word/definition, idiom/meaning, a follow-up question required. A1: personal information on fictional ID cards ('How do you spell it?'). A2: routines and last weekend (fictional). B1: present perfect experiences, collocation halves. B2: needs/haves negotiation and paraphrasing definitions without reading them aloud.
catalog.contentShape: Pair items (with the set field for uniqueness) are cut into card halves carrying a hidden 2-character check code. speaking-prompt or survey items with mode 'find-someone' fill the grid, each with followUps[]. character items supply fictional profiles. category-list sets of 4 supply the swap mode. A class-size input drives exact card counts.
catalog.delightDetails: The pair-check codes let the teacher verify a match in 2 s without reading every card. A teacher card covers odd class sizes. The screen keeps the question frame and a 'Say it again, please' repair chip visible. The hand-count debrief turns into a live bar chart and ready-made report sentences. Pairs roll straight into the next game in the lesson playlist.
catalog.teacherControls: Class size, mingle radius (free, row or table), timer, card type, fictional or real prompts, print, check-pair key, debrief counts, whether a follow-up is required.
catalog.risks: Movement in crowded rooms: seated and row-mingle options exist. Noise: the noise meter helps, and the mingle is short. Privacy in 'Find someone who': fictional cards are the default for Genç, and sensitive topics are never used. Social exclusion: random cards decide partners, students never choose. It depends on printing; the fallback is a numbered on-screen list students copy from ('You are number 7: write this word').

reviewVerdicts: age-level: keep-with-changes -> Team Maker / lesson-playlist utility (pairs roll into the next game); c21 survey/chart game for the debrief

issues: It depends on printing and cutting. Many Turkish public-school teachers have no easy printer access, and cutting 28-40 card halves takes 10-15 minutes before the lesson. The fallback (students copy 'You are number 7: write this word') costs 5+ minutes of silent copying in class and gives the whole trick away, because everyone can see the full list on the screen.

Absent students break the pairs. The class size is fixed at print time. On the day, 3 students are missing, so 3 orphan halves circulate, 3 students search forever, and the round never ends. The design only covers odd numbers, not absences.

Verifying pair codes is a bottleneck. With 14 pairs, the teacher types 28 two-character codes on a smart-board on-screen keyboard while standing, about 2-3 minutes of typing while 26 students wait and get loud. At the board the '2 s per pair' claim does not hold.

Dead time at the tail: after about 3 minutes, 22 students are matched and idle while the last 3 pairs search. Matched 10-year-olds get noisy and wander, and the last pairs are usually the weakest or shyest students, now in a public spotlight.

The 'never show your card' rule collapses within 30 seconds with 10-12 year-olds. They flash cards and speak Turkish ('seninki ne?'). Nothing on screen or in the rules makes asking in English necessary rather than just suggested, so the language work quietly disappears.

Row mingle at fixed double desks is only half a solution. Students in the middle of a row cannot reach the row behind without climbing, and any pair split across the room cannot meet under row radius unless the card dealing respects that radius. The engine doesn't know the seating.
The noise meter assumes a microphone. Most FATİH boards and school PCs have none, or the browser mic permission gets blocked, so the headline chaos control is often missing.

Find Someone Who with fictional role cards for Genç groups turns the task into 'find the card that says X', which is really a card search, not a personal question. The 3x3 grid gets done in 2 minutes by strong students, who then dominate by 'helping'. The early finishers have no extension.

Mode 3 'Takas' (Go Fish in groups of 4) means 7 separate printed decks, 7 unmonitored groups and nothing for the screen to do. It is a different game glued on, it adds prep, and the teacher cannot check the English at 7 tables.

The screen's role is thin: a timer, a frame and a debrief. The concept is a print-kit generator more than one of the 10 'proper' homepage games, so it may disappoint a teacher who expects a showpiece.

Adults: with 10 students the mingle is great once, but Find Someone Who and the Networking Mixer wear out fast in a weekly evening course. The B2 needs/haves negotiation needs careful design, or it stalls with 2-3 people who have nothing to trade.
Stopping at any moment: in Mode 1 there is no natural stop before every pair is found. The planned 'pairs become teams' hook fails if the teacher stops early, because unmatched students have no team.
fixes: Print sheets sorted by pair, with both halves side by side and the pairs numbered in order. The teacher deals from the top of the stack and stops when students run out, so there are never orphan halves. The leftover odd student gets the teacher card. Add a 'Bugün kaç kişi?' step that works without reprinting: print N+4 pairs and skip the extra ones.

Replace code typing with tapping. The screen shows a grid of numbered pair buttons (1-20), each half carries only its pair number in a tiny corner, and the teacher taps number 7 when pair 7 stands up. Better still, let the pair check itself: each half shows the same small colour and shape on the back, flipped only at the end. The screen then does a whole-class 'Show me!' reveal, where all pairs flip together and a random 3 read out their match aloud. That makes one 20-second moment instead of 14 separate checks.

Tail management: when 70% have matched, the screen switches to 'Eşini bulanlar: yardım et!'. Matched pairs must ask one unmatched person a question frame in English, or else get a pair task for matched students (one extra question on the screen for them to discuss). A hard timer ends the round, and any leftovers are paired by the screen so nobody ends up alone.

Make English necessary: at the check, each pair must say a scripted frame aloud ('I've got a ___. She's got a ___.'). A2 and above: pairs whose halves only make sense together (question/answer, sentence halves) must read both halves in order to count. Hide the answer key from the projected screen.

Seating-aware dealing: in row-mingle mode, ask for the number of rows and desks per row, then print the halves so each partner sits within 1 row. Allow a 'pass cards' seated variant, where cards travel along a row every 20 s on a screen cue, as the default for Oyun Parkı in crowded rooms.
Make the noise meter optional and add a no-mic control: a big 'Freeze!' button with a sound and a full-screen hand signal, plus a 3-2-1 reset countdown the teacher can trigger with one tap.

Find Someone Who for Genç: use safe real prompts by default ('can whistle', 'likes pizza', 'has a pet' from a vetted whitelist) and keep fictional cards for sensitive topics only. Each name must come with one follow-up answer written in the square, and a name can be used at most once per grid (anti-domination). Early finishers go on to 'full card' and then 'find a new name for each square'.
Drop Mode 3 'Takas' or spin it off as a separate printable. Keep this game at two modes, Eşini Bul and Kimde Var?, to cut prep and cognitive load.

Laminate-friendly reuse: save every generated card set under a seed or class-profile name so the teacher can reprint the same set, and offer a 'reshuffle pairs, same cards' option so a laminated deck is reused with new partners. For adults, keep a bank of 10+ mixer themes so a weekly course can rotate.

No-printer fallback: each student sees only their own card via a projected QR code or a 'number wheel' reveal ('Row 2, desk 3: look away — now!') instead of the full list, or a phone-free 'teacher reads your word into your ear' mode with the list on the teacher's phone view only.

Position it as a lesson-opener and team-maker utility inside the playlist, not one of the flagship 10 games. Make the handoff robust: if the round is stopped early, the screen auto-assigns the unmatched students to teams.

Pacing defaults: Oyun Parkı runs 3 minutes of mingle and a 1-minute Show me!, 6 minutes total. Stüdyo runs 8-10 minutes with a 'What surprised you?' debrief of 3 prompts. A visible 'stop now' button always leads to a clean debrief with whatever data exists, and the hand-count debrief needs no more than 9 taps.

reviews.mergeWith: Team Maker / lesson-playlist utility (pairs roll into the next game); c21 survey/chart game for the debrief
issues: The screen does little. The language happens on paper and in the room, and the software is a timer, a code checker and a debrief. It does not meet the teacher's 'polished, proper game playable from the homepage' bar. It works better as a lesson-flow tool (warm-up plus team-maker) than as one of the 10 flagship games.

A1 Genç children who barely read cannot do Mode 2. A text grid like 'Find someone who can swim / has been to Ankara' needs reading and writing names in Latin script under time pressure. A 3x3 grid is still 9 text prompts. The level tuning makes pictures a card-type option for Mode 1 only, not for the Mode 2 grid.

The A1T identical picture pairs ('Have you got a panda?') are only a naming drill. 9-year-olds will simply show their cards, and the 'never show your card' rule can't be enforced once they are mingling. The language work drops to near zero while the activity still looks successful.

Row mingle conflicts with random pairing. If halves are dealt at random, a student's partner is often outside the allowed radius (their own row and the row behind), so the mode cannot finish. The design does not say how card distribution matches the seating.

Checking every pair by typing both 2-character codes is slow in a 40-student Turkish state class: 20 pairs × 2 codes arrive in a burst at the end, with a queue and noise. The design also says 'each pair reads out its match', which duplicates the check and takes about 5 minutes.

Pairs from LLM prompts risk ambiguous matches. Two definitions can fit one word, sentence halves can combine several ways, and present/past pairs can be matched by form alone. One ambiguous pair in a 40-card mingle breaks the whole activity, and there is no uniqueness check beyond a 'set' field.

Fictional role cards as the default for Genç turn 'Find someone who' into reading a line off a card. That removes the real curiosity which makes the activity motivating for 12-14 year-olds, and they notice. Privacy is solved at the cost of authentic communication.

LLM-made 'real' prompts drift into unsafe or non-universal territory (family, religion, money, travel abroad, having a pet or a phone), which can expose low-income students. 'Has been to Kapadokya' and 'has a game high score' already rank students by privilege.

Nothing controls the mingle language. In a crowded room, Turkish takes over within 30 seconds. The single visible question frame helps A1-A2 but does nothing for the B1/B2 follow-up question requirement, which the teacher cannot check across 40 students.

B2 needs/haves negotiation and 'paraphrase without reading aloud' are strong production tasks. Everything below B1 is mostly formulaic Q/A, so production barely scales across A1-A2 beyond swapping the frame.

Mode 3 'Takas' (Go Fish with category-list sets of 4) is a different game with its own dealing logic and turn rules. It makes the kids' ruleset harder to explain (3 modes, each with its own rules) and wants its own set-uniqueness validation.

The printing dependency is real for Turkish public schools, where same-day printing is often impossible. The fallback of copying 'You are number 7: write this word' from a 40-line screen list is slow and error-prone for A1T/A2T, and it exposes all the answers on the projector.
Oyun Parkı says 'nobody is left out', but in a mingle, shy or low-status children end up last. The 'duos found' counter in Arena makes the last pair visibly lose.
fixes: Reposition the game as 'Sınıfı Dolaş: warm-up + team-maker' inside the lesson playlist, or merge its team-making role into a shared Team Maker utility. Don't count it as one of the core 10 unless the screen gains a real game layer, such as a live 'pairs found' constellation where each confirmed pair lights a star and together they reveal a picture.

Give Oyun Parkı a picture-only Mode 2: a 3x3 grid of icons (swim, bike, cat, pizza) with the question frame read aloud by audio. Students tick and draw a smiley or write the classmate's number instead of their name. A1T gets 2x2 or 3x3 with at most 1 frame ('Can you...?').

For A1T, drop identical pairs. Use 'information-gap' pairs where the two halves differ but match on one feature (a panda with a red hat / a word card 'red hat'), or split pictures (the top and bottom halves of one animal), so the question carries meaning and showing the card doesn't solve it.

Make the dealing seat-aware. The teacher enters rows × seats (or picks a layout), and the engine prints cards in seating order so that each partner is inside the chosen radius. Each card carries a small seat index for dealing, not for matching.

Replace per-code typing with a group reveal. Every pair shares a hidden matching symbol under a fold line, and pairs unfold together when the teacher calls 'Check!'. The screen shows only the colour/shape legend and a pair counter the teacher taps. Keep optional code entry for disputes, and require only 3-4 random pairs to read aloud, chosen by the screen.

Add a pair validator for LLM and built-in content: reject pair sets where a left half plausibly matches more than one right half (a second LLM pass or an embedding-similarity check), keep a word-band check against words.js per level, and show a 'possible duplicate' warning before printing. Cap card types per level (no sentence halves below A2).

For Genç, default to a curated 'safe real' prompt whitelist (can/likes/favourite-type prompts about abilities and preferences, never possessions, travel, family or money) and offer fictional cards as the alternative. Apply the same blocklist to LLM prompts in all groups and remove privilege-ranking examples.

Keep a sticky screen 'language strip' that rotates the target frame, a short-answer model and one repair chip. Add a 30-second 'freeze' mid-mingle where the screen picks a random student to say their last question aloud (spot-check English). For B1+, require the follow-up answer to be written as a 3-4 word note on the grid, so the teacher can verify it.

Make the debrief the production core at every level. A1: the screen shows 'X of us can swim' with a count and the class chants it. A2-B1: pairs report 'Ayşe can ... but she can't ...'. B2: groups write a 2-sentence summary from the bar chart (comparatives, quantifiers: 'most of us', 'hardly anyone').
Cut Mode 3 from the kids' ruleset, or ship it as its own seated micro-game. Oyun Parkı should expose one mode per session, with pictogram rules (ask, answer, find).

Offer a no-print fallback: the screen shows only a big card number while the teacher whispers or points, or the teacher uses a reusable laminated card set that the system saves per topic. The printable should be an A4 cut-sheet at 8 or 12 cards per page with large icons.

Remove the duo counter in Arena, or show only the class total. When 80% are paired, the screen switches to a 'help mode': remaining students raise their cards and the class helps with questions, so there is no visible last pair.
Tie the time and card count to level: A1T at most 6 min with pictures and 1 frame; B2 adults up to 15 min with negotiation. Add a class-size input guard that suggests seated mode above 30.

issues: It isn't really a screen game. About 90% of the play happens on printed paper. The projector shows a timer, a question frame and a chart. Next to Hangman, the board game or the RPG it will feel like a worksheet generator with a stopwatch. It overlaps the Material Maker (printable cards) more than any other game in the suite, so it doesn't count cleanly toward 'at least 10 proper games'.

Printing is a hard dependency, and many Turkish state schools have no printer in the classroom. The teacher also spends 5-10 minutes cutting per class. The proposed fallback ('You are number 7: write this word' on a shared screen) shows every card to everyone. In Eşini Bul that ruins the 'never show your card' mechanic, because students can match from memory.

The pair-check flow is slower than claimed. With 36 students there are 18 pairs, and typing 36 two-character codes on a smartboard keyboard takes well over 2 s each. The teacher becomes the bottleneck while the rest of the class waits.

Absences break exact card counts. Cards printed the night before for 32 students no longer fit when 3 are absent: orphan halves appear and one student can't find a partner. The design only covers class sizes that are known and odd.

Ambiguity is the main LLM risk. Mingle clues must match exactly one card: 'Something you wear on your head' fits both hat and cap, and 'Have you got an animal that lives in the sea?' fits two cards. Sentence halves often recombine grammatically ('I have lived here / since 2010' vs '/ for two years'). The generator cannot see cross-pair collisions without a set-level check.

The A1T/A2T picture pairs need a large picture library that doesn't exist. words.js has no images. Emoji rendering differs between the projector PC and the printer, and some emoji are culturally off or too small when printed.

Mode 3 'Takas' (Go Fish) is a third ruleset. It needs sets of 4 per group, more cutting and more rules, and adds little the other modes don't already give. This is scope creep for an S-size build and it dilutes the polish.

Find Someone Who with real prompts has privacy and sensitivity edge cases: family, money, travel abroad, pets, religious holidays and health all expose socio-economic differences. An LLM given a free Turkish prompt will produce these ('has been abroad', 'has a PlayStation').
The noise meter needs microphone permission. School PCs often have no mic or block the permission, so it can't be a core feature.

Mingling 40 children aged 9-11 in rows of fixed desks turns chaotic quickly. The design does include row mingle, but the screen does nothing to structure the movement: there are no rounds, no freeze signal and no visual of who should ask whom.
'Whole-class response every turn' (from the kids checklist) is vague here, because there are no turns. The pass/fail against that checklist has to be defined for a mingle format.
fixes: Make pair checks self-verifying instead of typed. Print both halves of a pair with the same shape and colour glyph (★ blue, ▲ red, ...) on a fold-under flap or on the back, and pairs flip to confirm. The teacher then taps one big '+1 çift' button, and the screen counter and celebration run from that. Keep typed codes only as an optional dispute tool.

Add absence-proof printing. Number the pairs in priority order (1A/1B ... 18A/18B) and print a 'Bugün kaç kişi?' strip. At the start the teacher enters today's headcount and the screen says 'Remove pairs 17 and 18'. For an odd count, the teacher takes a named 'Öğretmen kartı'. Two spare pairs are always printed.

Replace the leaky no-print fallback with a 'Gizli Ajan' reveal ritual. Everyone closes their eyes, the screen calls 'Number 7, open your eyes!' and flashes that card for 3 s, then the next. Kids love it, it keeps the cards secret, and it needs no printer. Also offer 'copy on a slip' only for Mode 2, where secrecy doesn't matter.

Add a set-level validator after LLM generation. It dedupes lemmas and headwords and rejects near-synonyms using words.js (same definition head, same category tag). For clue-to-card items it runs a second cheap LLM pass that answers 'which cards could this clue match?' and rejects the set if any clue matches more than one card. For sentence halves it checks every cross-combination with that judge pass. It prefers curated built-in packs for A1T/A2T.

Start with a curated icon set of about 150-200 self-hosted SVGs (animals, food, clothes, school, family, jobs, places) plus OpenMoji SVGs with credited licences, instead of system emoji. Only allow picture modes for words that have an icon, and fall back to word/word pairs otherwise.
Drop Mode 3 'Takas' from v1. Park it as a later variant, or move it into the Memory/Match game, where sets already exist. That leaves two modes done well.

Strengthen the screen layer so it feels like a game. Run the mingle in 90-second rounds with music and a big 'FREEZE!' stop signal (a clap icon plus a sound). Keep the question frame and the 'Say it again, please' / 'How do you spell it?' repair chips on screen at all times. Add a live 'pairs found' constellation where each pair lights up a star, with the class goal 'Light up the sky!'. In Arena show a duo counter against the clock. Finish with a reveal animation that turns the pairs into team cards for the next game (a hand-off to the team-maker).

Make the Mode 2 debrief a proper payoff. Use big +/- steppers per square for smartboard input, a live bar chart, and rule-based report sentences using quantifiers keyed to level (A1: 'Twelve students can swim'; B1: 'Most of us have...', 'Hardly anyone...'). Export to the class profile or c21 without any names.

Hard-code a sensitivity blocklist for Find Someone Who: no money, possessions, travel abroad, family structure, religion, health, body or appearance. Apply it to both LLM output and teacher-typed prompts. Genç groups default to fictional role cards, and 'real' mode is Stüdyo-only unless the teacher overrides it.
Make the noise meter an optional progressive enhancement. It is hidden unless getUserMedia succeeds, and a manual teacher 'Sessiz!' button always exists.

Print from a print-CSS A4 layout: 12 cards per page, dashed cut lines, card numbers in the corner, and the kids and adult skins in greyscale-friendly ink (light fills, heavy outlines) to spare school printers. Add a one-page teacher key listing the pairs, the glyphs and the removal order.

Rewrite the kids checklist for this format. Define the whole-class response moment as a round-end chant (after FREEZE the class reads the frame together). No one is left out, because the teacher card and the pair-removal order guarantee a partner for everyone.
Position it honestly in the suite as a warm-up and team-maker ('Isınma' shelf) that feeds the other games. Don't count it as one of the 10 flagship games unless the screen layer above is built.

catalog.rankReason: Find Someone Who / mingle: valuable teaching, but the screen does little and it depends on printing. Keep it as a printable warm-up and team-maker utility that takes Tanışma Tombala from c16. It needs absence-proof pair printing, tap-to-confirm pair numbers, and picture grids for kids.

catalog.name: Kulaktan Kulağa (Whisper Chain, Paper Telephone & Dictogloss)
catalog.familiarAs: Kulaktan kulağa / Chinese whispers / Telephone, Gartic Phone-style paper chain (write-draw-write), Dictogloss
catalog.oneLiner: A sentence travels down each desk row by whisper, or by write-draw-write on folded paper, and the screen shows word by word how much of it survived; a dictogloss mode rebuilds a short text heard twice.
catalog.howItPlays: MODE A 'Fısıltı Zinciri' (rows are teams): (1) Seeding happens with no phones. Either the screen shows 'Row starters look now; everyone else heads down' for 5 s (answer-leak guard), or the teacher hands out printed, numbered, folded seed slips, or the seed appears on the teacher's Kumanda. Each row gets a different sentence of equal length and target. (2) Each student whispers once down the row. A row may spend one 'Say again' token. (3) The last student writes the sentence on a mini-whiteboard; A1T students point to one of four pictures on screen instead. (4) Reveal: the teacher taps the arrived words from chips. The engine aligns them with the original and colours words kept, changed or lost. Points go to kept content words, plus a bonus if the target structure survived (third-person -s, a past form). A 'Plot twist of the day' prize celebrates the funniest drift. (5) The class says the original sentence together. MODE B 'Kâğıt Telefon' (age 12 and up, adults): printable strips. Student 1 writes a sentence from a prompt in the target grammar and folds it. Student 2 draws it and folds so only the drawing shows. Student 3 describes the drawing in writing, and so on. The screen runs 45-60 s step timers and calls 'Pass!'. At the reveal, rows read their chains aloud, the class votes for the most surprising chain, and the teacher ticks target use. MODE C 'Yeniden Kur' (dictogloss, B groups): TTS or the teacher reads a 40-140 word text twice. Students jot key words, then teams rebuild the text in 6 minutes. The reveal highlights the idea units (from the text's sentences[] and content words) and the target structures each team got.
catalog.playerSetup: Mode A: desk rows as teams (4-8 rows of 4-6), which fits fixed-desk classrooms. Mode B: groups of 4-6. Mode C: groups of 3-4. All teams play at the same time.
catalog.adultVersion: Stüdyo uses the whisper chain as a 5-minute warmer built on drift traps: numbers (thirteen/thirty, fifteen/fifty), names, and minimal-pair words. The reveal links each drift to a sound item and its mouth tip. Dictogloss is the main adult mode, with news-style anecdotes at level; its reveal feeds missed structures into Kaçırılanlar. Paper Telephone with neutral prompts works as an icebreaker for new courses. There are no penalties, and the game is calm and quiet by design.
catalog.teenVersion: OYUN PARKI 'Gogo's Secret' has three rules, all shown as pictograms: whisper once, pass it on, the last friend points to the picture. Seeds are 2-4 word picture phrases ('a big red ball'). The last student chooses among four pictures that differ in one detail (red/blue, on/under), so nobody writes. Every row gets a sticker for trying and an extra one for a match. Gogo says the original, and the whole class repeats it twice: a whole-class moment, no elimination, no scores below zero. ARENA 'Signal Relay': squads 'transmit a code' of 6-12 words with a built-in twist (a number, a name, a past form), and the reveal shows 'Signal integrity %'. The 'Draw & Guess Chain' is the highlight for this age, because the Gartic-style format is familiar to them. Stats: Most words saved, Best glow-up.
catalog.levelTuning: A1T: 2-4 word picture phrases, answered by pointing. A2T: 5-8 words, answered by writing with a word bank. B1T: 8-12 words with one target structure, written. B2T: 12-16 words with two clauses, plus Paper Telephone. A1 adults: 5-7 words carrying numbers, times and names (practical listening). A2: 8-10 words. B1: 12-15 words, dictogloss of about 60 words. B2: dictogloss of 100-140 words with 3 target structures and idea-unit scoring.
catalog.sessionMinutes: 5-8 (whisper warmer); 15-20 (Paper Telephone or dictogloss)
catalog.contentShape: Seed sentences come from vocab.example, gap text with the answer filled in, or order tokens joined, and are balanced per row by length, word level and target. Kids' final choices use 4 picture options that differ in one attribute (an mcq with fmt 'picture'). Dictogloss uses a text item (sentences[] and words computed) plus target tags. Printable seed slips and fold strips are generated per row.
catalog.delightDetails: The reveal animates lost words dropping out and replacements sliding in. Drift traps (numbers, names) are planted on purpose and explained afterwards. A 'Say again' token per row adds strategy. The noise meter shows 'whisper level', so this is a game that rewards quiet. At the end, TTS plays the original and the drifted version back to back. The printables carry row numbers and fold lines.
catalog.teacherControls: Seed delivery (screen peek, printed slips or Kumanda), sentence length and target, number of repeats, final answer mode (point, write or say), dictogloss speed and number of readings, TTS or Öğretmen okur, a key to accept a variant.
catalog.risks: Whispering into ears can feel uncomfortable or unhygienic, so allow a hand-cupped whisper or a written pass. Some students distort the sentence on purpose; scoring by kept words rewards accuracy. The seed can leak when projected, so use printables or the peek screen. Dictogloss is too heavy below B1T. Students with hearing impairments should use the paper modes.
sources: C:/lg/docs/classroom-games-roadmap.md G04 (Dikteyle yeniden kurma), dropped from the clusters

issues: Three games in one card. Mode A (whisper), Mode B (paper telephone) and Mode C (dictogloss) each have different setup, timing, grouping and prep. The teacher faces a mode menu before the class even starts, and Mode C is a well-known teaching technique rather than a game; the screen adds little to it beyond a timer and the highlighted reveal.

Reveal bottleneck (28 kids, 6-7 rows). Having the teacher 'tap the arrived words from chips' means rebuilding each row's sentence word by word from a chip pool. At about 30-60 s per row, that is 4-6 minutes of the teacher's back to the class, and the 25 students who are not on stage lose focus exactly then. This is the biggest source of dead time and chaos.

Low active ratio in the whisper phase. Only one student per row is active at any moment. With 5-6 per row, each student is 'on' for about 10 s out of a 60-90 s chain. Everyone else talks, turns around to listen in, or leaks the sentence. The pitch that 'all teams play at the same time' hides the fact that most individuals are idle.

Seed leak on a smart board. 'Row starters look, everyone else heads down' for 5 s does not hold up with 10-12 year-olds; someone always peeks. Printed slips cost prep time and printer access, which is often missing in public schools. The Kumanda option makes the teacher walk to each row starter, so 6-7 trips.

Noise escalates. Seven rows whispering at once in a 28-student room quickly becomes loud talking, because students must raise their voice over their neighbours. A 'whisper level' noise meter punishes the whole room for a volume that parallel play itself causes, and noise meters on a smart-board mic are unreliable.

Fairness and one weak link. A single weak or mischievous student in the chain decides the whole row's score, and fixed desk rows mean the same weak link breaks the same row every round. Deliberate sabotage is common at 10-12, and 'scoring by kept words' does not deter a saboteur who does not care about points. It also shames the student where the chain broke, since everyone can trace it.
Row sizes are unequal in real classrooms (e.g. rows of 4, 5 and 6 when two kids are absent). Longer chains drift more, so scores are not comparable, and the design gives no length normalisation.

The Oyun Parkı pointing end is a guess. With four pictures that differ in one detail, even a totally garbled whisper leaves a 25% chance, and rows with nothing left still 'match'. The whisper stops mattering. Also, with every row pointing at the same projected four pictures, rows copy each other.

Mode B's paper chain needs strips printed per row, folding instructions and 45-60 s step timers. For 10-12 year-olds, the drawing steps run long (they keep drawing), 'Pass!' causes chaos, and strips get lost or torn. Arena 'Draw & Guess Chain' is the most fun part, but it is also the most logistics-heavy, and it assumes 12+ (the target class is 10-12).

Adult evening course of 10: whisper chains of 5 are fine, but adults find whispering into each other's ears awkward (and it is a hygiene issue). The 'hand-cupped' option does not really solve that, so many will want the written pass, which is slow and turns the game into dictation. Two teams of 5 give only two reveals, which is short and thin.

Dictogloss timing: two readings, note-taking and 6 minutes of rebuilding make about 12-15 minutes before any feedback. For the idea-unit reveal, the teacher must enter each team's reconstructed text, or the screen has nothing to compare against. That input step is not designed and is impossible on one screen without typing each team's paragraph.
Stopping at any moment: a chain half-way down a row has no graceful stop. Paper mode left mid-cycle loses the reveal, which is the payoff. The design has no 'end now, reveal what we have' path.
Replayability is fine for 2-3 rounds but then drops, because the same row order and the same last student get the same outcome. Round 2 is predictable unless positions rotate.
fixes: Split the scope. Ship Mode A 'Fısıltı Zinciri' plus a lightweight Draw-chain as this game. Move dictogloss (Mode C) into a separate listening/reading tool, or into Kaçırılanlar/Material Maker, instead of making it a game mode.

Replace chip-building with tap-to-toggle on the original. The screen shows the original sentence as big word tiles. The last student says the arrived sentence out loud, and the teacher taps only the words that were LOST or CHANGED (one tap cycles kept, changed, lost). Target: under 15 s per row, done from a phone Kumanda so the teacher faces the class.
Make the reveal a whole-class moment. Before each row's reveal, everyone else votes by hand ('How many words survived? 3, 5 or all?') or predicts the original, so the 20+ spectators have a job.

Stagger or rotate to raise the active ratio. Run two short sentences at the same time, one travelling front-to-back and one back-to-front (they cross mid-row), or have every student in the row whisper at once in pairs down the chain (pair-relay). After each round, rotate who starts and who finishes (the last student becomes the starter), so the weak link moves and no one is always the one who 'broke' it.

Seed delivery without leakage: the default for children is a 'Kumanda peek'. The row starters walk to the teacher's phone or the board one at a time while a full-screen cover (a countdown with a mascot) plays for the others. Or the board shows the seed as a PICTURE only, and each starter builds the phrase themselves (the picture is safe to show). Keep printables optional.

Normalise for chain length: the score is kept words times a length factor (e.g. rows of 4 aim for 100%, rows of 6 get 1.2x). Or better, publish no inter-row ranking for kids; show only each row's own 'signal integrity' against its previous round (self-improvement).

Deter sabotage by rewarding the chain, not the individual. Add a 'Reverse check': after the reveal, the last student whispers back up the chain. Also have a teacher 'mulligan' key that silently voids a round, and never show which position broke.

Kids' ending: pick the four picture options so that at least two slots test the whisper (e.g. colour AND preposition in 2x2 combos), which makes guessing 25% but a partial match visibly partial. Let each row point on its own at once on a 3-2-1 signal (fingers 1-4), so rows cannot copy.
Noise: drop the mic noise meter, or make it cosmetic only. Instead, use a 'library voice' pictogram and a teacher-held 'Shh' key that freezes timers.

Add a 'Bitir ve göster' key that ends any phase at once and reveals whatever exists (for paper mode, it jumps to the reading-aloud of partial chains). Show a visible total-time bar with a hard cap (8 min whisper / 15 min draw).

Adults: offer a 'written whisper' by default (a sticky note with 3-second viewing, passed along) and treat whispering as optional. Use drift traps (numbers, names, minimal pairs) as the core and tie each lost word to the pronunciation tip. It works well with 10 people as two chains plus a crossover round.

Draw-chain for 10-12: cap the chain at 4 steps (write, draw, write, draw), 40 s per step with a visible 10 s warning, and use a single A4 folded in four with printed fold lines (one sheet per row). No strips.
Include a one-screen pictogram rule card (3 rules for Oyun Parkı) that stays visible, and a 20-second demo round with the teacher and front row before scoring starts.

issues: Mode A gives each student very little language. In a row of 6, each student hears and repeats one sentence once, which is about 5 seconds of L2 per round. The other rows wait, and 4 of the 6 students in a row are idle most of the time. This is the classic weakness of telephone as an ESL activity: it is fun, but thin on learning.

The A1 teen seeding assumes the row starter can read the phrase from the peek screen or a slip. Many A1 children aged 9-10 cannot decode 'a big red ball' reliably, so the first link already drifts on reading, not listening. The starter also has no model pronunciation, so a wrong form travels down the row.

Whispering is low-fidelity input by nature. Weak rows can reinforce mispronunciations, and the design only corrects this at the reveal. There is no step where the last student says the sentence aloud before the reveal, so speaking production is close to zero.
The 'Plot twist of the day' prize for the funniest drift contradicts the kept-word scoring. Children of 9-13 will distort on purpose to win the funny prize, especially in Arena.

The reveal does not scale. With 6-8 rows, the teacher taps the arrived words from chips for every row and reads each mini-whiteboard. That can take 3-5 minutes of the whole class waiting, which breaks the 5-8 minute warmer claim and loses kids' attention.

The A1T picture options that differ in one attribute (red/blue, on/under) need a composable illustration system. An LLM prompt cannot produce these pictures, and vocab.example cannot either. As written, the teacher's free-text path does not work for A1T and A2T.

Seed sentences taken from vocab.example (Oxford) are uneven. They carry off-level words, odd register and different lengths, so 'balanced per row by length, word level and target' is unrealistic without an LLM rewrite plus a level check against words.js bands.

In crowded Turkish classes (30-40 students, fixed desks), simultaneous whispering leaks between rows, and kids fall back to Turkish or mouthing. The 'whisper level' noise meter cannot tell which row is loud.
B2 adults find Mode A trivial and a bit childish. Only the drift-trap warmer (thirteen/thirty) and the dictogloss carry them. A1 adults at 5-7 words with numbers and times fit well.

Dictogloss is a different activity: listening, note-taking and group text reconstruction. Bundled with telephone games, it makes the scope three games, not size M. Idea-unit scoring by the teacher for 8 groups is heavy unless the engine does the matching.

In Paper Telephone, A2 teens and A1-A2 adults cannot write a description of a drawing freely in 45-60 s, so the chain collapses into Turkish or single words. Drawing steps also eat time that produces no language.

The kids checklist is mostly met: 3 rules, stickers, a whole-class repeat, no negatives. But ear-whispering for hygiene and personal space, and hearing-impaired students, are only handled as a side note.
fixes: Make an audio-first seed the default for Oyun Parkı and A-levels. The row starter sees a picture and hears TTS once through the teacher device, or the teacher says it quietly. Reading the seed becomes optional. The pupil then passes on a modelled pronunciation.

Build seeds from a constrained template grammar per level (A1T: [size] [colour] [noun] [prep] [place]; A2: subject + verb-s + object + time) with composable SVG sprites or icons. The LLM fills the slots with whitelisted words from words.js bands, and the engine generates the 4 one-attribute-different picture options. The teacher's free-text prompt then works for kids too.

Add a 'Say it!' step: before the reveal, the last student of each row says the sentence aloud to the class. The whole class then chorally repeats the original. This turns every round into production plus a whole-class moment.

Default the reveal to one tap per row: 4-option chips built from the original plus 3 engine-made drift distractors (a changed number, a dropped -s, a swapped noun). Keep word-by-word chip alignment as an optional 'detailed reveal' for a single spotlight row.

Cut the idle time: run two staggered sentences per row (from the front and from the back). Or give waiting students a 'detective' job: they hold picture cards and point when their row's sentence mentions them.
Move the 'funniest drift' prize to Paper Telephone only. In Whisper Chain, reward only accuracy and 'Best save' (a row that recovered a word using its Say-again token).

Use an LLM rewrite pass for seeds (source vocab.example or a gap item, plus the level profile). Pass it through a validator for word cap and CEFR band, and pair rows by exact word count and target tag.

Give Paper Telephone at A2 and low B1 a word bank and sentence frames on the strip ('I can see a ... who is ...'). Cut the draw step to 30 s, and let the teacher pick 'write-write' chains with no drawing for adults.

Split Dictogloss 'Yeniden Kur' into its own listening/writing game (B1T+, B1-B2 adults), or park it as a phase-2 mode. The engine should score idea units automatically from sentences[] by content-word overlap from typed team versions, or from a tick-list the teacher confirms.

For Stüdyo, lead with the 'Drift Traps' pronunciation warmer: minimal pairs, numbers, names, -ed endings, linked to sound items. Frame it as a listening diagnostic, not a party game, so B1-B2 adults don't find it babyish.

Make the hand-cupped or written pass and 'Kâğıt Fısıltı' (pass a folded slip after reading it for 3 s and writing it from memory) first-class options, not risk footnotes. Let the noise meter show a per-row indicator only when the teacher enables it.

issues: This is three games under one name. Whisper chain, write-draw-write and dictogloss have different setups, timings, scoring and reveal screens. Building all three at 'M' size is optimistic: it is closer to L. Shipping all three half-finished breaks the 'proper, polished game' bar.

The screen does very little. During play it is mostly a peek screen and a timer, and the game happens in students' ears and on paper. It only feels like a real game at the reveal, so the reveal carries the whole polish budget. Mode B is a countdown plus 'Pass!' with nothing else to it, and next to Gartic Phone it will feel like a PowerPoint.

The reveal has an input bottleneck. For every row, the teacher reads a mini-whiteboard and taps the arrived words from chips. That means 6-8 rows x 8-15 words on a smartboard, with chips that only hold the original words. Changed words (the whole point of drift) cannot be entered from the original chips, and typing on a smartboard is slow and error-prone. The drift reveal takes 20-40 s per row with a class waiting, and pacing dies.

Some claims go past what the build can do. 'Plot twist of the day', 'Best glow-up' and the funniest-drift prize all need someone to judge them, and it can only be the teacher, which adds taps. 'Signal integrity %' and target-structure-survived detection need a reliable token alignment plus morphology checks (third-person -s, past forms). These are doable with LCS plus lemma rules, but they break on contractions, numbers written as digits or words, and spelling errors on whiteboards.

The noise meter works against the design. All rows whisper at once in a 30-40 student room, so the mic cannot tell rows apart. It also needs a mic permission prompt on school PCs and smartboards, which are often blocked. It adds risk for a gimmick.

The kids' picture choice needs a real art pipeline. It needs four pictures that differ in exactly one attribute (red/blue, on/under, big/small). An LLM cannot make these, and stock clipart will not have controlled variants. Without them the Oyun Parkı version cannot ship.

The kids' whole-class moment comes only at the end of each round. Five students wait while one whispers, then the rest wait again. At 9-11 the middle of a long row goes off-task. The row structure also means one weak or mischievous student ruins the row's result, and the kids' checklist cannot fully cover that.

Adult fit is doubtful. Whispering into a colleague's ear is childish or uncomfortable for many adult Turkish learners, and adults will ask for the written pass. Once that happens it is just a dictation relay. Dictogloss is valuable, but it is a teaching technique, not a party game. As a 'game' it will be judged against the other nine and will feel like a listening exercise.

Mode C overlaps with any reading/listening game in the suite (Reading Detective, text items). Mode B overlaps with the Draw or Act and Draw & Guess mechanics that use taboo-card/character items. Only Mode A is unique.

LLM content risk is moderate. Seeds and dictogloss texts are easy to generate, but 'drift traps' and 'balanced per row by length, level and target' need a deterministic check afterwards. LLMs miscount words, sneak in off-level words and forget the target structure. Turkish free-text prompts will often produce topics, not sentences, which means a second generation step.

The seed leak guard ('everyone else heads down for 5 s') is unreliable in practice. With different sentences per row on one screen, every starter sees every row's seed. Printed slips add a print step that many teachers skip.
fixes: Make Mode A 'Fısıltı Zinciri' the game and build it to full polish. Ship Mode C 'Yeniden Kur' as a Stüdyo/B-level variant inside the same shell, sharing the alignment and reveal engine. Move Mode B 'Kâğıt Telefon' to a printable extra, or merge it into the Draw & Guess/Draw or Act game if the suite has one.

Redesign reveal input as fast judging, not transcription. For each row, show the original as big chips. The teacher taps a chip to cycle kept -> changed -> lost, and for 'changed' picks from 2-3 engine-predicted drift chips (minimal-pair partner, number twin 13/30, a similar name) or a quick 'other' toggle. Keep the target to 5 s per row. Offer an optional phone Kumanda where a row captain types what arrived, with the TV as fallback.

Put the seeds on the Kumanda by default, then printable slips, and make the projected peek the last option. On the peek screen show one row's seed at a time: 'Row 3 starter, look now' for 4 s, with the other rows' starters turned away. Always generate printable numbered slips as a one-click PDF.
